en: Table of Contents for the *Jingtu zhigui ji* (Collection on the Pointing to the Destination of the Pure Land),
Volume One:
Section One, Original Teachings (*Yuanjiaomen*).
The teaching arises dependent upon conditions: the causal ground of Amitābha, the three sages of his causal stage,
the excellence of the Pure Land, the protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas, the instructions of Mañjuśrī, the affinity with the Buddha,
the two gates of subduing and gathering, and their manifestation through the mind alone.
Chapter Two: The Fourfold Benefits; The Eighteen Sages Who Formed the Society on Mount Lu;
The Founding Ancestors of the Lotus Society; The Successive Generations Who Upheld the Tradition;
and the Essential Teachings.

Taking the contemplation of the mind as the primary principle, one contemplates the general and specific aspects of Buddha-remembrance, the four lands and their purity or defilement, the superiority or inferiority of the three bodies,
the nine grades of the three classes of practitioners, and the six stages of realization that clarify the Buddha’s land of tranquil light (*jigō*) as being endowed with marks,
supreme, wondrous, and skillful means; for there is no phenomenon outside of the mind.
Non-arising yet arising, arising is itself non-arising;
the Pure Land is mind-only, like the moon appearing when the water is clear or as polishing a mirror.
Within the ten kinds of non-obstruction, raising one includes the whole.
The third section, the Gateway of Dharma Characteristics,
distinguishes between the two types of goodness— difficult and easy, concentrated and dispersed— within the Path,
and clarifies the suffering and bliss of the two lands in the Western Quarter: the ten difficulties of *Sahā* and the ten ease of the Pure Land.
All belong to the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), emerging through both the horizontal and vertical paths;

they encompass the dual cultivation of Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, the relative laxity or urgency of the vehicle and precepts, the authenticity or falsity of demons and Buddhas, and the superiority or inferiority of Tuṣita.
Yongming’s critical discernment reveals that when the Dharma is free from the four attachments, its principle accords with contemplation.
The Fourth Gate: The Contemplative Wisdom that Guides Practice, Discovers Karmic Manifestations,
and Distinguishes the Quantity of Roots of Goodness through the Six Identities.
The single mind and threefold contemplation; the sixteen subtle contemplations; the earnest contemplation of the setting sun;
the contemplation of the Buddha’s honored special marks and signs based on the mind; the earnest contemplation of the white tuft of hair;
the contemplation of the coarse as manifesting the subtle; and the five gates of skillful means for universal contemplation while seated in meditation.
The Fifth Dharma-Gate of the Practice of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi for Abandoning Discursive Thought through the Four Teachings:
Reciting the Holy Names, the Fourfold Vows and Practices, Prostrating to the Buddhas, and Repentance.
The Ritual for the Morning Ten Recitations, Vowing and Directing Merit Toward Rebirth, and the Mantra of the Path of Practice;
Cultivating Realization According to a Fixed Schedule; the Two Practices of Joy and Aversion;
the Three Superior Minds; Daily Binding of the Mind to the Object; and Entering Contemplation at the Time of Sleep.
At the time of death, one should maintain right mindfulness through three types of pure karma:
filially supporting one's parents, cultivating the ten wholesome deeds, and being fully endowed with the various precepts;
furthermore, one should resolve for Bodhicitta, read and recite Mahayana sutras, draw near to virtuous friends, and listen to the True Dharma.
The Sixth Section: The Gate of Verification, from the Lower Scroll of *Ten Kinds of Faith: One Mind Without Distraction*.
The Bodhisattva’s Rebirth; Nāgārjuna’s Rebirth; Three Visions of Sacred Phenomena at the Sites of Master Huiyuan;
the Final Exhortation of the Wise One (Zhiyi); the Meritorious Deeds of Shandao; Remin’s Vision of the Buddha;
the Manifestation of the Buddha’s Radiant Sound and Light; and Practicing the Path on a Remote Peak.
The Underworld Authorities venerate the Lotus Society of the West Lake;
Imperial Calligraphy for the Seven-Jeweled Lotus Boat of the Lotus Society; Vowing to Attain the Golden Terrace;
Burning and Destroying the Immortal Scriptures; Solemn Reverence to Extinguish Transgressions; The Valiant and Talented Enter the Underworld.
Secret Cultivation of Pure Deeds; Seeing the Buddha at the Hour of Death; Preaching the Dharma at the Hour of Death;
Offering Money for the Painting of Buddhas; Uninterrupted Mindfulness; The Ferryman’s Proof of the Western Land;
Paintings of Seven-Jeweled Buddhas to Awaken the Deluded; Self-Transformation through Standing Meditation in Longshu.
Chapter Seven: The Gate of Resolving Doubts Concerning the Rebirth of Empress Gudu, Female Beings, Evil Beings, and Spirit-Birds.
This Dharma is difficult to believe; the Pure Land is not provisional. To clarify the five delusions, it is shown that the Buddha’s words are not false.
One must have correct faith in cause and effect. Yet, one's own hindrances and obscurations render the body and mind hollow and deceitful.
Lust and killing follow one another as causes, manifesting as the karmic signs at the moment of death.
Not seeking further advancement; the assembly of virtuous people; awakening to former errors;
the ten kinds of obstacles and difficulties; the city of doubt; falling back; rebirth through the ten recitations;
the non-arising of even small roots of goodness; the non-arising of the two vehicles; and the clarification of the sacred name.
The twelve images of the Tathāgatas are the true body; in the fasting hall, the establishment of images represents the dual cultivation of the sudden and gradual approaches.
Using principle to subdue phenomena, one abandons the four kinds of emotional attachments.
To speak of emptiness while losing its gains, or to contravene the scriptures and deviate from the sages, is to fail in one’s final years.
To lose the great for the sake of the small is the first of the ten failures; by not cultivating these [failures], one will forever be free from demonic interference.
Through the three powers of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, one is like a lion’s sinew string or a stone boat that does not sink;
with a single thought, one is reborn, like an image appearing in a mirror, drawn forth by the strength of one's vows.
Chapter Eight: Seeking the Buddha’s Protection to Repudiate Error;
Regarding the Deviation from the Fundamental Tenet and Loss of the Essential Meaning through the Erroneous Attachment to Partial Emptiness, wherein Doubt is Profound and Obstructions are Heavy.
They preach deceptive and false doctrines, claiming to have attained what they have not;

they propagate heterodox theories on embryonic respiration and perverse "silent illumination" meditation; they possess secret formulas for immortality and utterly deny cause and effect, willingly plunging themselves into the mire of suffering.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* (Broad Gate), the ninth;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus) concerning the bestowal of predictions; the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Flower Ornament); the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Perfection of Wisdom) as the ultimate culmination; the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* (Mindfulness of the Buddha);

the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (King of Jewels); the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (Contemplation of the Buddha); the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Heap of Jewels) regarding the ten mental states; and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Heroic Progression) concerning the rising and sinking of thoughts.

Chapter Ten: Encouraging Practice through the Composition of the *Awakening of Faith*, the Return to the Attribution of its Authorship to Vasubandhu, the Commentary on the Treatise, the Resolution of the Ten Doubts,
the Installation of Images at the Time of Death, the Cremation, and the Ten Recitations, as well as Ancient and Modern Writings.
Ciyun exhorted the cultivation of the wondrous contemplation on the weighing of merits,
whose function is profound and ensures one never regresses; by reciting the Buddha's name aloud and prostrating to the Buddha,
one obtains blessings in the present life, and as a monk, through reciting the Buddha's name, one attains nobility and wealth while studying the Way.
Various virtues support one another; one should encourage the cultivation of beneficial causes and reflect upon how negligence leads to failure.
One must contemplate what lies beyond this life and prepare for unforeseen circumstances; the merit lies in mastery.
These are the ten kinds of benefits.
*Jingtu zhiguī jí* (A Collection on Pointing to the Goal of the Pure Land) Table of Contents for Volume One of the *Jingtu zhiguī jí*,
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dayou of Beichen Monastery in Wujun.
The Original Teaching, Part One:

The Great Sage of the Western Quarter appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition, desiring to enable sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Because their capacities were divided into sharp and dull, [he taught] for over forty years... three... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)

Throughout more than a hundred assemblies, he expounded the teachings according to the capacities of beings. Although these differed as Great or Small, Partial or Perfect, they were all skillful means for the sake of the Dharma of the One Vehicle.
When the truth was revealed at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, they all returned to the single reality, and his original intent was thus fulfilled.
It is the same for all Buddhas of the three periods who appear in the world to deliver sentient beings; yet, if one seeks that which is most simple and easy, so that even a beginner...

For an ordinary person of mind who seeks sudden awakening to the Supreme Vehicle and swift ascent to the stage of non-retrogression, there is nothing more direct or essential than the gateway of the Pure Land Dharma-door.
To discuss this at length: the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is primordially manifest; it does not depend on external instruction.
Unsurpassed Bodhi is inherently possessed; it is not attained through cultivation. Nevertheless, the depths of delusion are profound and heavy.
Sinking into eternal kalpas, if one does not encounter the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, virtuous friends,
and spiritual mentors who provide instruction through skillful means, by what means could one understand birth and death and enter the Buddha’s wisdom?
It was from the time the Bhikṣu Dharmākara encountered the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and made the forty-eight vows that this Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha first began.
Its origins lie prior to the *rajas-bindu* kalpas; thus, Amitābha is now manifest in Qingtai, and Kāśyapa proclaimed it in Zhugan.

Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have extolled it with broad tongues throughout the lands of the ten directions. It serves as the primary cause for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods.
The transmission of this teaching has come down from of old. As for Yuan [Hui] of the Eastern Jin...
The Duke formed a society at Mount Lu specifically to propagate the bequeathed teachings of the Buddhas of the past. Thus it is said:
"Although the various samādhis are numerous in name, those of high merit that are easy to advance in take mindfulness of the Buddha as primary.

One thereby knows that when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas practiced on the causal ground, they all cultivated this very dharma; and when they delivered sentient beings upon reaching the stage of fruition, they all preached this very dharma. Now, if one wishes to...
For those who have resolved the great matter of birth and death and roam the ocean of the Buddhas' nature—how could they not follow this path?
The Preface to the Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai states: "Now, as for the Land of Bliss and..."
The realm of suffering is like gold and jewels compared to mud and sand; the womb-hells are like the longing for a magnificent pond; and thorny forests are comparable to the jade tree.

This is truly because the mind distinguishes between defilement and purity, thereby perceiving the rise and fall of the two lands; because conduct opens the way to good and evil, one beholds the coarseness and subtlety of the two directions.

It is like how a form being upright results in a straight shadow, and a source being turbid results in murky flow. Thus, we know that if one desires to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, [one must cultivate purity].
On this soil, one must necessarily cultivate the sixteen sublime contemplations and aspire to behold the World-Honored Amitābha; one must practice the three types of pure karma.
Yet, transformation proceeds gradually through events, and the teaching arises in reliance upon conditions. Thus, when King Ajātaśatru committed patricide, Vaidehī made her piteous plea;

the Great Sage bestowed his compassion and expounded the Dharma according to the occasion. He radiated the luster of his jade-like countenance and manifested auspicious signs from his precious terraces. Although [the teachings] are vast...
He reveals the precious realm and takes refuge in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), so that those with affinity in the later age may follow this sublime contemplation.
The setting sun hanging like a drum serves as a sign for the method of directing one's thoughts; the great waters freezing into ice truly represent the ground of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
The wind whistling through jeweled leaves resonates together with celestial music, and the ripples on the golden lotuses harmonize their echoes with the sutras. Contemplate the *uṣṇīṣa*.

While attending upon him, he contemplated the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-tuft between the brows) and beheld the Tathāgata; when the Buddha closed his eyes and passed away, he leaped high onto the precious dais.
As the inscription was completed and the seal broken, he was born through transformation seated upon a golden lotus. Transcending the three grades of rebirth, he crossed over horizontally;
surpassing the five sufferings, he galloped forth eternally. This may truly be called the subtle practice, the wondrous contemplation, and the essential art of the ultimate Way.
The *Sūtra on the Immeasurable Life of Amitābha’s Ground* states: "In the distant past, eons ago, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Dīpaṃkara (Dīpaṅkara).
Next was named Prabhāsa (Prabhāraśmi), and next was named Nāgarāja (Nāgasvara). Following this sequence, up to the fifty-third Buddha, who was named Lokendra (Lokendrajaya)."

O King, at that time there was a king who, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, felt great joy in his heart. He abandoned his kingdom to leave the household life and became known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.

For him, the Buddha extensively described two hundred and ten billion Buddha-fields—the various differences in their adornments, the goodness or evil of the lands, and the coarseness or subtlety of the realms of humans and devas.
Having heard this, Dharmākara beheld them all and made a great vow, saying: "If..."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any beings in my land who are hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment" (and so forth).
After the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these forty-eight vows, the great earth shook, and the heavens rained down jewels and other treasures.
With single-minded devotion, he adorned Buddha-lands and established sentient beings in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

He has now attained Buddhahood and currently resides in the Western World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), which is adorned with myriad jewels and is more pure and sublime than all worlds in the ten directions.

There is no Mount Sumeru, sun, moon, or great ocean; it is neither cold nor hot, but is always temperate and harmonious—all of which is accomplished through the great vows of the Tathāgata in the past.

The *Sambhadrā-bodhisattva-caryā-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Flower of Compassion from the Ground of the Three Sages) states: In the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a wheel-turning king named Araṇemin who ruled over the four continents.
This king had a great minister named Ratnasāgara, who was of the brahmin caste and begot a son endowed with the marks and signs of excellence.
Having fulfilled [the requirements], he left the household life and attained Buddhahood, becoming known as the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha.

He preached the Dharma for the king, who, together with his thousand sons, invited the Buddha to receive offerings for a full two hundred and fifty years. When the Buddha entered samādhi, he emitted a great radiance that manifested the worlds of the ten directions, whether pure or defiled.
Emerging from concentration, the Buddha was addressed by the king: "For what reason do some worlds appear pure?"
"It is impure. The Buddha said, "By the power of their vows, bodhisattvas take up pure lands that are free from the five turbidities.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, by the power of their vows, take up impure lands. The King said, "I now make this vow: when I attain Buddhahood..."
Within that land, there are no three evil realms; all things are of a true golden color and adorned with various ornaments. The Buddha said to the King:
"In the western direction, after one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this world shall change its name to Sukhāvatī.
You shall become a Buddha, titled Amitāyus Tathāgata. At that time, the Buddha again addressed the eldest prince, Animiṣa.
"I shall now designate you as Avalokiteśvara. After the parinirvāṇa of Amitāyus Buddha, you shall attain the path of Buddhahood and be named the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain King.
Furthermore, he addressed the second daughter, Princess Māyā: 'Next, you shall become a Buddha and be named the Tathāgata Virtue Abiding Jewel King.
By the power of your vows, you shall take up a pure land,' and he further designated her name."
"You have attained the Great Power (Mahāsthāmaprāpta).
Regarding the excellence of the Pure Land, Liu Zhiyou’s *Record of the Pure Land Cloister* states: 'Tens of thousands of li to the west of the Central Plains lies a land called India.'"
This is the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni manifested himself. That Buddha said:

"To the west, beyond a hundred thousand billion buddha-fields, there is a world called Sukhāvatī. The Buddha there is named Amitāyus Tathāgata. In that land, there are no three poisons or eight difficulties;
it is adorned with various jewels. Its inhabitants are free from the ten entanglements and nine afflictions, and they take the multitude of sages as their friends."
If there are those who, with a sincere heart and great vow, take refuge in this land, provided their power of mindfulness is sufficient, they shall be reborn in that realm.
Thereafter, having transcended the three realms, they shall never regress from the path to Buddhahood;
these words are not deceptive.
Zhang Lun’s Imperial Calligraphy on the Record of the Lotus Society states:

"I, your servant, have often read the scriptures of India and learned of that which is called the World of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha, whose radiance is immeasurable and whose lifespan is immeasurable. When he first ascended the throne and assumed his station..."
He cast them aside and did not dwell in them; he awakened alone in transcendence, realizing the mind and attaining sainthood. By the power of his great vows, he universally delivers all beings.
His land is entirely adorned with various jewels, exquisitely and perfectly beautiful. The ground is made of pure gold, free from the dangers of mountains, rivers, hills, and valleys.
Its climate is perpetually spring-like, without the fluctuations of yin and yang, cold or heat. There is no hunger, cold, old age, sickness, or birth.

Regarding the suffering of death, there is no turbidity of the five realms of rebirth dwelling together. By means of these various supernatural powers and skillful means, he manifests rare and wondrous events to skillfully guide sentient beings.
Sentient beings, filled with joy, give rise to faith; within their daily lives, they are able to produce even a single thought of awakening.
By recollecting the name of that Buddha, this single thought-moment becomes pure and fully matured, merging with True Suchness (tathatā) and becoming one with the Dharma-nature (dharmatā).
When the illusory body perishes, this nature does not cease; in a single kṣaṇa, the Buddha-land appears before one, like taking back a deposited object by presenting its left-hand tally.
The *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Protection and Recollection of Amitābha* states:
"Just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha, so too in the east is there Akṣobhya Buddha; likewise in the south, west, north, above, and below."

At that time, there were Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in every direction. Each, within his own land, extended his broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and spoke these words of truth:
"All you sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas. If there are good men or good women..."

Those people who hear this sutra and accept and uphold it, as well as those who hear the names of the various Buddhas—all such persons shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and all shall attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The title of this scripture, *The Sutra on the Inconceivable Merit of Praise and the Protection and Remembrance by All Buddhas*, consists of sixteen characters in total; this is the original text.

Regarding the title of the sutra, Master Kumārajīva omitted certain details and placed it after the section on the six directions, using the name of the Buddha as the title because the name of Amitābha is what all people delight to hear.
When the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty retranslated it, he titled it the *Sūtra on the Buddhas of the Ten Directions Praising and Upholding the Pure Land*;
"upholding" (*shèshòu*) refers to protective mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, this version includes the words of the Buddhas of the ten directions, stating that upon hearing this sūtra...
One who practices according to these teachings will certainly be sustained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who reside in the ten directions throughout ten *gaṅgā*-sands of world-systems;
they shall all be born in the Land of Utmost Bliss of the Buddha Amitāyus.

Regarding the *Mañjuśrī-śikṣā* (The Instructions of Mañjuśrī) from the Dali period of the Tang dynasty: The Dharma Master Fazhao, while on pilgrimage to Mount Wutai, was granted a vision by Mañjuśrī of the Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery.
Fazhao entered the lecture hall and saw Mañjuśrī seated to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand bodhisattvas.

As he was preaching the Dharma, Zhao paid his respects and inquired: "The sentient beings of the final age possess shallow and inferior wisdom; there is no way for their Buddha-nature and the ground of the mind to manifest.
I do not know what Dharma gate they should cultivate that would be most essential. Mañjuśrī said: "Regarding what you have asked..."

"Now is precisely the right time. Among all gates of practice, none is equal to the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Because I recollected the Buddha in the past, I attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and illumination.
Zhao then asked: "How should one recollect? Mañjuśrī replied: "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha, whose power of vows is inconceivable.
You should fix your mindfulness upon him without allowing it to be interrupted; at the end of your life, you will certainly [attain rebirth]."

He was certain to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Having finished speaking, Zhao [the Emperor] rubbed his head in blessing. Upon hearing this, Zhao leaped for joy and propagated the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation extensively wherever he went.
Emperor Dezong issued an imperial decree to welcome him into the palace, where he taught the palace ladies to recite the Buddha’s name. Thus, the Way of the Dharma flourished greatly.
The Layman Xiangshan, who shared a karmic affinity with the Buddha, said: "Observe closely all the sentient beings within this Sahā world, as numerous as its motes of dust.

Among them, there are none—whether wise or foolish, noble or humble, young or old—who, when they resolve to take refuge in the Buddha, do not first raise their hands in palms-joined salutation toward the West."
When those beset by fear, calamity, or suffering open their mouths and utter a sound, they invariably first call upon Amitābha Buddha.

Furthermore, whether it be images cast in metal or molded from clay, carvings in stone, woven patterns, or even children playing by stamping water or piling sand—all such acts take Amitābha Buddha as their primary object.
One does not know how this comes to be, yet it is so. Viewed from this perspective, he is indeed that [Tathāgata].
It is evident that this being has made a great vow regarding these sentient beings, and that these sentient beings possess a profound karmic affinity for that land.
Otherwise, since there have been many Buddhas throughout the three directions and four quarters across the past, present, and future, why would it be only this one who acts in such a manner?
The Inscription for the Amitābha Stūpa at Mount Nanyue by Chan Master Mugwan Zhong. Its brief account states: "How magnificent is the Way of the Buddha of Enlightenment!
It possesses two gates: subduing and gathering. To harmonize capacities and succor all beings, Śākyamuni manifested an impure land to subdue them. [The text continues: "To cause..."
When the thought of wearying aversion toward suffering arises, Amitābha manifests the Pure Land to gather [beings] therein, causing them to develop a resolute aspiration for joyful delight.
As for the defiled land, it is characterized by the unevenness of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, and the afflictions of warfare, famine, and pestilence.

As for the Pure Land, it is adorned with jeweled ponds and golden ground, and possesses the peace and happiness of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna. Thus, Tiantai said: "It truly depends on the mind."
By distinguishing between defilement and purity, one perceives the rise and fall of the two lands; by practicing good and evil, one beholds the coarseness and subtlety of the two directions.
From this it may be known that purity and impurity reside here, and not there.

One who embodies right contemplation realizes that the sufferings of war and the like in those realms are also a single aspect of the transformative power of adversity. Yet, while treading upon such pain and evil, ordinary beings—
Deluded by passion, they still take suffering for pleasure; their inversion is extreme, and it is truly lamentable. Someone may ask:
"To rejoice in purity and loathe impurity is to not yet have forgotten grasping and rejecting. How could the Sage transform people through the way of dualistic views? I reply: Does the Sūtra not say:
"Though one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land to teach and transform others"?
All sentient beings are indeed ablaze with both delight and aversion, yet they do not perceive the characteristics of such delight and aversion; this is what constitutes attainment.
Regarding the manifestation of the mind alone, the Layman Wugong said:
"The Land of Ultimate Bliss is ten thousand billion lands away from here, yet for an ordinary person at the moment of death, it is reached in an instant."
As for "attaining," it is simply because one's own mind is fundamentally wondrous. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"You still do not understand that all these floating dust-like, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise right where they are and perish right where they are. Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is false birth;

through the separation of causes and conditions, what is falsely called 'extinction' occurs. Yet you fail to realize that this arising and ceasing, coming and going, is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, which is eternal."
Abiding in wondrous clarity, within the true and eternal nature, one seeks for coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death, yet finds nothing at all.

Inferring from this, at the moment of death, as defiled conditions depart, the Sahā world perishes as an illusion right where it stands; as pure conditions converge, the Land of Ultimate Bliss arises as an illusion right where it stands.
This ceasing here and arising there occurs with no interval between them, not even enough to admit a hair—how could it last for even a single moment?
How can one discuss this? It is rather seeing that throughout the entire day one engages in taking and rejecting, yet never truly takes or rejects (from the *Xinxinlu*).
Regarding the four kinds of benefit, Chan Master Ciyun said: "The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One saves all sentient beings by means of four methods. The first is to manifest..."
First, he manifests the primary and secondary marks, causing those who observe them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.

Second, he manifests the teaching of the Dharma, causing those who hear it to attain awakening and enter the Path. Third, he manifests transformative deeds, causing those who see or hear them to obtain the benefits of all dharmas.
Fourth, his name is disseminated throughout the ten directions, causing those who hear it to uphold and keep it in mind, whereby their transgressions are extinguished and goodness arises. And...
One attains liberation and deliverance.
Master Lingzhi Zhao of Lushan Jieshe said:
"The teachings and contemplations of Amitābha are recorded in the Great Canon; they are certainly not few. However, the Buddha..."
The transformation spread eastward. For several hundred years, almost no one in the world was aware of it. Dharma Master Huiyuan resided at Donglin on Mount Lu;

with his singular spiritual genius, he became a pioneer for the world. He excavated a pond and planted lotuses, established a hall, and made a vow to exclusively cultivate the Pure Land practice, naming it the White Lotus Society (*Bailian She*).
Renowned monks and great scholars of the time arrived there spontaneously without prior invitation. Huidi... [text continues]
Huiyuan was a preeminent talent of the Śākya school. Liao Yimin and Lei Cizong were both eminent figures among literary scholars;
they all held him in high esteem, sought his instruction, and joined his society. Consequently, when later generations discuss the Pure Land, they invariably cite Donglin as its origin.
The Eighteen Great Virtuous Elders:
Master Huìyuǎn of Dōnglín (Distinguished Awakening), Master Huìyǒng of Xīlín (Awakened Quiescence),
the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas from Kaśmīra (translated as "Awakened Clarity"), and the Śramaṇa Buddhabhadra from India.
Dharmakṣema (translated here as Juexian), Donglin Pujie Dashi Daosheng,
Yanmen Fashi Huichi, Fashi Sengrui, Tanchang, Tanshun, Tanshen, Daobing, Daojing,
Liu Yimin Zhongsu of Pengcheng, and Lei Cizhong Lun of Yuzhang.
Zhou Xuzhi Daozu of Yanmen; Zhang Ye Laimin of Nanyang; Zhang Quan Xiushuo of Nanyang;
and Zong Bing Shaowen of Nanyang—these were the patriarchs established for the Lotus Society.

Master Shizhi Xiao said: "Since the establishment of the Lotus Society took Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu as its progenitor, there have been no generations passing without those who have continued this path.
All of them have looked up to embody the Buddha’s compassion and grandly opened the gates of salvation.

Though separated by different eras, they shared the same spirit; all were excellent guides for the multitude. What is recorded in the biographies is truly impossible to conceal; thus, throughout the successive dynasties..."
Those who recorded these accounts have preserved them as a succession of patriarchs:
first, Dharma Master Guangming of Chang’an, whose name was Shandao; second, the Upoṣadha Master of Mount Nanyue, whose name was Chengyuan;
third, the National Teacher of Yunfeng Wuhui, whose name was Fazhao; fourth, Dharma Master Taiyan of Xinding, whose name was...
1. Shaokang; 2. Chan Master Yongming Zhijue, whose name was Yanshou; 3. Dharma Master Zhaoying Yuanjing, whose name was Xingchang;
4. Chan Master Changlu Cijue, whose name was Zongze.
Throughout successive dynasties, this has been held in high esteem;
Zen Master Zhendie said: "Buddha to Buddha, the hand is passed; from patriarch to patriarch, it is transmitted. There is only this one matter, and no other.
Although the Elder Śākyamuni dwelt in the world for seventy-nine years and preached the Dharma in over three hundred assemblies, he spoke of nothing but the Pure Land."

The teachings were repeated with such earnestness and frequency that they never ceased. Could this not be considered the swift path for transcending the mundane world and entering the state of sagehood?
The eighteen great worthies and one hundred and twenty-three individuals of Mount Lu all left behind auspicious responses, which are fully recorded in the historical annals.
The writings on Pure Land biographies and the texts on pure practice composed by the masters of successive generations are none other than the legacy of the patriarchs and sages.
In his final testament, whether profound or shallow, skillful or clumsy, every single word and phrase returns to the good.

When the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, he described the practice of his own mind, saying: "The three contemplations within a single mind directly reveal the one mind.
In its very place, it is emptiness; in its entire substance, it is the provisional. It is both empty and existent, yet neither empty nor existent; it cannot be grasped or settled upon. It is not...

It cannot be grasped through deliberation; where the path of the mind is severed, that very state is named Buddhahood. Thus, as for the teaching of the Pure Land, it reached its full perfection at Tiantai.
It is so brilliantly clear, like the sun and moon being raised high to illuminate the vast void.
Section Two: The Gate of the Fundamental Purpose.
Some may find it difficult for sentient beings to attain birth in the Pure Land through the practice of *nienfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name).

Yet, if even the most ignorant men and women can uphold the sacred name with sincere faith and without doubt, there are none who will not attain birth. Others may consider this practice easy; however, this is not so unless one has planted roots of merit in past lives.
Those who possess profound depth, who penetrate the subtle essence, and who do not stagnate in partial or inferior views cannot fathom their inner sanctum.

The *Mahāyāna-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that those who cultivate goodness with a doubting mind fail to comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom and are born in a womb-palace for five hundred years, where they do not behold the Triple Gem;
yet the cause for rebirth in the highest grade truly lies in understanding the primary truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, one knows that clarity regarding the fundamental principle is essential.
This is the precursor to the myriad practices. How could those who cultivate the karma of purity afford to be lax?

This sutra takes mental visualization as its primary principle; it takes the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence. As for what is called "the Buddha’s teaching on the contemplation of Amitāyus Buddha":

The Buddha is the supreme object of contemplation. By mentioning his primary retribution-body (*vipāka-phala*), his secondary environmental fruits (*niśraya-phala*) are included; by describing the Master of Transformation, his retinue is encompassed.
Although there are sixteen modes of contemplation, speaking of the Buddha alone suffices to complete them. The Venerable Ziming of Siming, in his *Miaozongchao*, comments:

"The Sūtra takes 'contemplating the Buddha' as its title, while this Commentary now takes 'mental contemplation' as its core principle. These two are not different; only when they are thus unified is it correct."

Now, upon observation, it is clear that the perfect understanding (*yuan-jie*) is fundamentally different from that of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). The Small Vehicle is ignorant of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), viewing the Buddha as existing externally;
therefore, they hold that the essence of the mind and the Buddha are distinct. Practitioners of the Mahāyāna know that their own single mind possesses the nature of all Buddhas.

By relying on objects to cultivate contemplation, the marks of the Buddha then manifest. Now, observing Amitābha’s environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu* and *sambhoga-kāya*) as conditions, one perfumes the nature of the mind which inherently possesses them.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss and its inhabitants arise through the power of perfuming; they are born from what the mind inherently possesses. How could they ever be separate from the nature of the mind?

The entire mind is Buddha, and the entire Buddha is mind. To contemplate the mind all day is to contemplate the Buddha all day. Therefore, both the sutra and its commentary establish this as their fundamental tenet.
Although the terminology differs, their meaning is no different. Furthermore, one must understand this: if one contemplates the Buddha, one must necessarily illumine the mind;

if one contemplates the mind exclusively, it does not necessarily rely upon the Buddha as its object. For example, in the *Ekākṣara-samādhi*, one directly contemplates a single thought-moment without relying on another Buddha as the focal object.
However, in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and in this method of contemplation, one begins by contemplating the reliance [upon the Buddha] in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

It is correct. One contemplates that the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are not separate from the nature of the mind; therefore, it is called "contemplation of the mind. It must be understood that this contemplation does not exclusively contemplate the mind.
If one were to divide it into internal and external, this belongs to external contemplation, because it relies upon those environments and inhabitants as the object of observation.

For this reason, the title of the sutra is called "Contemplating the Buddha" (*guanfo*). As for what is difficult or easy, one must now follow what is easy. The *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The Buddha-dharma is too..."

[The object of] height is vast; sentient beings are too numerous. For a beginner, this is difficult. Since the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in their threefold nature, contemplating the mind is easy.

This present method of contemplation does not merely contemplate the Buddha, but rather takes the mind as its basis for observation. By taking the lower to reveal the high, although one practices the contemplation of the Buddha, it is not called difficult.
Thus we know that the central tenet of this sutra is the contemplation of the mind, with the aim of seeing the Buddha; therefore, both [aspects] are attained.

The explanation of this meaning does not follow divergent paths; furthermore, one should understand that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu* constitutes my single thought-moment, and likewise, its entire substance constitutes sentient beings and Buddhas, the support and the supported, the sense organs and their objects.
From a single mind to a single speck of dust, down to a single atom, there is nothing that is not the entire *dharmadhātu* acting as such. Since each and every phenomenon is entirely...
Because it is the activity of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is sufficient to cite a single instance; this is precisely the entirety of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm.
Since it is the whole of the Dharma-realm, what single thing could there be that does not possess all phenomena? For every single phenomenon possesses all phenomena.
Therefore, our school establishes the principle that "it is only color" or "it is only fragrance," and so forth. If this is so, why do the sutras and treatises frequently [state otherwise]?
Is one mind established as the object of contemplation (*ālambana*) as a universal synthesis of all phenomena?

This is because when contemplating objects such as those of ordinary beings or Buddhas, the entities are separated and distinct, making it difficult to forget the duality of subject and object (*grāhaka-grāhya*). Contemplating the mind-phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), however, is both proximate and essential.

Since it is that which constructs [all things], its full significance is not yet manifest; furthermore, by taking that which contemplates as the very object of illumination, thoughts are easily severed. As the *Miaoxuan* states: "The three non-existences..."

Regarding the distinctions: contemplating the mind is easy; even when contemplating external objects, one must do so by way of the mind. This sutra specifically concerns contemplating the Buddha by way of the mind.
As for the general and specific aspects of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha):
The *Miaozong* states: "Vairocana pervades all places; all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.
This refers to the Buddha of the inherent virtue of sentient beings—neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect—which is precisely the essence of the perfect and eternal Great Enlightenment.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: 'That which is called the meaning of enlightenment refers to the essence of mind being free from thought. Being free from thought...'"

As for its characteristics: it is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading all things without exception. The single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharmakāya.

Based upon this Dharmakāya, it is termed "original enlightenment" (prakṛti-awakening). Therefore, one should know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is the inherent nature and virtue (prakṛti-guṇa) possessed by us ordinary beings from the very beginning.
Thus, among all the practices taught in the various scriptures, there are none that do not serve to reveal this.
Since the essence of awakening is one, these four samādhis are collectively termed "Buddha-remembrance" (nienfo). However, they differ in their respective meditative methods as gateways:

for instance, the *Ekavyūha-samādhi* directly contemplates the three paths to manifest the Buddha of the original nature; the *Vaipulya-samādhi* additionally involves the recitation of mantras; the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-samādhi* additionally involves the recitation of sutras;

the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi* additionally involves counting the breaths; and the *Bodhyanga-samādhi* proceeds through the three natures. These various samādhis proceed through their respective practices.

Although they differ, their mindfulness of the Buddha is the same, for both serve to reveal the essence of Great Enlightenment. While both involve mindfulness of the Buddha, this is a general approach that reveals the essence of all Buddhas.

However, this contemplative gate and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi rely upon the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī, employing subtle and wondrous observation specifically directed toward Amitābha to reveal the true essence of the Buddha. Although they rely upon those objects, one must...

Know that the environment and its inhabitants abide together within a single mind. The nature of the mind is all-pervasive; there is no phenomenon it does not create, and no phenomenon it does not possess.
If even a hair’s breadth of a phenomenon were to arise outside of the mind, it could not be called the contemplation of the Mahāyāna.

The *Sūtra Commentary on the Contemplation of the Purity and Impurity of the Four Great Elements* states: "This sūtra takes as its fundamental tenet that 'if the mind is pure through contemplation, then the Buddha-land is pure. There are four kinds of pure lands:

namely, the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, the Land of Traceless Transformation with Remaining Karmic Conditions, the Land of True Reward Free from Obstruction, and the Land of Eternal..."

This refers to the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*). Each of these lands possesses both purity and defilement, with varying degrees of severity in the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). There is purity and defilement in the Land of Shared Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), distinguished by the skillfulness or clumsiness of their realization through either gradual or sudden entry.

There is purity and defilement in the Land of Reward for True Reality (*tathatā-vipāka-bhūmi*), distinguished by partial realization or ultimate perfection. And there is purity and defilement in the Land of Tranquil Light, distinguished by the same.
The Sahā world is a mixture of evils; filled with thorns, rubble, and impurities, it is a realm of shared defilement. The Land of Peaceful Nurturing is pure and serene;

its ponds and streams possess the eight virtues, and its trees are arrayed with the seven treasures. It is close to *nirvāṇa*, for all its inhabitants belong to the stage of right determination; ordinary beings and sages dwell together there.

This refers to the Pure Land of the Superior Grade. Regarding "the stage where skillful means remain" (*upāya-avaśeṣa*): one cultivates the path of skillful means and severs the delusions of the four abodes;

hence it is called "skillful means. Because ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been exhausted, it is called "remaining. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Beyond the three realms there exists a Pure Land."
Within it, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born; they receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) rather than being born through the process of segmented birth (*paricchedotpatti*).
Within this [category], there are further distinctions of sharp and dull faculties; thus, one speaks of purity and impurity. As for the "True Reward Unobstructed Land" (*sambhoga-kṣetra anāvaraṇa*):

because one practices the true Dharma and thereby attains a superior retribution, matter and mind do not obstruct one another; hence it is called "unobstructed. It is inhabited exclusively by Bodhisattvas, with no followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

The *Renwang jing* states: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the retribution of fruition. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of "immeasurable clouds of incense terraces," which refers to the pure and wondrous five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of that land.

Within these, one enters either gradually or instantaneously; there is no further discussion of purity or defilement. As for the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa*): [...]* (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.)
Permanence is the Dharmakāya; tranquility is liberation; radiance is prajñā. These three dots are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither conjoined nor separate;
they are called the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa), the dwelling place where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and reside. It is the ultimate true permanence and the most supreme Pure Land.

The ultimate attainment is distinguished merely by the purity or impurity of the upper and lower realms; therefore, the core tenet of this sutra is that through the wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind, one can evoke a pure land.

*Miaozong* (The Wondrous Commentary) states: "The essential point of the Mahāyāna Dharma lies in the mind. It is easy to understand that the mind possesses [all phenomena], whereas it is difficult to comprehend that physical form possesses them.
Thus, whether contemplating oneself or others, all is the cultivation of the contemplation of the mind. Now, in contemplating the pure land, one must seek it within the mind."
Because the mind is capable of possessing all things, and because the mind is capable of creating them; when the mind is defiled, the land is defiled; when the mind is pure, the land is pure.

This is still a general indication and not yet a definitive discourse. The definitive point lies in the single mind: to suddenly cultivate the three contemplations. These contemplations observe the environment and the inhabitants of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Ultimate purity is called the purity of mental contemplation (*citta-vipaśyanā*). This contemplation is able to purify the lands of the four Buddhas.

It is precisely this that constitutes the essential purport of this sutra. Originally, this sutra was for the sake of Vaidehī, who, weary of the defilement of the cohabitation realm (*sahabhū-bhūmi*), sought the purity of the cohabitation realm.

Therefore, we discuss the sublime contemplation (*miao-guan*). One contemplates that [Pure Land] in terms of its environment and its inhabitants. If the three contemplations are perfected, the coarse defilements fall away first. It is not merely a matter of attaining a residual purity; where else could one be reborn?
One must know that the primary purpose is to be born in the "pure land of cohabitation" (*tongju jingtu*); thus, the three contemplations are taught.

This is truly because the subtlety of these contemplations can shatter the three delusions (*san-huo*), and they do not merely induce rebirth in the pure land of cohabitation alone. Rather, according to the depth or shallowness of the delusions severed, [one attains various levels of rebirth].

One naturally attains the three stages, such as "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*), just as one who is ill requires medicine. Originally for the sake of physical well-being, one seeks out an immortal’s formula, compiles it, and ingests it;
not only does the body become well, but the bones also become light. This physical well-being may be likened to being born in the Pure Land of Co-residence (*sahā-vihāra*).
The "light bones" may be used as a metaphor for the response to the three higher lands; though they constitute a single medicine, their efficacy is profound and superior.
Just as a single sublime contemplation can purify the four lands, so too do the three bodies vary in their degree of excellence.

The *Miaozong* states: "That which is called 'Buddha' refers to ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). Since both principle and wisdom have reached their consummation, the two aspects of the beginning and the fundamental are forgotten.
Being without marks and without name, it cannot be explained or demonstrated. For the sake of sentient beings, one accordingly establishes names and marks within the mundane world.

To say that the Buddha fundamentally has no body or lifespan means only that he lacks the three kinds of marks that follow worldly sentiments; it does not mean that the subtle [nature] inherent in his essence is non-existent."

The "wondrous body" and so forth are therefore the true Buddha’s ultimate gateway to all pure and defiled phenomena. If these were entirely non-existent, how would they differ from the ultimate truth expounded by the Hinayana?

Thus, that the ultimate is non-existent while the conventional is existent, or that the ultimate is existent while the conventional is non-existent, both accord with the *siddhānta* (the established tenets).

One must not hold to partiality or dogmatic attachment. It is like a valley responding to an echo: the magnitude follows the sound. It is like a mirror manifesting forms: beauty or ugliness resides in the substance.

Because it relies on the *savisaya-vijnana* (consciousness of objects) and perceives only emptiness, it belongs solely to the impermanent. If, however, one relies on the *karma-vijnana* (consciousness of karma) and perceives non-emptiness, [it is otherwise].

This very impermanence, in its entirety, is permanence. The permanent body is immeasurable and universally responds to the three lands; impermanence is limited and responds only to the land of common residence.
This is because it is only through the partial realization of the faculties of the true recompense that one perceives the body of other-enjoyment in the land of skillful means.

Although those who receive the teachings—whether via the Separate or Perfect Teachings—perceive slight variations in the excellence of the Buddha’s marks they behold, these are not bodies born of birth-and-death; they are all bodies of recompense-Buddhas.

If one dwells in a land of cohabitation where the capacities for all four teachings are present, those who receive the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) teachings are able to perceive the Reward Buddha (Baofo).

Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that [the Buddha] constantly resides on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the preaching of the Dharma continues until the end of the future;
likewise, in various Mahāyāna sūtras, it is taught that within the manifested form (yingxiang), one perceives this Dharma-nature body of sublime distinction (faxing zunte zhi shen).
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states that there are three grades for sentient beings of the ten directions who aspire to be born in that land. Regarding the superior grade:
they renounce their homes and abandon desires to become śramaṇas; they resolve upon bodhicitta and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus.

The Buddha said: "If there are those who cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land, at the time of their death, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them.
They shall immediately follow that Buddha and be born within precious lotuses, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression. As for those of the middle grade:
they give rise to the bodhicitta and vow to be born in that land; they single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha and observe the fast."

[Those who] observe the precepts, erect stupas and images, and provide food for śramaṇas—when such persons approach the end of their lives, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them.
They shall then follow the transformed Buddha to be reborn in that land, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression.

As for those of the lower grade who wish to be born in that land, they should resolve upon bodhicitta; if they hear the profound Dharma and do not give rise to doubt or confusion—even for a single [moment]...
"Mindfulness. One who mindfully contemplates that land will, at the time of death, see that Buddha in a dream and likewise attain rebirth there.
The *Tiantai Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "The nine grades of this sutra are intended to distinguish the superior, middling, and inferior levels of consciousness;

they correspond to the three classes of the Larger [Sukhāvatīvyūha] Sutra. The *Gushan Record of Collation and Correction* states: "The three classes of the Larger Sutra correspond only to the first six grades of the Contemplation Sutra, because those two..."
"This is because those of the three classes who are purely bright and virtuous do not equal the evil persons. Lingzhi said:

"The three classes of the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* all once gave rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment], which may be compared to the 'superior grade' of the *Contemplation Sūtra*. However, the middle and lower grades do not correspond to it;

moreover, their causal practices are entirely different from those of the present [sūtra]. Cao'an’s *Supplement to the Correct Explanation* states: "Tiantai [Zhiyi] harmonized the nine grades of the present sūtra with the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*..."

The three grades [of rebirth] are established based on the equality of their respective stages and positions; they do not concern the characteristics of the causal practices or the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.

Regarding the six levels of identity (*liu ji*), the *Fojiao miaozong* states: "All dharmas are none other than the Buddha; it is because of delusion that they are not known. Therefore, the Perfect and True Teaching (the *Yuanjiao*) does not...
Following deluded sentiments, one might directly claim that everything is the Buddha-dharma, that worldly phenomena are eternal, and that sentient beings are Buddhas.
Those who do not receive the teachings may possess the principle [of this truth], yet they are entirely unaware of it. If they hear these teachings, they will know it through the names;

if they enter the five grades of practice, they will know it through contemplation; those who enter the ten stages of faith will know it in a semblance; and throughout the forty-one stages, they will know it progressively.
This is true knowledge. If one attains the ultimate fruit, one realizes that all phenomena are entirely the Buddha-dharma.

The Dharma-realm has no exterior; it encompasses all things without contradiction. The form and mind, the environment and the inhabitants of both Buddhas and sentient beings, are of one and the same enlightened essence.

This body is profoundly still and tranquil, like a mirror devoid of sentience; when forms confront it, images arise, with not even a hair’s breadth of separation between the mountains and the finest details.

The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states that although the scriptures and treatises speak of the "formless" nature of the Land of Quiescent Light (*jiguang*), this refers to the fact that all defiled and obstructive marks have been exhausted;

it does not mean that there is nothing at all, like the vast empty sky. This is because when the three delusions are ultimately purified, then both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, [are perfected].

This is ultimately and clearly manifest. Thus, the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
The *Renwang jing* refers to these as the five aggregates of *dharmatā*. This is also the "permanence of worldly phenomena" (*lokadhātu-nityatā*) taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

In the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way; this is what is called the ultimate Land of Bliss, the ultimate gold and jewels, the ultimate lotus ponds, and the ultimate crystal trees.
Furthermore, this is established by exhausting the abandonment of defilement and reaching the ultimate source of purity.

Therefore, realms such as the domain of suffering are categorized as belonging to the three obstacles, while the Land of Bliss is composed of gold and jewels as its *sukhāvatī* (Land of Peaceful Light).

However, if one speaks in terms of the equality of the pure and the defiled, then even the ultimate realm of suffering, with its sands and mud, constitutes the *sukhāvatī*. Regarding these two explanations:
However, in accordance with the *siddhānta*, there is nothing that is not perfectly consummate. Question: The Buddha’s unsurpassed recompense is the phenomenon that is identical to principle;
thus, it may be discussed in terms of gold and so forth. Ultimate quiescent radiance is the principle that is identical to phenomena; how could there be gold and such things therein?

If these were equally present, then since phenomena and principle would be conflated, how could one distinguish between the two lands? Answer: The Buddha’s unsurpassed recompense is the ultimate beginning.

Awakening. Ultimate primordial awakening (*mūla-awakening*) is the supreme quiescent light. Since the initial and the fundamental have reached their ultimate limit, how could they be divided into two distinct entities?

One should know that although the two lands are distinguished as the phenomenal (*śa*) and the principle (*li*), they are in reality neither existent nor non-existent. How could the truly good and wondrous existence not be the principle?

How could the principle of the secret treasury be the same as the "small emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) of the Hinayana? Therefore, these two names—phenomenal and principle—refer to a single essence. Because it is the restoration to the original state, it is called [the Name].

This is the unsurpassed act of retribution. Because it is the restoration to the fundamental source, it is termed the principle of the Supreme Dharma-realm (Sajō-kōmyō). Thus, the *Myōraku-ki* states:

"The four virtues attained through cultivation and the four virtues inherent in the original nature are equal in their two meanings; only then do they constitute the characteristics of the body and land of Vairocana.

Furthermore, the *Jōmyō-sho* explicitly takes the Dharma-realm as the Buddha’s *niṣyanda-phala* (dependent retribution). Therefore, one should know that it is a fixed error to insist that the land of retribution possesses gold and jewels.

...and so forth. That [the Pure Land] is definitively non-existent in the Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light (Jigō) is merely a confusion regarding the name; it shows a complete lack of understanding of the meaning.

The Venerable Master of the Four Clarities (Shimmyō Sonja) said: "The realm of Ultimate Bliss (Gokuraku) is, in fact, the manifestation of provisional means by the Buddha of Enlightenment. Since both the sutras and the treatises state this...
Taking the teaching of the Pure Land as a supreme skillful means, we know through verification that this is the Tathāgata’s skillful exercise of expedient power (*upāya*).

However, the name "expedient" is not restricted [to the provisional]; it also applies to the ultimate reality. One must distinguish between them clearly before one can understand what to reject and what to adopt. Expedient means external to the essence must be shattered;
expedient means internal to the essence must be cultivated. A principle divorced from phenomena is coarse; the reality that is identical with the expedient is truly wondrous.
Therefore, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) contains no teaching of other Buddhas, whereas the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) speaks of oceans of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*).
This is because the nature of mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm without exception; since the principle is ultimate, the phenomena are vast. Because the flowers are large, the ponds must be deep.

These lands appear like the jewels of Indra, manifesting in infinite layers, thereby revealing the principle of the *jiguo* (light of tranquility). Bodies are like celestial delicacies, each being a response to karmic retribution.
They are not the same; they rather manifest the nature of Vairocana. How could the Land of Ultimate Bliss not be included within the Mind-Only?

Therefore, within the Tathāgatagarbha, the seven great elements are fully present, manifesting according to conditions and known according to capacity; thus, it can manifest both the hells and the celestial palaces.
Is it not the case that one creates a defiled land or a pure land? Although the fundamental nature is inherently complete, it is manifested through the mind.
Amitābha, with his unconditioned compassion, took up the Land of Ultimate Bliss; Śākyamuni, with his eloquence of joyful speech, revealed the gateway to rebirth there.
These are all skillful means of expedient methods to gather in those beings who are submerged in saṃsāra, ensuring that those who fear falling back do not regress.
To enable those who have not yet cultivated skillful observation to observe, there are many provisional manifestations (*upāya-nimitta*) of the Pure Land. Now, I shall briefly discuss these two.

Thus, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "When beginners in the Mahāyāna possess right faith, because they do not constantly encounter the Buddha in this land, they may fear that their faith will lack its necessary conditions and thus regress or be lost.
One should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to ensure they do not regress; one need only..."

If one focuses one’s mindfulness exclusively on Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss as the *tathatā*-dharma-body, one will certainly be born in that land because one dwells in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
How could focusing one’s mindfulness on the *tathatā*-dharma-body differ from the correct faith of the Mahāyāna?

Since it takes that Buddha as its object, it is able to draw one’s rebirth toward the Pure Land; this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, one contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
The Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings possess weak and inferior mental conceptions; lacking the divine eye, they cannot perceive from afar.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess extraordinary skillful means (upāya) to enable them to see. This is primarily due to the spiritual power of Śākyamuni and the vow-mind of Amitābha.

If one contemplates with sincerity, one will certainly be able to behold [him]. This, too, is the extraordinary and wondrous skillful means of the Buddha, the King of Awakening. Such is this provisional and skillful method.
Since this is discussed in terms of the Perfect [Teaching], it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the subtle and wondrous skillful means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Therefore, the devas and humans, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicles, and the gradualist mahāsattvas who fill the world—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—exhaust their thoughts and measurements yet cannot perceive or awaken to it.
Only Buddha after Buddha can thoroughly exhaust its meaning; this is the Perfect Faith.
[Only] through perfect understanding can one truly engage in cultivation (Reply to Yang Wengong).

Master Ciyun of the Xianchan Temple said: "Some say that the Pure Land is within the mind; why must one seek it externally? When the mind is pure, [the land is pure]. Following this, the mind is purified. Then...
"The Buddha-lands are pure; why then must one seek birth in a pure land in another direction from afar? The commentary states: "My son, you have not yet mastered the meaning of the 'mind-land.
You seem to think that my mind is confined within the square inch of the chest, and thus you perceive the West as being situated far beyond the borders of this realm.
If this were the case, how could it be said that 'when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure'? As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Since the Buddha-dharma is all-pervasive, the mind-dharma is likewise all-pervasive.

If each possessed its own separate direction, how could they be said to be without distinction? Furthermore, it is said that the mind wanders through the dharma-realm as if through empty space; yet how could empty space have any divisions?

If one realizes that a single thought-moment is all-pervasive, then a single speck of dust is also all-pervasive; thus, even a distance of ten million billion lands is contained within the span of a few steps.
How could they exist outside the mind? When people of the world discuss the principle of emptiness, they dismiss cause and effect;

when they discuss their own minds, they do not believe that there are dharmas external to the mind. Is this not merely slandering the Dharma? It is also slandering one's own mind. That such calamity should lead to a fall for ten thousand kalpas is truly lamentable.
Regarding "arising from non-arising," Chan Master Zhanglu Ze said: "To take thought as thought and to take arising as arising is the error of eternalism.
To take non-thought as non-thought and to take non-arising as non-arising is the delusion of nihilism."
To contemplate while being without contemplation, and to arise while being without arising, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, on the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is received; thus, there are no Buddhas to be contemplated and no Pure Land to be born into.

Yet, within the gateway of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned; thus, all faculties are universally gathered, for there exists the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, which is the essential means for returning to the source.
This method reveals the single gate for rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, one may recite the Buddha’s name all day long without contradicting the state of non-thought;

and while fervently seeking rebirth, one does not deviate from the principle of non-arising. Consequently, ordinary beings and sages each abide in their own respective positions, yet there is a mutual resonance between them through the Way.
Though they do not travel back and forth between east and west, the spirit transcends to the Pure Land. This is something that cannot be subjected to further questioning or refutation.
Furthermore,

in the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* by the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master Lingzhi, it is asked: "When one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty, the mind is pure and the land is pure."
"Why is it necessary to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land? Answer: "If one truly penetrates the principle, whether speaking or remaining silent, all is as it should be;
there is no hindrance to practice. What prevents one from reciting the Buddha’s name? If one disparages the recitation of the Buddha’s name, one has not yet attained the status of a realized person.

Why is this so? Having realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one does not dwell in signs (*nimitta*). Constantly reciting the Buddha’s name, one does not stagnate in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Thus, one transcends the two extremes. From... [text continues]
Accommodating the Middle Way, every thought-moment accords with the Dharma-body of Amitābha, and every sound flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

At the moment of death, one will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level. Is this not what is meant by "when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure"? Thus, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* says:
The wise person ardently seeks birth in the Pure Land, yet realizes that the essence of birth is unattainable; this is true non-arising.
It does not mean that there is a separate non-arising apart from arising. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Although one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty..."
This refers to constantly cultivating the Pure Land and transforming all sentient beings.

Regarding the Pure Land as being solely the mind—desiring to realize the Pure Land of the Mind—one must first understand that all phenomena are mutually interfused. Ordinary people do not understand this, and consequently cling to the "square inch" of the physical heart-mind.

Take the mind as the pure land. Since the adornments of the Buddha-lands described in the sutras are all merely symbolic manifestations and lack any substantial reality, one must avoid the fault of slandering the Dharma by realizing that there are no phenomena external to the mind; thus it is said, "mind-only. As the sutra states:
It is like a hundred thousand lamps illuminating a single room; their light fills it entirely, without destruction or confusion.

From the form and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the sentient beings of the nine realms—down to a single speck of dust or a single hair—and whatever single dharma one may cite, each is but one lamp among those hundred thousand lamps.
A practitioner’s single thought-moment is as if situated at one lamp in the east, while Amitābha’s Pure Land is [as if] at another.
It is like a single lamp in the west: because its light pervades everywhere, the one is all, and all is one.
Outside the mind there is no land; outside the land there is no mind. This is the principle within phenomena: the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
Because there is neither destruction nor confusion, this lamp and that lamp do not interfere with one another; the mind is simply the mind, and the Buddha is simply the Buddha. Pure.
This very land is itself the Pure Land. It is the sentient beings of this land who, by recollecting the Buddha of that land, seek rebirth there;
this is the principle within the phenomenon, namely the Western Pure Land. Although one may distinguish between the phenomenal and the principled, they are in reality not two separate paths.

If one is restricted to the West alone without realizing that it is "mind-only," then one attains the phenomenon but loses the principle; though such a state may not yet accord with the ultimate principle, through the Buddha’s spiritual power...
Therefore, one may still attain rebirth; though one may dwell in the lowest grade, there shall be no falling back.

If one restricts oneself to one's own mind and does not seek the Western Land, then both practice and principle are lost. Because one does not seek rebirth, one fails to attain it; this is the loss of practice.

Because they do not know that there are no phenomena external to the mind, they dogmatically cling to the square inch [of the chest] as being the mind, thereby obscuring the principle of the perfect interfusion of mind and phenomena.
This is a failure to grasp the truth.
When the water is clear, the moon appears.
The Layman Yang Cigong, a Master of the Unconditioned, said: "The Sage of Great Vows comes from the Pure Land; yet in coming, there is truly no coming.
The ordinary person of deep resolve goes to the Pure Land; yet in going, there is truly no going. He does not come here, and I do not go there."
And why is it that when the holy and the ordinary meet, both attain communion? The radiance of Amitābha is like the pure, full moon, shining universally throughout the ten directions.
When the water is clear and still, the moon manifests its entire form; yet the moon does not suddenly come there to take up the water.
When the water is turbid and moving, the moon lacks a fixed reflection; yet the moon does not suddenly depart from the water. While it is in the water, [it remains as such].

There are distinctions of clarity and turbidity, motion and stillness; yet regarding the moon, there is no grasping or rejecting, no coming or going. Thus, the Householder Vimukta in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* said:
"One knows that all Buddhas are like reflections and one's own mind is like water. Those Tathāgatas do not come here, nor do I go to them.
If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha in the Land of Peace and Bliss, I can do so according to my will."
One sees it immediately. This shows that when sentient beings focus their attention, they will certainly see Amitābha; Amitābha comes to welcome them, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away.
These are words of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) in accordance with one's nature, not provisional teachings. (Preface to the *Jueyi ji*) Zen Master Tiantiyi Huai asked students in his quarters:
"If one says to abandon the defiled and take up the pure, or to loathe this world and rejoice in that, this is merely the sentiment of grasping and rejecting."
[The assembly] gave rise to deluded thoughts. If one says there is no Pure Land, it contradicts the Buddha’s words. "How should those who cultivate the Pure Land practice?
The assembly remained silent. [Huiyuan] answered for himself again, saying: "To be born, one is certainly born; to go, one truly does not go. He further said:

"It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its reflection sinking into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no intention of retaining the reflection."

Regarding the mind, the *Polishing the Mirror Sūtra* (*Mojing jing*) states: "It is like polishing a mirror; when the grime is exhausted, the brilliance appears. An ancient mirror buried in dust, though its radiance is inherently present, [cannot manifest]..."

It is manifested through polishing; this is the meaning of cultivation and accomplishment. Although it is manifested through polishing, it is entirely inherent from the beginning and does not come from without;

this is the meaning of innate virtue (*dharmatā-guṇa*). If one were to dogmatically insist that the radiance is inherently present and not obtained through polishing, then an ancient mirror buried in dust should still be able to reflect objects—this would be the error of clinging to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
If one were to dogmatically insist that it is obtained only through polishing, [then it would not be inherent].

If that were so, then rubbing a tile would also result in a mirror; this is the error of clinging to [the notion of] causes and conditions. The Sūtra says, "This mind makes a Buddha," which is spoken in reference to the cultivation of virtue.
It means that although sentient beings possess the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya*), they must necessarily rely on the function of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
It is only after this that realization is attained. As for the statement "this mind is Buddha," it is spoken in terms of the inherent virtues of nature (*xingde*).

This means that although the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is manifested through cultivation and realization, it is entirely the original existence of these inherent virtues; it is not obtained from another source.

The ten kinds of non-obstruction are the mind contemplating the Buddha. By relying on objects to manifest the nature, every moment of mind is free from dependence, and every phenomenon is entirely true.

There are those who do not understand this and thus groundlessly give rise to doubt and slander; hence there are those who cling to the internal mind as being the Buddha while refusing to seek it externally, or who cling to themselves...
Those who claim there is no need for other Buddhas; those who cling to the emptiness of all phenomena while disbelieving in the existence of Buddhas;

and those who cling to the idea that everything is spontaneously accomplished without relying on cultivation and realization—all these merely fail to follow the holy teachings and fail to comprehend the essence of reality.
Whatever one clings to becomes a false view; it negates cause and effect, indulges in deluded sentiments, mistakes gravel for gold, and attempts to cook rice from sand.
Now, by means of ten kinds of non-obstruction, I shall manifest the perfect integration of the Pure Land and sweep away all clinging attachments.
This clarifies and gives rise to right faith.
When the mind and its objects are one with the Dharma-nature (*tathatā*), for the practitioner, a single thought-moment is the observing mind, and Amitābha’s Pure Land is the observed object.
Because there is no phenomenon outside of the mind, the pure lands of all Buddhas are entirely one's own mind. Because there is no dharma outside of...
