Because it is without mind, this mind is entirely the dharma-body of all Buddhas. Mind and objects are ungraspable, yet mind and objects are vividly present;

they mutually vanish and mutually exist, beyond thought and beyond discourse. Thus the Sūtra says: "When you all contemplate the Buddha in your minds, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs...
[Section Two: The Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature. This is the Pure Land of the Sole Mind.]
The principle of original possession means that the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature (*xing*). Making a vow for rebirth is a matter of following conditions;

it is the realization of cultivation through the nature (*xing*). Because cultivation and nature are non-dual, although the pure lands of all Buddhas are primordially manifest, one must necessarily achieve rebirth therein through the fulfillment of pure karma.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. All...

The Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is an ocean born from the mind and thoughts. Third, the principle of cause and effect is identical because sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essence.
While the Buddhas have already attained awakening and sentient beings remain in delusion, although delusion and awakening differ, their nature is eternally equal.

Therefore, to practice mindfulness of the Buddha is to be mindful of the fundamental nature of all sentient beings. Thus, a sutra says: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. (Omission) Fourth, both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously transcended.
All phenomena are fundamentally empty, and not even a speck of dust can be found. Yet, as they arise in accordance with conditions, each phenomenon appears vividly and distinctly.
Because all dharmas are empty, neither mind nor Buddha can be apprehended. Because all dharmas are provisional, mind and Buddha appear vividly.
Because all dharmas are within [the nature of reality], mind and Buddha are non-dual. They are neither existent nor empty, transcending thought and beyond discourse.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The physical dimensions of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life are boundless; they are not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings. Yet that Tathāgata...

Due to the power of past vows, those who possess recollection and contemplation will certainly attain accomplishment. Furthermore, a sutra states: "The physical body is not the Buddha; voice likewise is not.
Yet, one does not perceive the Buddha apart from form and sound—this is the power of his spiritual transformations. (5) Regarding the mutual fusion of the environment and the inhabitants:

the adornment of the land is the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution), while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the *sambhoga-vipāka* (the primary retribution). A single mind possesses all.
In every land, within each and every atom, all Buddhas and the sentient beings of the nine realms appear; this is because their essential nature is fundamentally the same.
Therefore, the setting sun and the lands of ice, along with their adornments, are manifestations of the mind alone. The water-birds and the forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
(6) Regarding the identity of superiority and inferiority: the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas arises from the Truth as a response, like reflections appearing in a mirror.

The image [of the Buddha] reflects beauty or ugliness according to the capacity [of the beholder], just as water gives rise to waves that vary in size according to the wind. Because capacities possess sharpness or dullness, there must be distinctions of superior and inferior;
yet the essence of the Dharmakāya is fundamentally unmoving. Thus, a sutra says: "The supernatural powers of Amitābha Buddha are as he wishes;
throughout the lands of the ten directions, he manifests with sovereign ease—sometimes manifesting a great body that fills the void of space, or..."
The small body manifests as sixteen, eight, or ten feet; because one is identical to many, a single mind and a single atom pervade all Buddha-fields.
Because many are identical to one, all Buddha-fields are entirely contained within a single mind and a single atom.
In order to cause the mind to be single-minded and to achieve success with ease, one is directed to focus mindfulness on a single Buddha; yet, a single Buddha is all Buddhas.
Thus, a sutra says: "One who sees the Buddha of Infinite Life sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
[8] Mastery over breadth and narrowness: because the dharma-realm of the ten directions is not separate from a single mote of dust, a single mote of dust extends to...

Subtle. Its measure is equal to the Dharma-realm. Although Buddha-lands are vast, they do not depart from a single speck of dust; a journey of one hundred thousand leagues does not exceed the space of a square inch.
Thus, a sutra says: "Amitābha Buddha is not far from here; it is like seeing the reflection of one's own face in a mirror.
(9) There is no interval between past and present, because the three periods of time are not separate from a single thought-moment, and because the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be apprehended.
There is no past, because the posterior limit is unattainable; there is no future, because the intermediate limit is unattainable;

there is no present, because the world’s characteristics flow and change while its essence is eternally abiding. As the Sūtra says: "To contemplate that which is far distant is as if it were this very day."
In a mere moment, he visited and served all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions. His tenfold quiescence and function were unimpeded;

that is to say, while blazingly active in manifestation, he remained unmoved from the fundamental limit (*dharmadhātu*). It is like water giving rise to waves: the waves are entirely water. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, he manifests all dignified postures. And as the *Yìjīng* says: "Quiescent and unmoving, yet upon being stirred, it penetrates all. This is to function precisely within quiescence.

Therefore, one abandons defilement until it is exhausted and takes up purity until its source is reached. By means of this, there is constant quiescence; thus, although there is taking and abandoning, in reality there is no taking or abandoning.
Consequently, the fervent practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is equal to non-mindfulness, and the fervent aspiration for rebirth is equal to non-arising.

In the state where there is nothing to be seen, one is not hindered from seeing the Buddha; in the state where there is no arising, one spontaneously attains rebirth. By means of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]...
Because for the practitioner, whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, at all times everything is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As the Sūtra says:
"To adorn Buddha-lands is itself not adorning; to bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, there are in fact no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa."
This is what is meant by that. The ten kinds of unhindered Dharma-gates mentioned above are all explicit teachings of the Holy One, spoken from his own golden mouth.
If one thoroughly understands this principle, one does not even cling to these unhindered dharmas; how much less would one give rise to attachment based on the deluded sentiments of the world?
To practice such mindfulness of the Buddha is to mindfully recollect without recollection, to recollect while being without recollection, and to recollect others.
To contemplate the Buddha is precisely to contemplate one's own Buddha. To contemplate one Buddha is to contemplate all Buddhas.
To be born in one pure land is to be universally born in the pure lands of all Buddhas, yet there is no place of birth.
Chan Master Zhenxie Le said:
Someone asked, "The Pure Land of the Mind alone is inherently possessed by every person.
Why do you not directly accept this, yet instead seek it beyond ten quadrillion lands? He replied, "If you can understand that it is the Mind alone..."
The Pure Land—how could even ten million billion lands, as numerous as motes of dust, be considered distant?
Have you not seen how the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, taking a single step within a single pore, passes through worlds as numerous as the motes of dust in unspeakably many Buddha-fields?
Master Li said: "In the ocean of boundless lands, self and other are not separated; within the tip of a hair, the ten ages [of past and future] are present."
Now, from beginning to end, one does not depart from it, because it resides within the present thought. Thus, the World-Honored Amitābha is simply the single Buddha manifested within the mind.
If one points to the totality of the mind, it is not only that the Pure Land and the hells are manifestations of the mind alone;
as the Sūtra says: "The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky. Furthermore...
Question: Since it is perfectly interfused and unobstructed, why point specifically to the West? Answer:

It is precisely because the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused that every phenomenon does not depart from its own locus. Pure Land is omnipresent in all places; this is to take one and fully encompass the whole.
It is like the net of thousand-jeweled pearls in the palace of Śakra, where the light and shadows of the thousand pearls all enter into a single pearl, and that single pearl...
The light and shadow pervade the thousand beads; although each bead mutually pervades the others, this bead cannot be that bead, and that bead cannot be this bead.
They interpenetrate without being mixed, and they remain distinct without being divided. Although each one pervades all, yet none has a location.
The Pure Land of Amitābha is but one of the thousand beads. Each of the lands of the ten directions is likewise one of the ten beads.
Beings of the Three Vehicles, humans and devas, and those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—each and every one is none other than one of the thousand beads.
When a sage employs skillful means to focus single-mindedly on Amitābha Buddha, he directly points to one bead among the thousand; by seeing this one Buddha, one sees [all].

The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise perceive that the sentient beings of the nine realms, the ocean of lands as numerous as motes of dust, and the ten periods of time throughout antiquity and the present,
are all instantaneously perfected within a single seal, with no dharma remaining outside.
○ Section on the Characteristics of Dharmas, Number Three.
That which all Buddhas have realized is nothing other than the single principle. To investigate it to its ultimate conclusion, even this principle cannot be apprehended;
how then could there be any phenomenal characteristics? Nevertheless, this is merely a provisional statement. The Patriarch said: "Although the nature is one,"
Yet they lack a fixed, unitary nature; thus, the three thousand phenomena of form and mind appear with distinct characteristics in every detail.
Those who are deluded do not comprehend this, and there are even those who, clinging to a single principle, negate all differentiation. This is like rejecting the waves while seeking the water.

If one knows that differentiation is precisely the single principle, and that the single principle does not obstruct differentiation, it is like a person of great merit who takes a stone and transforms it into a jewel—what need is there for selection?
As the Sūtra says: "All worthy ones and sages are differentiated by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This is what is meant.
The Path has its difficulties and its ease;
as the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna states: "The Dharma of the Buddha has immeasurable gateways, just as there are difficult and easy paths in the world.
Traveling on land by foot is arduous, whereas traveling on water by boat is pleasant. The path of the Bodhisattva is likewise."

It is so. That which is difficult to practice can only be attained after a long time. As for those who fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, some may apply themselves with diligent effort;
yet by means of the skillful method of faith and easy practice, they may swiftly arrive [at the goal]. One should thus recollect the Buddha and invoke his name.
Such was the original vow of Amitābha Buddha: "If anyone recollects me, invokes my name, and takes refuge in me, they shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Bodhi. Therefore, one should always maintain mindfulness of it. The verse says:
If a person aspires to become a Buddha And keeps Amitābha in mind, They shall immediately attain his manifested body;
Therefore, I take refuge and pay homage. If a person wishes to swiftly reach The stage of non-retrogression, [One should likewise keep Amitābha in mind.]
One should, with a mind of reverence, uphold [this practice] and recite the Name.
If a person has planted roots of goodness but harbors doubt, the flower will not bloom; for one whose mind of faith is pure, the flower blooms and they behold the Buddha.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states: "Those who practice the Difficult Path seek *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) within the evil world of the five turbidities; this is exceedingly difficult."

It can be attained. Briefly stated, there are five [obstacles]: first, the outward appearance of goodness in non-Buddhists that confuses the Bodhisattva path; second, unscrupulous evil persons who destroy the superior virtues of others;
third, perverted wholesome fruits that can ruin pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); fourth, the self-interest of Śrāvakas which obstructs great compassion;
and fifth, relying solely on one's own power, like a lame person walking—such a person covers no more than a few li in a single day. It is easy [to fall into these].

Those who practice the Way are those who, having faith in the Buddha’s teachings and practicing the *nien-fo* samādhi, rely upon the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows to maintain their resolve for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
This is like a person traveling by boat on water, covering a thousand li in a mere moment;

it is also like a weak man following a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), who completes a circuit of the four continents in a single day and night. This is not due to his own strength, but the power of the Wheel-Turning King.

Regarding the two types of karma—concentrated and dispersed—the Great Master Tiantai’s *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "Roots may be sharp or dull, and practices may be concentrated or dispersed.

The samādhi of contemplating the Buddha is called 'concentrated'; the cultivation of other wholesome karmas is termed 'dispersed. The power of dispersed goodness is slight and cannot eliminate the five heinous crimes."

The *Great Sutra* (the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*) addresses this point, and thus speaks of "non-arising. This sutra clarifies the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and therefore one attains rebirth there.

Master Yulun of Shantang said: "The various Mahayana sutras exhort rebirth in the Pure Land through two types of causes: first, meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, non-concentrated practice (*vikṣipta*).

'Concentration' refers to contemplating the Buddha within one's own mind, visualizing the environment, the primary and secondary features, and the retinue of that Western Land as being fully present within the mind; everything is right where it is."
Emptiness is the entire body of the provisional; both extremes are unobtainable, and the Middle Way does not exist.

The three truths are perfectly interfused, fully present within a single mind. Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-realm body," and further, "This mind creates the Buddha;
this mind is the Buddha. This is the Tathāgata’s direct revelation of the Samādhi of Mind-Only, the essence of the perfect and eternal contemplation, through which one realizes that purity.
The land, the primary and secondary environments, and the mind—all are my own mind. Its nature is fully endowed with merit; thus, one takes the objective realm as the object of contemplation.
Outside the mind there is no Buddha; outside the nature there is no land. By contemplating this without ceasing, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Second is the practice of scattered goodness: employing a pure and sincere mind, one believes in the existence of the Western Land. With single-mindedness and without distraction, one fixes the mindfulness on Amitābha. Day and night, for one day or seven days, one continues without fail.

It is uninterrupted, with every thought following upon the next without interval. As the Sūtra says: "Holding fast to the Name, with a single mind and without distraction, at the moment of death, the Buddha and the assembly of sages will appear before one.
This refers solely to focusing the mind on that land; since it lacks the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), it is termed "scattered goodness" (*vikṣipta-kuśala*).

Therefore, one should dedicate the three kinds of pure karma with the vow to be reborn there, so that all may ascend to Sukhāvatī. Whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, and whether of sharp or dull faculties, these are all causes for the Pure Land;
all shall proceed toward non-arising and never again undergo regression.

Distinguishing between the Western [Buddhist] tradition and the Confucian classics of this land, he regards the Buddha as the Great Sage of the West. He states that Śākyamuni appeared in the kingdom of India (Tianzhu), and that his teachings subsequently flowed into the Central Plains (Zhongxia).
In the past, Faxian and Xuanzang traveled to the Western Heaven (Xitian) to seek the Dharma; both of them designated the Five Indias as their destination.
Regarding the language of the Zhugu (India): it is sometimes called Gandhāra, which is a phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit sound *Gandhāra*.

It is situated in the center of Jambudvīpa, while the land of Han lies to the east of Jambudvīpa; they are separated by only tens of thousands of li. Jambudvīpa is located to the south of Mount Sumeru;
together with the other three continents, these constitute one four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*). A thousand such four-continent world-systems [constitute a small chiliocosm].
This is called a small chiliocosm. A thousand small chiliocosms are called a medium chiliocosm. A thousand medium chiliocosms are called a great trichiliocosm.
This entire realm of transformation is the Sahā world, constituting a single buddha-field.
As stated in the sūtras, the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies to the west of the Sahā world, beyond a hundred trillion buddha-fields; each such field constitutes one buddha-field.

This is the Great Trichiliocosm. That Land of Ultimate Bliss is called *Sukhāvatī* in Sanskrit, which in the language of China means "Peaceful Nourishment" (*An-yang*) or "Pure Tranquility" (*Qing-tai*).
Amitābha Buddha currently resides there, preaching the Dharma. Those who cultivate the practices of purity and vow to be reborn there do so from this very place.
Although it lies beyond ten trillion *koṭis* of lands, it is not separate from one's own mind; such is the Buddha’s spiritual power.

Therefore, a single thought-moment is itself birth; it is truly not far away. Those in the world who study Buddhism are unacquainted with this teaching and all say that the Western Land is more than one hundred thousand *li* from here, merely pointing to the country of India.
Furthermore, the claim that it is eight thousand *li* is a groundless statement; only the commemorative writings of Liu Zhihou and Bai Letian describe it in some detail.

Regarding the suffering and happiness of the two lands, the Layman Wuwei said: "All sentient beings have not yet awakened to perfect enlightenment; they dwell within a great dream, rising and sinking through the six realms of existence without ever ceasing.
Though the heavens possess pleasure, when their retribution is exhausted, their signs of prosperity decline; as for the asuras, they are currently enraged, waging war against one another."
Superior! Among the animals that fly and run, they devour and mangle one another; among the ghosts and spirits in the dark realms, they are oppressed by hunger and thirst;

and in the long night of hell, they wail in agony. To be born into the human realm is indeed to be considered fortunate. Yet, one remains entangled by the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Only this Pure Land is free from all such suffering. Entrusting oneself to the womb of a lotus bud, one is spared the suffering of birth. Cold... [text ends]

Not shifting with the heat, there is no suffering of old age. The body is not subject to segmentation; there is no suffering of illness. Life span is immeasurable; there is no suffering of death. There are no parents, wives, or children;
there is no suffering of being separated from what one loves. One gathers with the assembly of supreme virtuous beings; there is no suffering of encountering what one hates.
Adorned with flowers, feasting on fragrant food, and enjoying precious jewels, there is no failure to obtain what one seeks and no poverty. Thus one contemplates and observes.

Emptiness and stillness mean there is no suffering of the aggregates (*skandha*). To compassionately rescue sentient beings—willingly taking birth when one wishes to do so and not abiding in quiescent extinction—this is not the way of the Two Vehicles.
To illuminate birth and death with wisdom and attain non-retrogression—this is not the way of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The three realms are utterly desolate, like the remote frontiers where hills, mounds, ravines, and pits abound, and where filth and decay accumulate; where streams and gullies are blocked and severed, who can provide a bridge or ford? Then there appeared...
Madmen wander lost within it; fierce beasts, *chi-mei* demons, and malevolent spirits dwell together, causing affliction and harm.
Weapons, fire, and water occasionally inflict violence and injury; wind, frost, and thunderbolts strike with such severity as to crush and terrify.

No city or domain is known where one may find refuge. Food, drink, and clothing are never sufficient; they endure these sufferings willingly, seeking no peace or happiness. There is a Buddha, Śākyamuni, who is the Great...
The "Teacher" refers to the Pure Land; it is the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Amitāyus Buddha is the Teacher of that Pure Land.
You sentient beings need only give rise to a sincere heart and recite the name of that Buddha, and you shall immediately attain rebirth there.
Once born in that land, there will be no afflictions. Those who do not hear or know this are truly to be pitied.
Regarding the "Ten Difficulties of the Sahā World" by Ciyun: it is difficult to attain the Way within the five turbidities, whereas cultivation in the Pure Land is easy.

Here, the ten difficulties of the Sahā world are contrasted with the ten ease of the Pure Land to distinguish between them. As for the ten difficulties: first, one does not constantly encounter the Buddha; the three realms are perilous.
First, although the Buddha is the guide, sentient beings’ karma is heavy; they are born at a time when they do not encounter a Buddha.
Since Śākyamuni has already entered parinirvāṇa and Maitreya has not yet appeared, the noble sages are hidden and false teachings flourish; thus, one does not hear the preaching of the Dharma.

Second, in this degenerate age of the Semblance Dharma, all that is spoken consists only of the heterodox and evil discourses of non-Buddhists; because one does not hear the True Dharma, one is led astray by evil friends. Third, one is enticed by evil companions.
1. Being bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*). 2. Associating with evil companions. 3. Seeking gain and offerings. 4. Misleading practitioners so that they fall into evil destinies. 5.

Being tormented and distracted by the four classes of Māras, and by the ninety-six kinds of heretics and wicked people who destroy and disrupt the True Dharma, thereby preventing the practitioner from attaining accomplishment.
6. The cycle of saṃsāra does not cease; one revolves through the six realms of existence like a water-wheel drawing from a well, without rest. 6.
It is difficult to escape the evil realms. One wanders through the three worlds, receiving retribution according to one's karma; even if born in the heavens, one cannot avoid falling back down.
Seventh, the seven types of worldly conditions obstruct the Path, as one is submerged in the toil of defilement; these constitute obstacles to the supramundane Dharma. Eighth, lifespans are short;
though humans may live for a hundred years, those who die prematurely are many. Time passes swiftly, and the Great Way of the Bodhisattvas is difficult to attain.

9. Because of the failure to accomplish [the goal]. There is the retrogression of practice; in this land, one must sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) through practice before one can become non-retrogressive.
This is because practitioners at the initial stage of the path cannot yet avoid falling back. 10. It is difficult to achieve in kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

For example, among those who heard the Dharma during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were those who regressed from the Great Vehicle and clung to the Lesser Vehicle, remaining on the stage of a śrāvaka for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. Although they passed through such a long duration of time, they had not yet...
Because one accomplishes the Great Way.
Regarding the "ten easinesses of the Pure Land":
first, one constantly attains the sight of the Buddha. Since the time the Buddha of Immeasurable Life attained the Way, ten... [years have passed].

First, it endures for a great kalpa, for it is eternally abiding and indestructible. Second, one constantly hears the sound of the Dharma, for the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, trees, forests, waters, and birds constantly proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Third, there is an assembly of sages and worthies, for Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve as supreme friends and all superior virtuous persons gather in one place.
Fourth, one is far removed from demonic activities; though there may be celestial Māras, they all protect the Buddha-Dharma.

1. To cause practitioners to achieve swift accomplishment. 2. Not to undergo cyclic existence; one is born through transformation within a lotus flower, so as never again to revolve within the miserable realms of birth and death.
3. To be forever separated from the evil paths; in that Buddha-land, the three evil paths do not exist, for even their names are unheard of.
4. To have superior conditions that assist the Path; jade towers and crystal palaces, precious garments and exquisite delicacies, all serve as [the means].

8. Because they possess the requisites for aiding the path to enlightenment; their lifespan is immeasurable, for the lifespan of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha, such that ordinary beings among humans and devas, even exhausting the full extent of their intellectual power, cannot know its number.
9. Because they enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
all sentient beings born there are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), as they do not regress. 10. Because they fulfill the practice of birth; they constantly follow and learn from the Buddhas.
Because one shall always attain unsurpassed bodhi throughout one's life.
As the *Miaozong chao* states:
"In this land, ordinary beings on the broad ground belong to the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). If they resolve their minds and practice, yet have not yet attained..."
Those who regress belong to the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*). Those who have already attained non-regression belong to the rightly determined group (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).

If one is born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*), regardless of whether their status is high or low—even those who have committed the five heinous crimes—if they attain rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death, they also attain non-regression;
therefore, it is said that all are of the rightly determined group.

Regarding the two modes of emergence—the horizontal and the vertical—Master Tongjiang discussed them as follows. As for the "vertical emergence," this refers to practitioners of the Three Vehicles who, relying upon the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the myriad practices of the Six Perfections, traverse the various stages and positions.
This is like attaining a degree in the civil service examinations; it requires talent and learning.

Just as one must have meritorious achievements to advance through successive official appointments, those who seek birth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name do so as if by hereditary succession, where merit is derived from one's ancestors;
furthermore, regardless of whether one possesses learning or not, it is like a general amnesty that promotes everyone universally.
Merit arises from the King [of Dharma]; regardless of the number of lifetimes, within the practice of "horizontal emergence" (*ōshutsu*), there are two types of goodness:

the determinate and the indeterminate. Shan-dao established two modes of cultivation: the exclusive and the miscellaneous. As for miscellaneous cultivation, it refers to the scattered cultivation of various virtuous deeds dedicated toward the adornment [of the Pure Land].
As for exclusive cultivation, one must exclusively prostrate to Amitābha Buddha with the body, without mixing in other forms of worship; with the mouth, one must exclusively...
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; do not recite other names. Your mind must focus exclusively on Amitābha Buddha and practice no other visualization.

If you practice with single-minded devotion, ten will be reborn for every ten, and a hundred for every hundred. If you practice in a mixed manner, among a thousand or ten thousand people, not even one or two will attain rebirth.
Today we see worldly people who perform three thousand prostrations to Amitābha daily, yet their daily recitation...
Regarding the "one hundred thousand recitations of Amitābha," there are those who practice seated meditation day and night, single-mindedly visualizing Amitābha;
that they all experience spiritual resonance can be verified through both the Exoteric and Esoteric methods of cultivation.
The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas consists of both the manifest and the secret. The manifest refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the holy teachings of the Tripitaka.

The secret refers to the performance of rituals in the maṇḍala and the recitation and upholding of secret mantras to decisively attain spiritual efficacy, such as the divine mantras for rebirth found within the Pure Land practices.
In the volume marked "Heng" of the Great Canon, there is one fascicle titled *The Ritual Manual for the Contemplative Practice of Amitāyus*. Gold... [text fragment].
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi has spoken this *Amitāyurdhāraṇī*. For those who practice the maṇḍala rites according to the Dharma, they will be reborn in the highest grade and realize the first bhūmi.

Furthermore, regarding the Heart Mantra of Amitāyus Tathāgata, the Root Mantra, the Fist Mudrā Mantra, and so forth, as well as the secret mantras of the various families, such as the Great Compassionate One and the Uṣṇīṣavijayā, their merits are exceedingly vast, as described in the sūtras.
It is said that those who cultivate pure karma and recite and uphold [the teachings] according to the Dharma will all be reborn in the Land of Bliss.

Regarding the relative urgency or laxity of the precepts versus the vehicle (*yāna*), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Laxity regarding the precepts is not what is called laxity; rather, laxity regarding the vehicle is what is called [laxity]."
"Relaxed. "Precepts" (śīla) refer to ceasing evil and practicing good; "Vehicle" (yāna) refers to understanding the ultimate truth (paramārtha). "Relaxed" means indolent and lacking diligence.
Regarding this, the Patriarch established four types of discernment (*catuḥ-prayoga*). First: "Urgent in precepts, relaxed in the vehicle.

Because one is urgent regarding the precepts, one is reborn among humans or devas—like an arrow shot into the sky that falls back once its momentum is spent. Because one is relaxed regarding the vehicle, although one hears the Great Dharma, it is as if one were deaf.
If one is mute, the Two Vehicles are urgent regarding precepts while lax regarding the Vehicle;

because they are lax regarding the precepts, they are born into evil realms, yet because they are urgent regarding the Vehicle, they constantly hear the Great Dharma—such as the eight classes of spirits and deities at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As the sutra says:

"It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell to hear the names of the Buddhas than to receive immeasurable bliss without hearing the names of the Buddhas. In the Three Vehicles, both [precepts and the Vehicle] are required.

If one is diligent, one will be reborn among humans or devas and constantly hear the Great Dharma; if one is lax in both the fourfold vehicle and the precepts, one will fall into the three evil realms and never again hear the Dharma.

Contemplating the intent of the two Mahāyāna schools, one knows that it is difficult to attain the essential meaning through hearing the Dharma, whereas the precepts and good deeds merely assist the path.
Therefore it is said: "It would be better to emulate Devadatta and dwell eternally in the earth."
Prison. One should not aspire to a temporary rebirth in heaven like that of Udraka Rāmaputra. Should those who study the Mahāyāna not be careful?

Regarding the distinction between the true and false Buddha and Māra, Dharma Master Zhāngān quotes the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, saying: "To sever the Truth of Origination is to subdue the Māra of Afflictions; to know the Truth of Suffering..."

This is the subduing of the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). Cultivating the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is the subduing of the Māra of the devas (*devaputramāra*). Realizing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is the subduing of the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the path of Māra will gradually arise to corrupt and disrupt the Buddha-dharma.
Just as fire seeks dryness and water seeks moisture, the heterodox cannot defile the orthodox. Throughout one's life, with a pure and sincere mind, one should remain firm and resolute in the truth.
If one possesses faith, recites with utmost sincerity, repents, and makes vows, I know that this person—whether in body or mind—is in communion with the spiritual affinity of Amitābha.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like a tree blown by the wind; its momentum inclines it toward the west, and when it finally falls, it falls in that direction."

They will inevitably lie down facing west. Even if their power of aspiration is feeble and their karmic offenses are deep and heavy, should signs of death appear and they invoke the Buddha’s name to seek salvation, then by the power of the Buddha, Māra shall be unable to act.

However, if those practitioners have accumulated much demonic karma—relying on the Buddha-dharma to seek fame and profit, appearing pure and upright on the outside while being utterly corrupt within, deceitful, hypocritical, and full of self-attachment—[they shall not be saved].
To exalt oneself: one cuts another’s thousand-foot height in half and boasts of one’s own single scoop of water as ten thousand bushels.
Such a person’s disposition connects them with demons; on the day of their death, they will not fall into the evil realms but will instead be born in a demonic palace—this is indeed fortunate.
One should know that all phenomena are but mind: when the mind is pure, the Buddhas welcome; when the mind is defiled, the demons receive.

This principle is easy to understand; why then need one harbor doubts or engage in the "Discernment of Demons"? Whether a Buddha is authentic or spurious is recognized only by those whose eyes of the Teaching are clear.
For the idle masses, at the moment of death, when the "wind-swords" dissolve the body and the spirit is thrown into turmoil, they will be struck with terror and panic;

how then will they have the leisure to discern whether a Buddha is genuine or demonic? In this world, there are those whose bellies are overflowing with greed and pride, preoccupied with right and wrong...
It fills the breast. During one's ordinary life, among the four māras, three cannot even be recognized.

At the moment of death, fearing a fall into the palace of Māra, one may say with the mouth that one will subdue the celestial māras, yet in the heart harbor thoughts of the method for "seated liberation" (sitting-departure).
To wish to be reborn as a human in a family of nobility and wealth—how truly laughable!

The Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is currently in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood in Tuṣita, will achieve enlightenment in the future. He presently resides in the inner garden of Tuṣita, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings.
The *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states that one must practice various samādhis and enter deeply into right concentration in order to attain rebirth there; there is no other way.

This is the meaning of employing skillful means to guide and lead others. Tuṣita is a heaven of the desire realm; its celestial maidens are attached to the five desires, indulging in them without relinquishing them.
In this Sahā world during the time of Śākyamuni, there were three hundred million households in the city of Śrāvastī who neither saw nor heard [the Dharma], let alone those in other lands.
It will be the same when Maitreya descends to be born. It is not like the purity of Amitābha’s land.
In this land, there are no evil realms or women; one constantly hears the sound of the Dharma and swiftly attains the stage of non-retrogression.
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states that in the Western Regions there were three bodhisattvas: the first named Asaṅga, the second Vasubandhu, and the third Siṃhabuddhi.
They made a vow to be reborn together in Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya. They swore that whoever arrived first would come back to inform the others. Later, Siṃhabuddhi alone—
He departed. He did not return for several years. After Vasubandhu had left, Asaṅga returned only after three years had passed. Asaṅga asked, "Why have you been gone so long?
Vasubandhu replied, "I went to that celestial palace and listened to Maitreya preach the Dharma from a single seat. I returned immediately upon his completion;
however, because the days there are long, three human years have already elapsed. He further said, "Siṃhabuddhi is experiencing celestial bliss there."
In the outer garden, Maitreya was not to be seen. If even that Bodhisattva who desires to be born in Tuṣita encounters such difficulties, how much more so for inferior ordinary beings?
Master Cien’s *General Praise of the Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The ten excellences of An-yang (Sukhāvatī) and the ten inferiorities of the celestial palaces.
Regarding the ten excellences: first, the excellence of the abode of the transforming Lord; second, the excellence of the long life of those to be transformed; third...

1. The land is not bound by the realms of existence; this is superior. 2. The four pure lands are free from desire; this is superior. 3. Women do not dwell there; this is superior. 4. There is no falling back from practice;
this is superior. 5. The pure lands are not defiled; this is superior. 6. The adornments of the lands are magnificent; this is superior. 7. Mindfulness of the Buddha gathers the emotions;
this is superior. 8. Ten recitations lead to rebirth there; this is superior. The celestial palaces are not like this; therefore, they are inferior in all ten respects.
Regarding Yongming’s Discernment:
Chan Master Yongming Zhijue received the essence of the single transmission from National Teacher Tiantai Shaokang and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land.

He invited scholars of the three schools to assemble and synthesize their various doctrines, resulting in the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles. Furthermore...
Fearing that students might cling to the view of emptiness as the true nature of reality, he composed the *Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Goodnesses*, stating:
"The six perfections, the myriad practices, and the *sāṃkhya* (Ganges-sand) number of Dharma-gates of the Mahayana Bodhisattva should all be cultivated in accordance with the nature.

Furthermore, regarding the four criteria for selecting between Zen meditation and Buddha-recitation, he stated: "First: 'If one has Zen but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray. When the realm of the *antarābhava* manifests—"

Previously, it was said that if one merely follows along with fleeting thoughts and clarifies only the principle of nature (li-xing), yet does not aspire for rebirth [in the Pure Land] and instead wanders through the Sahā world, there will be the danger of falling back and declining.
Regarding the "shadows and realms" (yin-jing): these are the manifestations of the shadow-demons (*skandha-māra*) within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

As clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, fifty kinds of demonic activities arise within the realms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Such a person initially fails to perceive that they are possessed by demons.
This refers to those who claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, yet through delusion and ignorance fall into the Avīci Hell.
Second: "There is no dhyāna, but there is the Pure Land; if ten thousand practice, ten thousand shall go. Once one has seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?

This means that while they have not clarified the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), they simply wish for rebirth; by virtue of the Buddha's power, they swiftly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. Third:
Possessing both meditative concentration and the Pure Land, one is like a tiger with horns; in this life, one becomes a teacher of humanity, and in the next life, one becomes a Buddha or a patriarch.

Having deeply penetrated the Buddha-dharma, one is thus able to serve as a teacher for humans and devas; furthermore, by making the vow for rebirth there, one swiftly attains the stage of non-retrogression.
"Ten thousand strings of cash wrapped around my waist, I ride a crane up to Yangzhou. Fourth: "No Chan, no Pure Land; iron beds and copper pillars.

Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no one to rely upon. Since you do not understand the principles of the Buddha and yet do not wish to attain rebirth there, you will sink into perpetual samsara;
by what means can you escape? If you wish to transcend birth and death and swiftly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression, you should..."
Regarding these four ways of selecting virtuous conduct, Master Zhendi of the Pure Compassion Dharma said:
"The teachings on the Pure Land have long been established in the sutras and śāstras; the explanations and analyses of various masters are likewise..."

This has already been explained in detail. Rebirth and its retribution manifest in alternation; they do not deceive us. There may be those in the world who harbor doubts, but this is merely because they obstruct themselves with ignorance and fail to harmonize principle with phenomena.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and utters 'Namo Buddha' just once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
How much more so for one who seeks rebirth here with a single-minded, undistracted heart? What doubt could there be?
Is it not so? Furthermore, if one’s perception of the good is not clear and the mind is not unified, then regarding the myriad phenomena of the world, in what direction would one not harbor doubt?
How much less so for the Buddha-dharma! In short, one should simply believe and accept it;
one ought not to doubt whether it exists or not. Thus, does the Pure Land truly exist? I say: No. Does it truly not exist? I say: No. It is also...
"Is it existent? "No. "Is it non-existent? "No. If this is so, where does the Pure Land fruit reside?
To be free from these various views is itself called the Pure Land; it is to see the Tathāgata.

If, upon hearing this teaching, one is neither startled nor terrified, know that such a person will certainly attain rebirth, yet there is no place of birth. This is because it is not through adornment that [the land is realized].
This serves as an adornment. When the mind of faith is pure, a single thought-moment is like a flower blooming; the entire body is revealed before one, complete with all marks and characteristics.
This mind is itself the Buddha—how could there be any doubt regarding the stage of the "Successor" (Upapadya)? Having transcended birth and death, one attains immeasurable life.
Should one be unable to believe and understand this, there are other expedient means in which the nine grades are fully present; practice according to your capacity, and it shall not be in vain.

Regarding the correspondence with principle through contemplation, the *Yongjia ji* states: "When the mind corresponds with emptiness, then whether one is reviled or praised, what cause for sorrow or joy?

When the body corresponds with emptiness, then whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, what suffering or pleasure? When the environment of dependent retribution corresponds with emptiness, then [regarding] giving..."
Regarding giving and taking away, what is gained and what is lost? Furthermore, when the mind corresponds with non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*), both attachment and aversion perish;
compassion universally rescues others. When the body corresponds with non-emptiness, it is internally like earth or wood, yet externally it manifests dignified deportment.

When the environment and its resources correspond with non-emptiness, craving and seeking are forever severed, yet material wealth is provided for the relief of others. Furthermore, when the mind corresponds with the non-...
When emptiness corresponds with that which is neither empty nor non-empty, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is first clarified, and one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
When the body corresponds with that which is neither empty nor non-empty, a single mote of dust enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), while all motes arise in samādhi.

When the environment and its conditions correspond with that which is neither empty nor non-empty, fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions adorn the land for those born through transformation. Yongjia’s statement here serves as a verification of cultivation.
This serves to verify whether one’s practice has reached fruition. If the three meanings are cultivated sequentially, one accomplishes the three contemplations in succession;
if they are cultivated in a manner of perfect fusion, then through the single mind’s three contemplations, one accords with emptiness, such that praise and slander are equal.
As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "View those enemies as if they were one's own parents; let the mind be without duality. People of the present day, however, [on their own...]

This means that those who claim to realize emptiness cannot possibly remain free from the perception of suffering and pleasure when reviled with a single word for the rest of their lives, nor from the perception of gain and loss when praised with a single phrase to the point of being unable to contain their joy;
nor can they remain unmoved by the application of incense or the slicing of their flesh with a blade, or by acts of giving and plundering.
Since they regard all these things as real yet speak of them as empty, they would be committing a great falsehood. How much less could they...
Is this not in accord with the Middle Way of non-emptiness? The true mark (*dharmatā*) first clarifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; herein, the Middle Way manifests before one.

When a single mote of dust enters right concentration (*samādhi*), all motes of dust arise from that samādhi. Thus, there is no obstruction to leaving this world and being born in that world of fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions within the adorned land.
This is the realm of the Pure Land; yet, many beginners who study the Buddha’s path look down upon it with contempt.
This is to be disparaged. How extreme is this perversion!
Wisdom guides conduct;
when the mind is upright, conduct is upright. Because wisdom is deviant, conduct is deviant. The practice cultivated by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas is based on *prajñā* (wisdom).
If these acts serve as a precursor, they all become causes for attaining Buddhahood and lead directly to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

When ordinary people practice virtue, they perceive it as truly existent; therefore, their retribution is experienced in the realms of humans and devas. When non-Buddhists perform asceticism, they take false views as primary;

therefore, their retribution is experienced in the three miserable paths (*apāya*). When those of the Two Vehicles cultivate practice, they focus their intent on partial emptiness; therefore, they realize only the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle. This is gradual cultivation.

Although the Great Being (Mahāsattva) integrates phenomena with principle through his reasoning, he still retains a sense of deliberate effort; thus, he has not yet been able to accord with reality in every single detail and consequently falls into the second [stage].
For the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, even a hair’s breadth of goodness is equal in measure to the Dharma-realm and is in perfect accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Not tending toward the Two Vehicles and not lingering in the three realms of existence, they realize that all phenomena are the principle of the inconceivable Three Truths; therefore, all are...
This is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. To cultivate the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha through inconceivable contemplation is the sublime practice of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching;
how could it be measured by the deluded attachments and false sentiments of ordinary people or non-Buddhists?
The *Wanshan tonggui ji* states:

"Now, the two wheels of good and evil and the two retributions of suffering and pleasure are all created by the three karmas, produced by the four conditions, accomplished by the six causes, and subsumed within the five fruits.
If, for even a single thought-moment, one harbors anger or engages in sexual misconduct..."
Killing is the karma of the hells. Stinginess and failing to practice generosity is the karma of hungry ghosts. Being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance is the karma of animals.
Arrogance and haughtiness are the karma of asuras. Firmly upholding the five precepts is the karma of humans. Diligently cultivating the ten wholesome actions is the karma of devas.
Realizing the emptiness of persons is the karma of śrāvakas. Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached is the karma of pratyekabuddhas. The six perfections...
Cultivating both [merit and wisdom] together is the karma of a bodhisattva; true compassion and equanimity are the karma of a Buddha.

If the mind is pure, one is born through transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees; if the mind is defiled, one receives a physical form in a defiled land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines.
These are all fruits of equal nature that can evoke superior conditions. Apart from the source of one's own mind, there is no separate essence.
Regarding the extent of the roots of goodness, the *Sūtra* states: "One cannot be born in that land by means of a small amount of roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions.

The Sub-commentary by the Vinaya Master of Great Wisdom (*Dazhi Lishi*) states: "If all meritorious deeds—such as giving, observing the precepts, meditating, reciting, and practicing asceticism—lack right faith..."
Dedicating merit and making vows are not the causes for rebirth; they are all termed "minor roots of goodness. If one relies on this sutra and upholds the Name, one will certainly attain rebirth.
Therefore, we know that invoking the Name constitutes many roots of goodness. Previously, I offered this interpretation, though some may have found it doubtful.
Recently, I obtained a stone-carved edition of the sutra from Xiangyang; beneath the phrase "single-mindedness without distraction," it states: "Exclusively invoke..."
Because one’s name is invoked, all transgressions are extinguished; this is precisely the cause and condition for manifold roots of goodness and merit.

That stone-scripture copy was written by people of the Liang and Chen dynasties, and its literary phrasing accords perfectly with the present commentary. Thus we know that the southern versions of the scriptures have been transmitted with errors and omissions.
One should understand that the Buddha-body is not a physical form; its fruition and virtue are so lofty and profound that it does not establish a specific, auspicious name.
The wondrous essence cannot be fully manifested; yet the Buddhas of the ten directions all possess distinct names, let alone my Amitābha, who receives sentient beings through their names.
Therefore, when one hears with the ears and recites with the mouth, the boundless holy virtues are gathered into the conscious mind, becoming forever the seed of Buddhahood.

One instantly eliminates the heavy sins of billions of kalpas and attains realization of unsurpassed Bodhi. Know for certain that this is not due to meager roots of goodness, but is the result of manifold merit.
Furthermore, regarding the "six identities" (*liu ji*), which serve to distinguish against confusion:

whenever the Great Master Tiantai explained the word "Buddha," he invariably clarified these six identities. This means that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is its entire substance present [within them].

Delusion is called the "identity of principle" (*li-ji*). Hearing the teaching and giving rise to understanding is called the "identity of name" (*ming-zi-ji*). Practicing in accordance with the principle is called the "identity of contemplative practice" (*guan-xing-ji*).
The great worthy and the near-sage are called the "identity of resemblance" (*xiang-si-ji*). Sharing what the Buddha has realized is called the "identity of partial truth" (*fen-zhen-ji*).

Reaching the ultimate unsurpassed state is called the "identity of finality" (*jiong-jing-ji*). Because there are these six, ordinary beings and sages do not become confused, thereby avoiding the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*). Because they are identical [in essence], both the beginning and the end are complete.
This prevents the arising of weariness. The six positions (ṣaḍ-avasthā) are always "immediate" (ji); this immediacy does not obstruct the six.

This meaning of the "six immediacies" originated from our own school and deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent. Yet many people erroneously cling to the defiled mind of birth and death and the painful realms of the five turbidities as being the pure mind and pure land;

this is the "impure as pure" among the four inversions of ordinary beings. When discussing all phenomena according to the Perfect Teaching, one must necessarily apply the framework of the six immediacies.
Distinguishing between the beginning and the end, I shall now propose this explanation to discuss the Pure Land, so that there may be no error or deviation.

If one says that all sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas—such that although they dwell within the five turbidities and the realm of defilement and undergo various retributive sufferings, their nature is fundamentally pure—this principle is precisely the fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) and purity of the Buddha.
If one hears that the nature is fundamentally pure and gives rise to deep faith...
Faith and understanding constitute the purity of name. Practicing in accordance with the nature through the inconceivable three contemplations constitutes the purity of contemplative practice.
Severing the secondary branches of ignorance and attaining the purity of the six sense organs constitutes the purity of semblance. This involves the partial destruction of fundamental ignorance.

To partially realize the secret treasury of the three virtues is partial true purity. When the three delusions are completely exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished, initial enlightenment becomes perfected and fundamental enlightenment is fully manifested;
one then achieves the pure *dharmakāya* and dwells in the land of eternal quiescence and light—this is ultimate purity.

Furthermore, although the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of sentient beings in the nine realms is inherently pure, because they have not yet heard the Great Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden, they are all defiled by the impurities of mind and land.

If these sentient beings, with a pure mind of faith, make a vow to be reborn there, then because their minds are focused, they will not depart from the present thought-moment and shall behold the pure realm of the Land of Bliss—the lotus ponds and jeweled trees.
Such individuals are those at the stage of "contemplative practice through names" (*nāma-śabda-caryā-bhūmi*).

Because the mind is pure, the land is pure. As the Sūtra says: "If one hears my teaching that the lifespan is long and far-reaching, and with a profound mind believes and understands it, then one sees the Buddha constantly on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma."

This is the purity of the land of expedient means (*upāya*). If one destroys fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), ascends to the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), and realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this person belongs to the stage of partial truth; their mind is pure and their land is pure. As the Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, one sees this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, level and even, with all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas dwelling therein. This is the purity of the land of true retribution (*samyag-vipāka*). If...

Having ascended to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), his wisdom and abandonment are perfected. This Sage of the ultimate fruit possesses a pure mind and a pure land. As the Sūtra says:
"Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Śākyamuni is named Vairocana.
Pervading all places, the dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*).

It is the Nirvana of the three virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—the realm where all Buddhas and Tathāgatas roam and reside; only this is termed ultimate. When the mind is pure, the land is pure.

Ignorant commoners, being worldly ordinary people who have not applied themselves to cultivation or realization, claim to be identical to the Buddha’s purity; they are like commoners falsely assuming the title [of royalty].
The sovereign brought about his own destruction; what crime could be greater than this slander of the Dharma?
○ Regarding the Fourth Gate of Contemplative Wisdom:
because the fundamental nature of sentient beings is endowed with all dharmas, one contemplates by observing that very nature; thus, all dharmas are seen as...
The mind manifests its realization; hundreds of thousands of billions of lands are reached without traveling. The eighty thousand marks and signs appear before one’s very eyes.
How great is the essence of the sublime contemplation of cultivating the mind—is it not the wondrous art that raises the dead and returns life?

Sentient beings have for kalpas been submerged in the ocean of suffering, nearly losing their Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom. Now, having received the teachings of the Perfect Vehicle, they come to know...
The mind makes the Buddha; knowing that the mind is the Buddha is like holding a torch while entering a dark chamber.
Because one contemplates the Buddha-body, one immediately perceives the Buddha-mind. Because one sees a single Buddha, one immediately sees all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Thus, in a mere instant, one can serve all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and universally hear all sounds, which exclusively proclaim the profound.
Within the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is nowhere that is not the Buddha-dharma. How inconceivable is the merit of wondrous contemplation!
It is the single mind and the threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*).
The Venerable Master of Siming said: "The three contemplations are that in a single thought-moment there is emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.

Their grand proclamation originated with the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening; tracing them back more recently to the Wisdom Teacher (Zhiyi), they arise entirely from the nature and are truly not accomplished through cultivation.

Thus, within a single mind, there are clearly three functions. That which is called 'emptiness' means that all things are empty, and the three contemplations are fully manifested as a sweeping purification."

This is the function of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "All is provisional" means that all things are provisional; this is the merit of establishing the teachings through the clarity of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

"The Middle" means that all things are the Middle; the three contemplations are entirely the essence of non-relationality (*anapekṣa*). Thus, while all day long one dispels characteristics, all dharmas are perfected;
while all day long one establishes teachings, not even a speck of dust remains; while all day long one transcends relationality, [the two extremes are eliminated].

Because the truths are blazingly radiant, the Prajñāpāramitā speaks of emptiness, whereby the eighty dharma-gates are revealed; Vimalakīrti establishes the Dharma, whereby the views and cravings of the triple world are all forgotten;
and in the One Vehicle of the Lotus Sūtra, the characteristics of the mundane world are eternally abiding—all of these arise from the mutual identity of the three contemplations.

Because it brings all phenomena to completion without exception: three is not three, and one is not one. It is not entered through sequential stages, nor is it observed through simultaneous distinctions.

It cannot be sought in terms of existence or non-existence, nor can it be grasped as a center or a periphery. Therefore, it is said that they are neither simultaneous nor distinct, neither vertical nor horizontal;
the three and the one are perfectly interfused, and cultivation and nature are merged in profound stillness. How could this be the domain of the conscious mind?
[The Master] says: What words can possibly express this? Therefore, he provisionally indicates it as "the wondrous contemplation that is inconceivable.
To speak is non-speaking; it is speaking without speaking. Once one has understood this, one may confront all objects and comprehend them through this contemplative illumination.
One may establish all practices and bring them to fulfillment through this contemplative guidance. One may discern all affairs and accomplish them through this contemplation.

Establish all teachings and expound them through this contemplation. For one who cultivates this contemplation, subject and object are necessarily forgotten, and grasping and rejecting are extinguished.
Thus, in true suchness there is no thought; when one turns toward it, the mind ceases. Though speaking and teaching all day long, it is no different from silence.
To abandon this is to inevitably join the ranks of the various Māras; to depart from this is not yet to transcend the various outsiders. Thus, Nāgārjuna said:
"Except for the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra. Kāśyapa said: "Prior to hearing the Great Nirvāṇa, all were but false views."
How magnificent! This is the wondrous core teaching of the single mind and the three contemplations.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Scripture on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha) states: "The Tathāgata now instructs Vaidehī and those of future ages..."

All sentient beings, by contemplating the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, shall—by the power of the Buddha—be able to behold that pure land as clearly as seeing one's own reflection in a bright mirror.

Upon beholding the most wondrous and joyful matters of that land, their hearts will be filled with joy, and they shall immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) at that very moment... [etc. The *Miaozong* says: "If one merely reads the text..."
This is not called practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). One must examine the characteristics explained in the sutras and bring them into a single thought-moment.

Using the subtle contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way, one illuminates the nature of the mind, which inherently possesses the Pure Land. By practicing accordingly, this very mind becomes the Buddha.
"This mind is the Buddha. This passage appears in the *Contemplation of the Buddha’s Image*; its meaning pervades both the beginning and the end.

It constitutes the inconceivable three contemplations and is the general essence of the sixteen contemplations—the sublime core of this entire sutra. Practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] who rely upon this for study will swiftly realize the non-arising of phenomena.
The first six [stages] concern the contemplation of the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*).
First is the contemplation of the earth, second the contemplation of water, third the contemplation of the ground, fourth the contemplation of trees, fifth the contemplation of ponds,
and sixth the general contemplation.
The second seven days consist of: (1) the visualization of the primary retribution;
(2) the visualization of the seven lotus seats; (3) the visualization of the images; (4) the visualization of the Buddha’s body; (5) the visualization of Avalokiteśvara;
(6) the visualization of Mahāsthāmaprāpta; (7) the universal visualization; and (8) the miscellaneous visualizations.
Third, the threefold contemplation of the nine grades:
first, the contemplation of the superior grade (14); second, the contemplation of the middle grade (15); third, the contemplation of the inferior grade (16).
First, one contemplates the setting sun, which appears like a suspended drum, causing the mind to dwell firmly, focused and unwavering. This has two intentions.
First, cause the mind to contemplate the sun so that it does not wander or scatter. Second, cause the mental visualization to be directed toward the western direction.

Next, contemplate clear water and further imagine it becoming ice. This is because the ground of that land is made of lapis lazuli; since this ground is difficult to visualize, one should first have them visualize ice.
If the perception of ice is accomplished, the jeweled ground becomes visible. For the time being, one relies on this world, using the setting sun and the ice as skillful means.

Next, one contemplates that land—its grounds, trees, ponds, and towers—until the contemplation of the towers is perfected and the jeweled lands all appear; therefore, this is called "contemplating the whole."

(Above, the contemplation of the *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* [the environment] is complete. Next, contemplate the *sambhoga-kāya* [the primary retribution]. Since one wishes to contemplate the Buddha, and the Buddha must necessarily be seated upon a throne, one first contemplates the flower-throne.
Furthermore, the true Buddha is difficult to perceive; one must necessarily contemplate an image. Once the contemplation of the image is perfected, the true Buddha can be seen.

Regarding the eighty thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one contemplates only the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows), which is like five Mount Sumerus. If this visualization is perfected, all eighty thousand will manifest. Next, contemplate Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
[One proceeds] to the true and ultimate form-body (*rūpakāya*). Next, one practices universal contemplation: first, one visualizes oneself being born in that land;

next, one contemplates the three sages entering into one's own heart. Next, one practices miscellaneous contemplation, observing the Buddha’s body and its superior or inferior transformative functions—how it can be both great and small, all fully encompassing the Dharma-realm (the above seven contemplations observe the primary retribution;
next, one observes the practitioners of the three grades). Next, one observes the practitioners of the three grades and nine ranks.

Cultivating causes brings about their corresponding fruits; thus, one should abandon the middle and inferior grades and cultivate the superior grade. All contemplations employ the characteristics shown in the sutras, which one should retain in mind as the objects of observation.
Furthermore, one must realize that this dharma is inherently possessed by one's own mind and is actualized through reliance upon these objects and mental conceptualization.

To cause the inherently endowed dharmas to illuminate the mind and eyes, such that one's contemplation accords with the sutras and is contemplated in accordance with the nature [of reality], is called "right contemplation.
To see characteristics that deviate from the sutras is to give rise to demonic activity; therefore, it is called "erroneous contemplation."

Regarding the contemplation of the setting sun, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Vaidehī, "You and all sentient beings should single-mindedly fix your attention on one place and contemplate the West.
How should you form this visualization? In general, when forming a visualization, no sentient being—unless they are born blind—"

Those who possess sight all see the sun set; at that time, one should give rise to this visualization: sitting upright and facing west, gaze intently at the sun, causing the mind to dwell firmly and the focused thought to remain unmoving.
When seeing the sun about to set, its form is like a suspended drum. Having seen the sun thus, [one should continue].
Whether with eyes closed or open, one should cause everything to be clearly perceived; this is the visualization of the sun, called the first contemplation. *Miaozong* says:

One first performs the visualization of the sun with the intention of binding the mind. Since the ordinary mind is dark and obscure, how could it otherwise be able to clearly perceive the wondrous realm of the Pure Land?

Therefore, one is instructed to focus the visualization exclusively on the form of the setting sun. By binding the mind to this single object and contemplating it without ceasing, the mind becomes concentrated.
When the mind is thus still and subtle, all manner of contemplative methods can be practiced. As for the method of binding the mind, the setting sun must be used.
This is intended to cause the concentrated visualization to proceed toward the west, for that is the direction where Amitābha resides.

Although a beginner practitioner understands that both the sense organs and their objects are entirely the Dharma-realm, their mental conceptions are weak and inferior, making it difficult to perceive the sublime signs.

Therefore, the Tathāgata established an alternative skillful means, taking the first sight of the setting sun as the object of focus, so that by visualizing it, the visualization may arise within the contemplation.

The Sun: A person of perfect capacity possesses wondrous understanding; they know that the mind capable of conceptualization inherently contains all phenomena of both the environment and its inhabitants.
Now, by means of this sun-like mind, they take as their object the very sun that is the mind itself, causing the sun of their original nature to manifest before them.

This is to take the dharma-realm mind as the object of the dharma-realm境 (object), thereby giving rise to the sun of the dharma-realm. Since all are the dharma-realm, how could they not be identical to emptiness and provisionality?
This is still a general indication. If one were to discuss the daily progress of accomplishing the three contemplations in detail:
because the faculties and objects are empty and quiescent, the mind-sun is unimpeded; because they are provisionally established through dependent origination, accumulated thoughts arise daily;

and because both the mind and the sun are the dharma-realm, they manifest as their own essence. These three contemplations are identical within a single mind; they are neither one nor three, yet they are three.
And they are one; this is inconceivable. If it were otherwise, it would not be the contemplation practiced by those of perfect capacity.
Regarding the contemplation of the image, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, fascicle eight, states: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter..."
Within the thoughts of all sentient beings, when you contemplate the Buddha, that very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
That mind creates the Buddha; that mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ right and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s contemplation.
Therefore, you should single-mindedly fix your mindfulness and clearly observe that Buddha’s [wondrous]...

The Master’s commentary states: "If one wishes to contemplate the Buddha-body, one must know the substance of contemplation. That substance is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*); its arising constitutes the capacity for contemplation.
It is in reliance upon this substance that the thesis is established—this is what is meant.

One must know that original enlightenment is precisely the Dharma-realm body of all Buddhas, because all Tathāgatas have no separate object of realization, as they fully realize the fundamental nature of sentient beings. If initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) were to possess functional efficacy..."
Thus, original enlightenment (benjue) is revealed; hence it is said that the Dharma-body arises from the mind and thoughts.

Furthermore, Amitābha and all Buddhas are one body and one wisdom, and their functional application is likewise so. When the body of Amitābha manifests, it is the body of all Buddhas; when the marks of all Buddhas are clarified, they are the essence of Amitābha.
To discuss this in terms of practice is precisely the inconceivable threefold contemplation (san guan), for whether through negation or affirmation, [it leads to realization].
These are called the two contemplations of emptiness and the provisional. That which neither destroys nor establishes is called the Middle Way contemplation.

When one acts by being entirely within [the truth], then the three truths are both destroyed and established; when one is entirely within while acting, then the three truths are neither destroyed nor established.
The emptiness and the provisional within the middle are called "acting," for they can destroy the three delusions and establish the three dharmas; thus, they evoke the three bodies of the Buddhas.
The Perfect Response (yuan-ying) can fulfill my mind. The three bodies as the fruit are precisely within emptiness and the provisional;
this is what is meant by "name. Thus, delusion is entirely wisdom, and hindrances are entirely virtue. Therefore, the mind is the Responsive Buddha, and the mind is the Fruitional Buddha.
One should know that practicing these three contemplations with this single mind is the general essence of the sixteen contemplations and the sublime core of this sutra. These words appear here.
The meaning [of this] pervades from beginning to end. Therefore, practitioners should employ this intent when cultivating the causes for the Pure Land.

Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha’s body in the ninth chapter of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Wuliangshou jing), the "Contemplation of the Buddha’s Body," it says: "The body of Amitāyus Buddha is like [the radiance of] a hundred thousand..."
There were ten trillion Yāma heavens. The Buddha’s body was the color of Jāmbūnada gold, sixty million *nayuta* of Ganges-sands of *yojana* in height.
The white tuft of hair between his brows curled to the right, as magnificent as five Mount Sumerus.
His eyes were like the waters of the four great oceans, with their blue and white clearly distinguished. From all the pores of his body, he emitted radiance, like Mount Sumeru.
Mountain. The halo of that Buddha is like ten billion trichiliocosms.
Within that halo, there are transformation Buddhas as numerous as the sands of ten million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges Rivers.
Each transformation Buddha is likewise attended by a multitude of countless transformation Bodhisattvas. Amitāyus Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks; each mark...
Each possesses eighty-four thousand secondary marks of physical excellence (*anuvyañjana*). Each mark, in turn, has eighty-four thousand rays of light.
Each ray of light shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, embracing and never abandoning those sentient beings who mindfully recite the Buddha’s name.

The manifestations of these lights, marks, and secondary signs, as well as the emanated Buddhas, cannot be fully described; one should simply contemplate them with mindfulness so that they may be seen by the eye of the mind. Having seen this—
As for the matter: it is to see all Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the Buddhas, it is called the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).

One who performs this contemplation is said to contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas; because they contemplate the Buddha-bodies, they also see the Buddha-minds. The Buddha-mind is great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*).
By means of unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), it gathers in all sentient beings. One who performs this contemplation, upon casting off the body...
In future lives, one will be born before all Buddhas and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The *Amitābha-sūtra* (Guan wuliangshoufo jing) states: "One who contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life enters through a single mark and excellence; they need only contemplate the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows."
