Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dayou of Beichen Monastery in Wu Commandery.
Section Six: Testimonies of Verification.
Regarding those who practiced the *nien-fo* samādhi, attained rebirth, ascended to the stage of non-retrogression, and left behind auspicious responses in the world: if...
They are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and its fine motes of dust, beyond all calculation. What is recorded in the biographies constitutes but one or two out of ten million;
yet by citing these one or two examples, one can understand the vastness of the ten million. This allows students to admire the former practitioners and take them as models.
By establishing vows based on right faith and engaging in cultivation, progressing ever forward without ceasing, then now—
Those who practice these samādhis are all superior practitioners who have purified their lands and attained non-retrogression.

In the *Sūtra on the Rebirth of Bodhisattvas in the Land of Immeasurable Life*, Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "In this world, how many bodhisattvas will attain rebirth in the [Land of] Ultimate Bliss?"
"Joyful," the Buddha told Maitreya, "in this world there are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land.
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, and each is equal to you, Maitreya."
Countless bodhisattvas of minor practice and those who have cultivated few meritorious deeds shall all be reborn there.

It is not only in my land that this is so; in other buddha-fields as well—such as the Buddha-field of the Buddha Dūriprabha, where there are eighteen billion bodhisattvas—all shall likewise be reborn.
In the immeasurable buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions, those who attain rebirth are exceedingly numerous and beyond counting.
If I were to explain it in full, I could not exhaust it all.
A verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* concerning Nāgārjuna’s rebirth says: "O Mahāmati, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, in a future age..."
There is one who upholds my Dharma: in the land of South India, there was a bhikṣu of great fame and virtue named Nāgārjuna.
He was able to refute the doctrines of existence and non-existence and manifest my unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma within the world.

Having attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), he was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī). Regarding the three translations of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, this is the seven-fascicle version translated by Śikṣānanda.
In the text, within the fourth fascicle:

Regarding the traces left by Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu—Master Huiyuan was extensively learned in the classics and histories and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. He heard that Dharma Master Daoan was lecturing on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Upon reading the sutras, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He sighed and said, "The divergent theories of the nine schools are all nothing but chaff and husks.
He immediately shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk. He profoundly elucidated the principles of Buddhism. During the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty, he passed through Xunyang;

admiring the purity and loftiness of Mount Kuanglu, the Regional Inspector Huan Yi established Donglin Monastery for him to reside in. For thirty years, he did not let his shadow leave the mountain. Whenever he saw off guests, he would do so at Tiger Creek.
[The region] served as his domain. When Emperor An of the Jin dynasty returned to the capital from Jiangling, the imperial carriage visited Xunyang.

Some advised the Master to go and pay his respects, but the Master cited illness and did not proceed. The Emperor then dispatched an envoy to inquire after his well-being. Xie Lingyun, who was arrogant toward others due to his own talent, was struck with solemn reverence and submitted to the Master’s virtue upon their first meeting.
He dug two ponds, diverted water to plant lotuses, and requested to join the community; however, the Master declined him on the grounds that his mind was too distracted.
He brought them to rest. One hundred and twenty-three eminent monks and great scholars alike renounced the world and its honors to follow the Master in his travels and stay.

Liao Yimin composed a vow, establishing sincerity and making aspirations; throughout the six periods of the day, they practiced meditation and recitation without ceasing, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Consequently, those who cultivate the Pure Land practice have taken the Donglin Lotus Society as their model for all ages.
Thus it was. On three occasions he beheld the sacred countenance [of the Buddha].
Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu cultivated pure deeds with diligence; he resided at Donglin for thirty years. Initially, during the eleventh year...
During this interval, he beheld the forms of the Buddhas three times, yet he did not let others know.

Nineteen years later, on the final evening of the seventh month, while at the Prajñā Terrace, he was just rising from meditative absorption when he suddenly saw Amitābha Buddha filling the void of space.

Within his circular halo were various transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance at his left and right. He also saw the flowing water and its radiance divided into ten [streams].
The four limbs flowed up and down as he expounded the sublime Dharma. The Buddha said, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you.
Seven days from now, you shall be born in my land. He also saw Buddhayaśas, Huichi, and Tanshun at the side of the Buddha;
stepping forward, he bowed and said, "My masters intended to be before me—why have you arrived so late? Having thus recognized the timing, [he departed].
Upon his arrival, he said to his disciples, "When I first resided here, I beheld the holy form three times; now I have seen it once more.
It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. On the sixth day of the eighth month of the Bingchen year of the Yixi era, he sat upright and entered nirvana.
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, the Wise One, was at Shicheng Temple in eastern Shan. As he was about to enter nirvana, he said to his disciples:
"I know my life is here; I shall not advance further. Today, I cease my chiseling and snap my strings. He then chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha.
The title of the *Sūtra on the Buddha of Longevity* concludes. It further states: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land with lotus ponds and jewel trees;
though it is easy to travel there, no one does so. Yet when the signs of the Great Vehicle appear, even those who repent for a single thought may attain rebirth.

How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and meditative concentration, whose holy path and power of practice ensure that their merit is not in vain. The characteristics of the Brahma-sound truly do not deceive people."—Zhi Lang.
[The disciple] asked, "I venture to ask: what stage of realization have you entered? After passing away from this life, where will you be reborn? Who is it that we should look up to as our model?
The Master said, "I do not lead a following; I shall simply purify my six sense faculties. By sacrificing myself to benefit others, I shall reach at least the fifth stage [of the Ten Abidings].

As for your question regarding where I am reborn: my teachers, friends, and attendants, all following Avalokiteśvara, will come to welcome me. As for whom one should look up to as a model, have you not heard of Pó..."
"The Prātimokṣa is your Great Master; the four kinds of samādhi are your enlightened guides. He further instructed the *karmadāna*:
"When a person's life is about to end, hearing the sound of bells and chimes increases their right mindfulness. Let it be long and let it be sustained until the breath has ceased.
Why then do you strike the chime only when the body has grown cold? None of the worldly mourning rites should be performed. Having finished speaking, he raised his voice and sang:
The names of the Three Jewels. As if entering samādhi,
the master of virtuous guidance and practice,
the Venerable Shandao of Chang’an during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, visited the Nine Grades Practice Hall of Master Chao of Xihe.
He sighed and said, "This is truly the essential gateway for entering the Buddha-way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish;
only this Dharma-gate allows for swift transcendence of birth and death. From then on, for thirty years, he practiced the Way without ceasing.

With whatever offerings he received, he transcribed one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and painted more than three hundred wall murals depicting the transformations of the Pure Land. Both monastics and laypeople [received...]

As for those who were transformed [by his teachings], their number was beyond calculation. When someone asked whether reciting the Buddha’s name leads to rebirth in the Pure Land, he replied, "According to what you have recited, I shall fulfill your vow.
Every time he recited the Buddha’s name once, a ray of light issued from his mouth. Emperor Gaozong bestowed upon the temple the plaque-name "Guangming" (Radiant Light).
He composed a verse of exhortation for the world that said: "Gradually the skin becomes like chicken-skin and the hair turns white like a crane; Look, look at the gait—how it falters!"
In our declining years, even if gold and jade fill the halls, one cannot avoid decay, frailty, old age, and illness.
No matter how many kinds of happiness you may possess, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the path of direct cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
When the surviving disciples saw the Buddha’s bowl, they followed the Dharma Master of Mount Lu in forming a religious society (*śamgha*). They composed a vow to commemorate this auspicious event;

there were one hundred and twenty-three virtuous members in the society, of whom eighteen were the most eminent, and the Master was the most outstanding among them all. Throughout his life, the Master constantly recited the name of the Buddha.
At that time, he saw the body of Amitābha Buddha, purple-gold in color, appearing before his chamber.

The Duke, filled with both shame and joy, wept bitterly and said, "How may I obtain for myself the Tathāgata to personally stroke my head and clothe my body with His robes? Suddenly, the Buddha stroked his head and drew His *kāṣāya* robe over him.
On another day, he again saw himself traveling through a great pond of the seven treasures, which was perfectly clear and transparent.
It was boundless. Blue and white lotuses were interspersed throughout. A man pointed to the water in the pond and said, "This is water of eight virtues;
you may drink from it. The official drank the water, which was sweet and delicious. Upon waking, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores.

The official said, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have now reached their fulfillment. Who will act as the assembly of the six harmonies to bear witness for me? After a short while, a monk appeared...

The assembly gathered together. The Master faced the honored image, burned incense, and prostrated twice, making this vow: "By virtue of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that Amitābha Buddha exists.
This incense is offered to Śākyamuni Tathāgata; next, it is offered to Amitābha Buddha, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
May all sentient beings be born together in the Pure Land. Having made this vow, he rose.
Having finished, he knelt for a long time until his death.
The manifestation of sound and light was the Buddha.
During the early Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Xiao Kang, a native of Xian-du in Jing-yun, was at Baima [Monastery] in Luoyang.
At the temple, he saw characters within the hall emitting light. He reached out to grasp them; they were the text for converting and guiding composed by Master Shandao.
Kang said, "If I have a karmic affinity with the Pure Land, may this radiance appear once more. Before he had finished speaking, the light flashed forth.
Kang declared, "Though kalpa-stones may be worn away, my vow shall never change. He then proceeded to the portrait hall of Shandao in Chang’an and made extensive offerings.
While he was making offerings, another monk said to him, "If you wish to transform others, you should go to Xinding—this is the present-day city of Yanzhou.
When Hui Kang arrived there, no one recognized him. He then begged for money, luring small children by saying, "Amitābha Buddha is your original teacher;
if you can recite his name even once, I will give you a coin. The children, eager to obtain the money, all followed him.
He urged them to practice mindfulness. After more than a month had passed, those waiting for money grew numerous. Kang said, "Recite the Buddha's name ten times, and I will give you one coin.
In this way, for an entire year, people mindful of the Buddha filled the roads. Subsequently, at Mount Oryong, he established a Pure Land practice hall.

He constructed a three-tiered altar and gathered a great assembly. At midnight, they performed the ritual circumambulation; every time he chanted the Buddha’s name once, the multitude saw a Buddha appear.
[The light] issued from his mouth; as he chanted ten times in succession, there appeared ten Buddhas, like a string of pearls.

Kang said, "Those of you who have seen the Buddhas will certainly attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. The assembly numbered several thousand, yet some did not see them at all. Later, he gave these instructions to both the monastic and lay communities.
"You should now direct your mind toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and cultivate a spirit of diligence; regarding Jambudvīpa, you should give rise to a mind of weary detachment.

Having spoken these words, he emitted several rays of light and suddenly passed away. National Teacher Shao of Tiantai later reconstructed his stupa, and the world has universally regarded him as an incarnation of Shandao.
Chan Master Yongming Yijue practiced the Way on a separate peak.
At the invitation of the King of Wuyue, Zhongyi, he resided at Lingyin Temple for two years before moving to Yongming.
He maintained a daily liturgy of one hundred and eight items, never failing to perform them even for a moment. When students came to inquire about the Dharma, he pointed directly to their own minds.

The Master took awakening as his standard. By evening, he would go to a separate peak to practice the Way and recite the Buddha’s name; he considered this difficult to sustain himself and did not wish to force others to do so.

Nevertheless, those who followed him in secret were always several hundred in number. On clear nights when the moon was bright, the sounds of conch shells, celestial music, and heavenly instruments were occasionally heard in the air.
The King often sighed, saying, "From antiquity, there has never been one who sought the Western Paradise as he does."
This was most earnest; he specifically constructed the Xiangyan Hall to fulfill his aspiration.

Regarding the Master Yongming Shou, the Director of the Netherworld said: "He is the standard for the Chan school and the preeminent figure among those of the Pure Land practice. Thus it was established.
He caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish and exhorted ten million people to cultivate wholesome deeds (*śukla-karman*). At the end of his life, he knew in advance that the time had come;

his *śarīra* relics were arranged like scales upon his body. Once, there was a monk from Fuzhou who circumambulated the Chan Master’s stupa for years. When people asked him the reason for this, [he replied:]...
He then said: "Recently, I fell ill and entered the underworld. Because my lifespan in the world of the living had not yet ended, I was permitted to return to life.

In the left side of the hall, I saw a painted portrait of a monk whom the King paid homage to with great reverence. I then questioned the presiding official: 'Who is this person? The official replied:
'This is Chan Master Shou of Yongming Temple in Hangzhou. There is no one among the deceased who does not pass through the underworld.'"
The judgment was that this person alone had practiced with such diligence as to be reborn directly in the highest grade of Sukhāvatī.
The King, considering this a rare occurrence, had his image painted and honored it with devotion.

Regarding the West Lake Society during the Chunhua era of the Song dynasty: Dharma Master Shengchang of Qiantang resided at Nan Zhaoqing Temple on West Lake and devoted himself exclusively to pure deeds.

He established a society for pure conduct (*śubha-karma*), with the eminent statesman Wang Wenzheng Gong Dan serving as its president. All the scholar-officials who joined the assembly were known as "Pure Ones."

The monastic community consisted of eighty lay associates and one thousand bhikṣus. The Dharma Master pricked his finger and wrote out the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in blood as a solemn vow.
Song Bai, the Director of the Hanlin Academy, composed the inscription for the stele, the gist of which states:
"The Master admired Master Huiyuan and established a society at Mount Lu; he changed the name 'White Lotus' to 'Pure Conduct. While Master Huiyuan lived during a period of decline..."
At that time, those he befriended were for the most part recluses who had withdrawn from the world;

yet, as the Superior Man flourished in an era of peace and stability, those with whom he associated were largely virtuous men holding official rank. Looking forward, there were many renowned scholars; looking back, his role as a bridge across the stream was never-ending.
Yuan Sunhe inscribed the names of the members of the society on the back of the stele. Su Yijian of the Hanlin Academy composed a preface to the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," stating: "I..."

One should spread one’s hair to receive his feet and gouge out one’s flesh to request the Dharma; even for such things, one would not decline, so how much less could I, with my meager writing and shallow learning, feel any regret?

Master Cijue (Fahua), the eminent abbot of Changlu, was proficient in both the teachings and their realization, excelling equally in understanding and practice. He established the Pure Rules for the Chan Forest and composed the *Guijing wen* (Mirror of Precedents).
His *Zuochanyan yi* (Protocol for Seated Meditation) elucidated perfect understanding and prohibited idle talk. Furthermore, he upheld purity and issued admonitions on frugality.

He washed his face and spoke throughout the land, saying: "There is no one who does not take this as a model to broaden the benefit of all sentient beings and swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression.

Nothing compares to the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land. In the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, he gathered a great assembly of monastics and laypeople to establish the Lotus Supreme Assembly.
One night, he dreamed of a man about thirty years of age, wearing a tall cap and white robes, with a refined and beautiful countenance. The man came forward, bowed, and said:

Desiring to participate in the assembly of the *Gongsheng* (Public Victory), he requested that his name be written down. The Chan Master asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Puhui" (Universal Wisdom).
When the writing was finished, he said again, "My elder brother also once had his name entered. The Chan Master asked, "Who is your elder brother? He replied, "Puxian" (Universal Virtue).

Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished. Upon waking, he suddenly realized: "These are the two great Bodhisattvas from the 'Chapter on Leaving the World' (*Lishi jian pin*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*."
Thus, we know that when a follower of the Buddha performs Buddhist deeds and assists in propagating the Buddha’s transformation, they will evoke the secret assistance of sages and worthies.

For those who participate in this assembly, how could it be anything other than a minor cause? Although the name and title of Samantabhadra have been changed, and it is unknown who he is, he is said to be at the head of the two bodhisattvas.

The Imperial Inscription for the Lotus Society (Lianshe) from the Qiandao era of the Song dynasty: Zhang Lun, the Regional Commander-in-Chief of the Two Zhe circuits, vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land;

he exhorted himself with diligent perseverance and focused his thoughts solely upon the Buddha. All members of his household, both old and young, followed his transformation. He excavated a pond and planted lotuses, emulating the establishment of the society at Donglin.
In accordance with this bequeathed intent, he daily led his wife and children to recite the Buddha’s name ten thousand times.

Every year, during the final months of spring and autumn, he would travel to the Pujing Aranya (Monastery) in Wushu to share this practice with those who believe in the Way. Those who saw or heard of it rejoiced and gathered like clouds from all directions.
His Majesty, the Most August Guangyao Shousheng [Emperor Gaozong].
The Emperor personally applied the imperial brush to write the two great characters "Lotus Society" (Lian-she) as a gift. Yuan Lun bowed deeply and ascended to receive them;
these celestial writings and dragon-pen strokes descended from Heaven, their radiant aura brilliant and magnificent, dazzling the eyes of ten thousand people.

This was not merely to be transmitted within Yunlin to magnify his singular encounter, but so that all who behold them throughout the world and in future generations may universally bring them to mind.
The Buddha’s samādhi has ultimately brought about the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi; the benefit it confers is truly beyond measure.
We have respectfully engraved this upon metal and stone, in order to respond to and exalt his magnificent and illustrious mandate.
Regarding the Chan Master Liang Daozhen:

he aspired to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, yet had not yet been able to advance in it. One night, he dreamed that several monks were traveling westward across the sea aboard a seven-jeweled flower boat.
Daozhen asked where they were going; they replied, "We are proceeding to the Land of Amitābha Buddha. Daozhen...

He then sought to join them as a passenger. The boatman said, "According to your intention, who would dare refuse you? However, for the merit of this single day’s practice, one transcends the kalpas of eternity.
Because you have not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and performed the ritual bathing of the monks, your vow is not yet fulfilled;
therefore, you cannot go with us. Upon waking, he was filled with deep gratitude and resolve. From that time forth, he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* day and night.

He did not cease his practice. When he opened his room to bathe the monks, two years later, he suddenly saw a man carrying a silver platform approach and say, "The Dharma Master’s retribution has ended;
you shall mount this platform. On the evening before his death, the people of the district saw a mountain cliff and rock wall.
A thousand torches blazed together in mutual brilliance until dawn. He immediately went to the mountain to inquire about it and learned that the treasure was lost;
was this not a sign of his rebirth?
He vowed to take up the golden platform.
Chan Master Huaiyu of Taizhou was extremely strict in observing the Vinaya. He wore plain cloth robes, ate only one meal a day, and sat upright for long periods without lying down.

He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand times and daily chanted the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times. In the first year of the Tianbao era, he saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas filling the void of space;
a person came bearing a silver platform to receive him. Huaiyu said, "I have spent my entire life chanting the Buddha’s name, vowing—"
He took up the golden platform. Why should it not be so? The assembly of saints then vanished. Yumi redoubled his diligent practice.

After twenty-one days, they appeared before him once more, with extraordinary light filling the room. He said to his disciples, "I have been born in the Pure Land," and he passed away with a smile on his face.
The District Magistrate, Duan Huairan, saw this and marveled at it, composing a verse of praise which said: "My Master, in a single thought-moment, has ascended to the First Stage."
At the Buddha’s country, the *sheng* (flute) appeared twice; there was only the ancient huai tree before the gate, its branches lowered solely to hang the golden platform.
During the Zhenghe era of the Song dynasty, at Xiangfu Temple in Sanqu, the Dharma Master Xianzhang experienced a similar manifestation of spiritual response.

After the burning and destruction of the *Xiánjīng* (Scripture of the Immortals), Dharma Master Tánluán of Bìgǔ during the Later Wei dynasty traveled to Mount Wutai in his youth. Moved by spiritual wonders, he left the household life;

however, his nature inclined toward the arts of speech. Hearing that the Recluse Táo possessed methods for longevity, he traveled a thousand *lǐ* to seek him out and received ten scrolls of the *Xiánjīng*. He said:
"Immortals can certainly be attained. Later, he returned to Luoyang and met Bodhiruci when the latter was three years old.
He then asked him, "In the Western Regions, there are arts for attaining longevity; can they truly ward off aging and prevent death? Bodhiruci smiled and said, "Longevity and immortality—"

"This is my Buddha-way. He then bestowed upon him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying: "If you study this, you shall no longer be born within the three realms, nor shall you again travel through the six paths of existence.
Whether fullness or emptiness, waxing or waning, calamity or fortune, success or failure—none of these shall reach you.

As for your lifespan, it shall be as vast as the sands of the Ganges and as enduring as the kalpa-stone. The number of grains of sand and stones is finite, but the measure of your lifespan is infinite."

"This is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Sengluan was greatly delighted; he subsequently burned the immortal scriptures and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
Despite the changes of cold and heat and the onset of illness, he never slackened even slightly. The Wei ruler admired him and titled him "Divine Luán.
One night, he saw a foreign monk in his room who said to him, "I am Nāgārjuna. I reside in the Pure [Land]..."
"It has been a long time since we last met. Because you share my same aspiration, I have come to see you. Ling asked, "What instructions do you wish to give me?
Shu replied, "That which has already passed cannot be reached; that which is yet to come cannot be pursued. Where does the present dwell? The white colt is difficult to turn back.

Having finished speaking, he vanished. Ling knew for himself that the time had arrived, so he immediately gathered the assembly to offer them exhortations, commanding them to recite the Buddha's name aloud while facing west.
He closed his eyes and passed away. The assembly heard the sound of pipes and strings coming from the west; after a long while, it finally ceased.
Regarding Wei Gong’s Eradication of Sin:

Wei Gong was a monk of Faxing Monastery in Jingzhou during the Tang dynasty. By nature he was arrogant and haughty, treating superiors with contempt and bullying subordinates, and he associated intimately with those of improper character.

When he had a little leisure, he would lecture on the sutras and recite the Buddha’s name, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). However, wine-drinkers and gambling companions flocked to his door;
days passed without him ever failing to engage in such deceptive acts. The temple monk Lingkui was of his kind. A villager mocked him, saying:
"Lingkui has committed every possible sin, and Weigong follows in his footsteps. There are thousands upon thousands of hells, yet neither of you seems weary of being pushed to the front of the line."
He entered and respectfully said: "I have already committed these deeds; my transgressions cannot be escaped.
However, I rely on the Master of the Pure Land who, out of compassion for my sins and evils, has pulled me from the mire and ashes. How could I fall again into the evil realms?
In the second year of the Qianning era, as Gong was nearing death, Kui returned from outside and saw several young attendants of extraordinary appearance, their clothing bright and clean. Kui...
He asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from the West. The Venerable Huigong asked, "Where is your monastery located?
Kui pointed toward the temple to show him. One man took a golden pitcher from his bosom; within the pitcher was a lotus flower, its petals closed like a fist.

In an instant, it opened wide until it was as large as a basin or bowl, its radiance shimmering and reflecting one another. They galloped swiftly toward the temple, but suddenly the man vanished. Kui then arrived at the temple.
Upon hearing the sound of the bell, the assembly gathered together and learned that Gōng had died. A strange light enveloped his chamber, and the sound of celestial music was heard.

Xuānkuī recounted what he had witnessed, and everyone was struck with wonder. Xuānkuī himself maintained his reputation for integrity and moral discipline, and thus became renowned as one of lofty character.
Xiongjun entered Míngtáng during the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty.
A monk from Chéngdū, Xiongjun’s courage and bravery surpassed those of ordinary men. He did not observe the monastic precepts, yet he was skilled at lecturing and preaching.
Whatever offerings and benefits he received, he used for improper purposes. He once left the monastic life to join the military, but soon fled due to the chaos of war. Furthermore, he...
The monk, who had strictly maintained his reputation and integrity, was generally one to fear and avoid [the consequences of evil].

However, upon hearing the sutra teaching that reciting the Buddha’s name even once extinguishes the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, he was filled with great joy and said, "I am fortunate indeed to have this. Although I have been unable to cease my offerings at the incense burner and strike the bell with loud voice and prostrations, my deportment and every movement are never without mindfulness.
Even upon my mat or between the walls of the latrine, I invariably turn away from the west. I consider that among the people of this world, none cultivate themselves as I do.
This is the purification of karma. Zhiyi of Siming revived the Great Teaching of Tiantai after it had fallen into decline, enabling people to see their nature and become Buddhas;
yet he still used this very method to transform others. Thus, it is clear that this profound Dharma-gate must not be discarded.
If one were to say, "Why must one be born there before becoming a Buddha? then by that logic, those who live as householders would likewise not need to leave the home-life.
Furthermore, those whose birth stars fall under Jia or Yi need not necessarily seek out teachers or inquire after the Way. May those who have not yet passed through the barrier take heed of this.
The Pure Land is not a provisional teaching.
Master Huìjué Yù said: "Some claim that the Pure Land is merely a skillful means of the Sage, intended to guide those of dull faculties and transform the vessels of ordinary beings.
If one could transcend directly and enter the stage of the Tathāgata all at once, what need would there be for the power of another?"
The answer is: Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra during the Buddha’s lifetime, and Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna after his parinirvāṇa;
as well as Zhizhe and Zhijue in this land—all of them made vows to be reborn there. Are they all to be considered of dull faculties?

When Śākyamuni, in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, exhorted his father King Śuddhodana and sixty thousand members of the Śākya clan to be born in the Pure Land, were they all to be considered merely ordinary vessels? Such individuals...

"Are the sages and worthies of old all inferior to those of sharp faculties and superior capacity today? Moreover, if this is treated as a provisional teaching (*upāya*), what then shall be considered the ultimate reality (*bhūta*)?
The distinction between the provisional and the real does not consist of a single path; were it not for one whose eye of the teachings is clear, how could one discern them?
I address you, O discerning ones: you should believe the words of the Buddha. The retribution for [disbelief] is no light matter; do not treat this with levity. Formerly, Sun Xin...

The Senior Scholar initially harbored doubts on this account. However, when he met with Yang Cigong and discussed the Way with Minister Wang Minzhong, their views were in perfect accord, and his doubts were thereby dispelled.
Both Cigong and Minzhong were Confucian scholars who studied Chan; yet they were now diligently seeking refuge in the Pure Land.
From this, one can know that the Pure Land is not a mere expedient devised by the Sage, but is indeed true Chan.
Regarding the dwelling of his companions:
Chan Master Changlu Yi’s *Record of the Lotus Assembly* states: "When those of initial resolve enter the Way, the power of their forbearance is not yet pure."
One must rely upon pure conditions as a dominant influence. Why? Because in this Sahā world, Śākyamuni has already passed into extinction and Maitreya has not yet been born;
whereas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the World-Honored One Amitābha currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.

In the Sahā world, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta merely look up to their illustrious names from afar; in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those two sublime beings personally serve as one’s supreme friends. In the Sahā world...

In this land, various māras compete to create obstacles, harassing and disturbing practitioners. In the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), amidst its great radiance, there are certainly no demonic affairs.
In the Sahā world, there are chaotic and depraved sounds, and the six colors of seductive beauty abound.

In the world of Ultimate Bliss, the waterfowl and the forest trees all proclaim the sublime Dharma. Their primary retribution is pure; truly, there are no women there. Thus, the conditions for cultivation are fully perfected.
It is not as it is in the West, where those of shallow faith recklessly give rise to doubt and slander. I have often reflected on this:

among the people of this land, there are none who do not weary of the clamor and vexation of the secular home and yearn for the tranquility of the *araṇya*. Thus, there are those who abandon their homes to leave the household life.
Thus, they earnestly offer praise [to the monastic life]. Yet, as for the myriad sufferings of this Sahā world, how could they merely be the clamor and vexation of a lay household?

And as for the leisurely ease of Sukhāvatī, how could it be simply the tranquility of an araṇya (hermitage)? To recognize that leaving home is beautiful, yet not to wish to be reborn [in the Pure Land], is the first delusion.

To toil with hardship across ten thousand *li* to seek out a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to illuminate the Great Matter and resolve the questions of life and death—yet [to fail to do so]... Mi... [text truncated]
The World-Honored One’s physical form, mind, and deeds are supreme; his power of vows is vast and profound. A single utterance of his perfect voice leaves nothing unclarified or unharmonized.
You wish to attend upon a spiritual friend yet do not desire to see the Buddha—this is your second delusion. In the vast assemblies of monasteries, all delight in dwelling there.
To wish not to rely upon the small assemblies of the Way-grounds while the number of those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss who are in their final birth before Buddhahood is exceedingly great,
and to desire to frequent groves of sages while not admiring the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude—
this is the third delusion. Furthermore, the people of this land have a maximum lifespan of no more than a hundred years, yet they are beset by childhood ignorance and old age.
In old age and illness, one is beset by successive afflictions; for the greater part of one's time, one dwells in a state of stupor and sleep.

Even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "shading of the corpse," and Śrāvakas still lack clarity upon emerging from the womb. Thus, of every inch of jade and every moment of time, nine-tenths are lost before one attains the stage of non-retrogression—this is truly a cause for heart-rending anxiety.
In the Western Land, lifespans are immeasurable; once one takes refuge within a lotus calyx, there is no further suffering of death. Such is the contrast.
Continuing without interruption until reaching Bodhi, one may be said to have attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), which can certainly be expected.
Yet, while the fleeting moments of the Sahā world flow on, one remains lost in the Pure Land for a long time; this is the fourth delusion.

Only when one’s rank is non-retrogressive and the fruit is the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), such that one is without desire amidst desires and not defiled while dwelling in the dust of the world, can one truly give rise to the [unconditioned].

Based on loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they exercise compassion that realizes the same essence as all beings; they enter back into the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*) and blend their light with the five turbidities.

Yet, those who have heard only superficially or possess limited wisdom, or who merely associate with minor roots of goodness, claim to have forever emerged from the four currents of existence and transcended the ten stages (*bhūmi*). They thus disparage the Pure Land.

To remain attached to this Sahā world, to close one’s eyes and return empty-handed, to wander aimlessly as if side-by-side with oxen and horses, and to follow in the footsteps of hell-beings—failing to realize who one truly is while claiming to compare oneself to a Bodhisattva of Great Power—this is the fifth delusion. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land. To fail to believe the sincere words of the Buddhas and to have no wish to be reborn in the Pure Land is [the sixth delusion].
Is this not utterly deluded?
The Buddha’s words are not false.
It was during the era of Emperor Wu (Kang Senghui) that the Dharma Master Kang Senghui first arrived at Jianye. The Lord of Wu, Sun Quan, questioned the Great Officer:
Kan Ze said, "How can the principles of the Buddha-dharma compare to the teachings of the Confucians and Laozi of this land? Kan Ze continued, "The Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle;
when compared with that of Confucius and Laozi, it is truly beyond comparison. Why is this? Confucius and Laozi established their teachings based on Heaven."
In exercising governance, one dares not disobey Heaven; when the Buddhas establish their teachings, the devas follow them in practice, dares not disobey the Buddha.

To speak from this perspective, it is clear that [the two] are truly not comparable. For what Confucius knew was merely the affairs of a single region, whereas the Buddha encompasses the entirety of the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, reaching to the furthest limits of empty space and all the lands as numerous as atoms—there is nothing within them that he does not know.

The teachings of Confucius and Laozi concern only the affairs of a single lifetime. The Buddha, however, exhausts the past and reaches the furthest limits of the future across kalpas as numerous as the atoms of infinite worlds;

therein, there is nothing he does not clearly perceive. This Dharma-gate of the Pure Land was proclaimed with a single voice by the broad and long tongue-mark of Śākyamuni Buddha, together with all the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
How can one, with the narrow and inferior knowledge and views of an ordinary person— sitting in a well and gazing at the sky—
give rise to doubt and fail to believe the words of truth proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata?
On Right Faith in Cause and Effect, Longshu said:
"If you wish to know the causes of your past lives, look at what you are experiencing in this life; if you wish to know the fruits of your future lives, look at what you are creating in this life.
Try observing those around you now: among the rich and poor, the noble and humble, the long-lived and short-lived, and the happy and suffering—what have they done to bring about such conditions?
Honor and disgrace, fortune and calamity, differ in their various forms. Although these are said to be the decrees of Heaven, how could Heaven act with partiality toward individuals?

It is because the actions performed in previous lives were different that the retributions received in this life are likewise different; Heaven merely presides over them. This is just like the government offices of the world:
how could they impose rewards or punishments upon people without cause? They do so only because there are those who have merit and deserve reward.

If one has committed a transgression, they must be punished; this is simply the governance of the Lord. Because such a person cannot be purely virtuous, they cannot receive purely auspicious retributions.
Thus, there are those who possess wealth and status yet meet an early death, while there are those who are poor and lowly yet live long lives.

Their resulting karmic fruits follow exactly what was done, like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound; there is not even a hair’s breadth of error. This has never been otherwise.
To sow hemp and obtain beans, or to sow millet and obtain grain, is simply because what is sown at the time of planting is small, while what is harvested at the time of reaping is great.
The commission of good or evil deeds is extremely slight, yet the retribution for receiving calamity or fortune is exceedingly vast. Thus it is said: "In spring one sows a single grain of millet;
in autumn one harvests ten thousand seeds. When a person performs good or evil in life, the resulting retribution is likewise so. This is indeed the natural law of transformation.
This is the principle. If the causes and effects of the mundane world are thus, then the causes and effects of those who cultivate the supramundane are likewise so.
How could one not believe in the Pure Land and practice accordingly?
Master Baiting said:
"Those who cultivate the practice of purity are always numerous, yet those who find its gate and proceed directly are few.
Those who discourse on the Pure Land are always numerous, yet those who grasp its essentials and point directly to it are perhaps rare. I have never heard of anyone [who... with such..."

Regarding those who obstruct and conceal themselves for the sake of preaching: that which most obstructs oneself is nothing other than craving; that which most conceals oneself is nothing other than doubt.
If one ensures that these two mental states—doubt and craving—are entirely without obstruction, then the single gateway to the Pure Land will never be interrupted.
The preface to the *Ten Doubts Treatise* by Wuyi says: "If craving is not heavy, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī."
Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty established a religious society on Mount Lu. He summoned Yuanming because he valued his ability to attain realization and sever worldly attachments;
yet he rejected Xie Lingyun because his mind was muddled and his thoughts could not be focused.
Is this not precisely because these two individuals represented the essential gateway to the Pure Land?

Regarding the falsity of body and mind, the Tang State Councilor Pei Xiu said: "O Great Assembly, that which you have constantly taken for 'my body' since beginningless time is a body formed by the provisional conjunction of earth, water, fire, and wind.
It assembles and disperses in an instant; it belongs to the category of impermanent phenomena and is not my true body. Great!

Since beginningless time, that which the multitude has constantly taken to be their "mind" is merely a mind of objective conceptualization and adventitious dust—a false and deluded mind that arises and ceases momentarily, belonging to the category of impermanent phenomena; it is not my mind.
My true body is this perfect, empty stillness; my true mind is this vast, numinous awareness. This empty stillness and numinous awareness constitute the divine function.
Sovereign, its nature contains myriad virtues, and its essence is free from a hundred negations. Like the pure lunar disc, it is perfectly full and without defect;
yet, shrouded by the clouds of delusion, one does not realize it oneself. Once false delusions are removed, the true mind is inherently pure.
The Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings—this mind of mine and theirs—are threefold non-different. This is the very substance of bodhicitta. To abandon this and...
To recognize [this] as recognition: this foul body and its deluded thoughts die and are reborn with every passing moment.
To suffer side by side with birds, beasts, and other such creatures—how could one who calls himself a man not feel shame?
Regarding the mutual causality of lust and killing, the *Longshu Jingtuwén* (The Text on the Pure Land of Longshu) states: "Food and drink, and men and women, are the great desires of human beings.

To restrain them as if they did not exist makes one a sage; to moderate them without indulgence makes one a worthy person; to indulge them without moderation makes one a base fool. This is because..."

Second, it is the locus where karma is created; they further assist one another in its arousal. For when food and drink are abundant, the blood and qi flourish, which causes lustful desire to increase.
When lustful desire increases, it conversely damages the blood and qi, necessitating reliance on food and drink for replenishment.
If both can be reduced and moderated, this is the way to settle the body and prolong life. Master Cijue said: "For humans, food and drink [are essential] daily..."
The moon waxes; coarse or refined, it merely serves to plug the wound of hunger. Once it has passed the three inches [of the mouth], what thing is it?
There is no need to employ the mind to calculate it minutely. The Realist Wild Man says: "Skin envelops bone, flesh, and pus and blood;

yet one forcibly feigns coquetry to deceive people. All heroes of the ten thousand ages have sat upon this; for a hundred years, all alike become dust in a single pit. If one can truly attain this precept, [one is liberated].

If these two matters persist in this world, by what cause would there be illness or premature death? After death, by what cause would there be rebirth in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal?
If you truly desire to seek birth in the Pure Land, you must vigilantly guard against these [transgressions].

Regarding the signs of karma at the time of death, the *Zongjing lu* quotes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says: "For example, when a person is about to die, they see the signs of the retribution they will receive according to their karma.
Those who have committed evil deeds see all that exists within the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts."
In the realm of manifold sufferings, they may see wardens holding weapons, who either rage or revile them as they seize and lead them away;

they also hear the sounds of wailing and lamentation. Or they may see the River of Ashes, the Cauldron of Boiling Water, the Mountain of Blades, and the Forest of Swords, subjected to various forms of oppression and affliction.
Those who have performed virtuous deeds, however, immediately see the immeasurable palaces of all the devas.
The celestial hosts and their various handmaidens are fully adorned with diverse garments; their palaces and gardens are all exquisitely beautiful.

Although they have not yet died, these objects already appear before them. Even when objects do not appear, they are merely false perceptions of the mind regarding the realms of suffering and pleasure, which originally have no source from which they emerge.
Matters of good and evil are summoned only by oneself; until one realizes the single mind, it is difficult to escape.
Regarding the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*):
the *Lingzhi Guanjing Shu* (Commentary on the Lingzhi Sūtra) states that there are those who make a vow, wishing that in all places where they are born before attaining the Way, they may encounter...
The Buddha heard the Dharma and left home as a *kumārabhūta*. Now, it is said that if one is born in the Pure Land, one will spontaneously encounter Buddhas and become a monk.
It is precisely because people do not understand the Pure Land that they harbor such aspirations. Masters of the Chan and Exegetical schools mostly hold this view.
One might test them by saying: "You have already attained birth as a male and become a monk; you ought to seek liberation immediately. Why then do you further seek [this]?"
"O man, you wish to leave the household life once more; is there not some further progress?

When good people assemble in the World of Ultimate Bliss, they are formed through pure karma and are born by transformation from lotus flowers, enjoying sovereign mastery. Such is the birth of those beings who go there."
Together with various superior and virtuous people, they gather in one place and attain non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed bodhi.
This is the true speech proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha]. To speak of it from one perspective alone:

there are indeed famous mountains and excellent lands, secluded dwellings and quiet chambers where no evil sounds are heard; there, virtuous people assemble and the teaching of the Way proceeds without ceasing. Furthermore, there are...
In villages and market towns, gangs of ruffians and evil cliques dwell together; they spend their days intoxicated with wine and addicted to lust, committing every kind of wickedness.
Those who study the Way must certainly abandon evil to follow goodness, draw near to the worthy and keep the petty at a distance;

only then can they enter the realm of the sages and worthies. Thus it is said: "To dwell with those of goodness is like entering a chamber of *zhī* and *lán* herbs"—after a long time, one becomes fragrant.
Yet one does not perceive its fragrance; thus, one undergoes transformation together with it.

Since the various Mahāyāna sūtras exhort and praise rebirth there, encourage intimacy with the noble ones and sages, and enable one to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, how could one fail to believe what the Buddha has taught and practice accordingly?
Upon awakening to his former errors, the Vinaya Master Lingzhi Zhao initially made a vow to always remain in this turbid world of Sahā to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
Furthermore, seeing the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, he read the account of Dharma Master Huibù, who said: "Although this land may be pure, it is not my wish. If only..."
"Rather than enjoying pleasure within the lotus flowers for two kalpas, how much better it would be to save sentient beings in the suffering realms of the three evil paths!

Because he stubbornly clung to this view, he lacked even a slight inclination toward the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Furthermore, seeing those who practiced the cultivation of the Pure Land, he gave rise to contempt and slander.

Later, he suffered from a grave illness; his physical strength and complexion grew feeble, his consciousness became dazed and lost, and he had no sense of direction. Eventually, as the illness progressed—
He was moved to tears and deeply reproached himself for his former errors. Although his aspiration was vast, his strength was not yet sufficient to sustain it;

he therefore consulted the *Ten Doubts on the Tiantai Teachings*. He noted that a bodhisattva at the initial stage who has not yet attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) must never be separated from the Buddha.
Furthermore, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he observed that even an ordinary person bound by all fetters can possess great compassion and vow to be born [in the Pure Land].

In this degenerate age, there is no way to save suffering sentient beings; it is like an infant who cannot be separated from its mother, or like a fledgling with weak wings that can only cling to a branch.
From then on, he completely abandoned all that he had studied throughout his life and devoted himself exclusively to seeking the teachings of the Pure Land school.

For more than twenty years, he never for a moment abandoned his studies; he investigated the principles and teachings in detail, scrutinized works from both ancient and modern times, and suddenly resolved all his doubts, causing his profound faith to deepen further.
The *Ten Kinds of Obstacles and Difficulties:
A Collection of Doubts* states: "There are ten types of people in the world who are unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death.

First, because they may not necessarily encounter virtuous friends, there is no principle for them to be exhorted to mindfulness. Second, because the suffering of karma entangles their bodies, they have no leisure to practice mindfulness."

Third, those who suffer from a stroke and lose the power of speech, unable to invoke the Buddha's name; fourth, those who are deranged and have lost their minds, making it difficult for them to focus their thoughts;
fifth, those who encounter water or fire, leaving them no leisure for sincere devotion; sixth, those who meet with jackals or wolves, finding themselves without virtuous friends.
Seventh, harboring evil thoughts at the time of death, which destroys one's faith. Eighth, eating to excess until satiated, leading to death through stupor and delusion.
Ninth, dying suddenly in the midst of military battle. Tenth, falling unexpectedly from a high cliff, resulting in injury to one’s life and limb.

These ten types of people will, at the moment of death, find themselves utterly unable to practice the Buddha-recitation. Therefore, one must cultivate it in advance so that pure karma may be perfected;
even if difficult circumstances arise, one will certainly receive the Buddha’s protection and deliverance.

Regarding the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Larger Sutra on Amitāyus), concerning the falling away from the City of Doubt, the Buddha told Maitreya: "If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious deeds;
who do not fully comprehend the Buddha’s wisdom, yet still believe in sin and merit, and practice the roots of goodness, vowing to be born in that land..."
The various sentient beings born in that palace have a lifespan of five hundred years. They constantly do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not see the Sangha;

for this reason, they are said there to be "womb-born. Within the city of the seven treasures, like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, once their five hundred years have ended, they finally reach the presence of Amitābha Buddha. Upon hearing the sutra, their minds fail to attain understanding. Because...

Because in previous lives one sought the Way with regret and doubt, believing for a moment and disbelieving for a moment, one should know that those who give rise to such uncertainty lose a great benefit.
In the *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra*, this is called the Land of Indolence; it is precisely the City of Doubt.

In Zhiyi’s *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra*, explaining the "contemplation of the sun," he states that the teaching commands correct contemplation in order to eliminate the doubting mind. The *Miaozong* (The Sublime Text) quotes the *Mahā-*.

The original text states: "If one does not understand the Buddha’s wisdom, then doubt and confusion will arise. Now, by means of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), one contemplates the sixteen objects;

thus, one thoroughly penetrates the Buddha’s wisdom and no longer gives rise to doubt or confusion. Those of middle and lower capacities who rely on this dedication and repent for their karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) possess the seeds of the vehicle and shall be born in that land.
There, they will swiftly behold the Triple Gem, avoid birth in border regions or within a womb, and so forth. — Yang Ci.

The Master said: "Once faith is established in a single thought, you have already cast the seed into the precious pond. As all virtues mutually support one another, you will certainly be born by transformation upon the golden ground.
Do not hastily regret or fall back, nor mistakenly recognize the City of Doubt. Immediately the lotus shall open, and you will attain the path of liberation.
This is the Land of Purity of the Mind and the Amitābha of Self-Nature; within this great radiance, there can never be any demonic interference."
*The Treatise on Resolving Ten Doubts Concerning Rebirth through Ten Recitations* asks: "Sentient beings have heavy karma; how can they attain rebirth through merely ten recitations? The answer is:

"Encountering a virtuous friend at the moment of death is entirely due to roots of goodness from past lives. If one lacked such prior causes, one would not even be able to encounter a virtuous teacher."

Consciousness. By what means are the ten recitations accomplished? If one were to claim that beginningless evil karma is heavy while the ten recitations at the moment of death are light, we shall now compare them by way of three aspects, rather than by the duration of time.
First, when creating evil in the mind, it arises from false and inverted views; whereas for one who recollects the Buddha, it arises from a spiritual friend hearing of Amitābha Buddha.
The name arises from true merit; how can one falsehood be compared to one truth?
It is like the sun’s light briefly reaching a dark room ten thousand years old—how could the long-accumulated darkness fail to be extinguished?

Second, at the time of committing offenses through conditions, they arise from a mind of delusion and darkness conditioned by false objects; whereas the mind that recollects the Buddha arises from hearing of the Buddha.
The names and titles of their merits arise from the mind directed toward unsurpassed bodhi. How could one true and one false be compared?

It is like a person struck by a poisoned arrow; though the shaft is deep and the venom is agonizing, wounding the flesh and breaking the bone, the moment they hear the drum of the medicine that eliminates it, the arrow is extracted and the poison removed.
How could the depth of the shaft and the severity of the venom prevent its removal? Third, this is for the sake of resolution.
When one commits a transgression, there is an interval and a subsequent thought; when one recollects the Buddha, there is no interval and no subsequent thought, and thus one immediately passes away.

Because the wholesome mind is so intense and sharp, one is reborn [in that state] instantly. It is like a great rope ten spans wide that a thousand men cannot restrain, yet a youth brandishing a sword divides it in two in an instant.
Or again, it is like a pile of firewood accumulated for a thousand years that is consumed by a single bean-sized spark.

Fire consumes everything in a short time. It is like a person who has cultivated the ten wholesome deeds throughout their life and ought to be reborn in heaven, yet at the moment of death gives rise to a single thought of resolute wrong view;
they immediately fall into the Avīci Hell. Because evil karma is deceptive and the mind is so fierce and sharp.

If even [the mere thought of] "I am able" can displace the wholesome karma of a lifetime and cause one to fall into the evil realms, how much more so when, at the moment of death, one recollects the Buddha with a fierce mind;
how could such genuine and uninterrupted wholesome karma fail to displace beginningless unwholesome karma and enable rebirth in the Pure Land?

Regarding the failure of minor good deeds to arise, Master Yungming Yi of Mount Guoshan’s *Amitābha’s Western Provisions* states: "Observe that in the world, people's minds for doing good are light, while their minds for doing evil are heavy.
How, then, can they be reborn in the Pure Land? Please verify this by examining present-day affairs. One's attitude toward a Buddha image is not as [respectful] as it is when meeting [a person]."
The great guest’s reverence and caution are such that he studies the scriptures and the Dharma less diligently than he exerts himself in seeking wealth and profit.

When censuring others, his breath is coarse and his speech is slick; when praising them, his breath is sluggish and his words are stilted. Or, if someone hates him, he conceals that person's virtues and broadcasts their faults.
If you hate others while loving yourself, you will conceal your shortcomings and exaggerate your virtues. You may accumulate evil deeds and become resentful when others speak privately of them;
or you may perform slight acts of goodness and harbor bitterness that no one recognizes them. Regarding evil matters, you may secretly spend a thousand pieces of gold yet remain silent about it;
yet when bestowing a single meal upon a virtuous person, you immediately boast of your own merit. All such mental states will cause you to sink into the miserable realms. If you wish—

If one seeks birth in the Pure Land with even a small amount of merit, is it not difficult? According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra), those of the Two Vehicles are not born there;
however, those of the middle grade in the three ranks—by maintaining the precepts, performing good deeds, and making the vow to be reborn there—attain the fruit of a Śrāvaka.
The *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra* states: "That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats.

If this is so, why does Vasubandhu’s treatise state that those of the two vehicles do not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]? One should know that these individuals originally possessed the Mahāyāna lineage;
having regressed from the Great Vehicle and remained in the Small Vehicle, they now hear the Great Dharma once again. Thus, their past seeds have now ripened, and they have made a vow.
Regarding rebirth and the provisional realization of the small fruits: one should know that in the pure realm of Sukhāvatī, the numinous birds proclaim the Dharma;

they are not born as a result of karmic retribution for transgressions. Although there are celestial Māras, they all protect the Buddha-Dharma. Thus, even if one realizes the fruits of the Two Vehicles, how could one still cling to the Lesser Path? The *Miaozong* states:

"The treatise speaks from the perspective of the fundamental and the initial, referring to the state of abiding during the stage of 'smallness,' and therefore says there is no birth. The Sūtra speaks from the perspective of the present."

It was taught toward those of great capacity; therefore, they attain birth [in the Pure Land]. Because they have turned their minds, they attain birth; because of their habitual practice, they realize the Small Vehicle.
Although they know the Great Vehicle, they realize the Small; yet, they do not cling to partial truth as the ultimate, and before long they will realize the Great.
To clarify the names of the Sages:

the Sanskrit term *namo* is translated here as "taking refuge" (*gui-ming*). The Sanskrit term *Amitābha* is translated as "Immeasurable Life" (*Wú-liàng-shòu*) and also as "Immeasurable Light" (*Wú-liàng-guāng*);
these are instances where the multiple meanings are not translated. The Sanskrit term *Buddha* is translated as "The Awakened One" (*Jué-zhě*), meaning one who has attained ultimate truth.

This is awakening. In the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, it is taught that by single-mindedly upholding the Name for one day up to seven days, one can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas;
this refers precisely to these six characters of the sacred Name. The Buddha’s Name is most concise, yet its merit is immeasurable;
it enables ordinary beings of the five turbidities to ascend to the stage of non-retrogression—what is called that which is difficult for all the world to believe.

This is the Dharma. According to secular tradition, during the days when Śākyamuni was in the world traveling to convert beings, he arrived at a lay residence and saw an elderly couple who were counting out one *dǒu* of grain while reciting the Buddha’s name.

They had recited the name of the Amitābha Buddha—identical in name and identical in title—three million six hundred thousand billion, one hundred and eleven thousand nine thousand five hundred times. When compared to the measure of grain, their count exceeded it.

The *Bao wang lun* (Treasure King Treatise), the *Wang gu jue yi ji* (Ancient Collection for Resolving Doubts), and the *Long shu jing tu wen* (Pure Land Text of Longshu) all record this teaching and exhort people to recite it.

However, since it is said to be the Buddha’s word, it must appear within the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*). As it does not appear in any of the sutras or treatises, one cannot follow its practice, and so forth.
[Commentary: According to this collection, within the section on the Dharma-gate of Practice, there is a statement that it is based on a sutra.]
In the *Sūtra of the Twelve Tathāgatas on Amitāyus*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "The radiance of the Buddha Amitāyus is most supreme;
it cannot be matched by the radiance of any other Buddhas. Therefore, the Buddha Amitāyus is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light and the Buddha of Boundless Light."
The Buddha Who Obstructs Light, and so on, up to the Buddha Who Surpasses the Sun and Moon; these twelve names are all alternative epithets for the single Buddha Amitābha.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, in the section on Śrī-Ābhāsvara’s Perfect Penetration, states: "I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
There appeared in the world Buddhas named the Twelve Tathāgatas of Immeasurable Light, who arose in succession throughout one kalpa.
The last of these Buddhas was named Surpassing the Light of Sun and Moon. That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (and so forth).

This means that in a kalpa prior to the kalpa of the Ganges-sand [eons], there were twelve Buddhas who appeared in sequence within a single kalpa; however, only the names of the first and the last Buddhas are mentioned.
It merely happens to coincide with the *Moheben* (Mahāvaipulya) version. Yet some take the twelve Buddha names from the *Moheben* to be the Buddhas encountered by Śrīkṣetra;
this is erroneous. Although their underlying principle (*li-ti*) is without distinction, their phenomenal manifestations (*shi-xiang*) differ.

Since it is said they appear successively over the course of one kalpa, the ancient Buddhas have long since entered parinirvāṇa; how could they be indiscriminately equated with the Buddhas currently preaching the Dharma?
Indeed. Failing to investigate the intent of the sutras and failing to distinguish between the differences and similarities of the present and the past—how can one be so utterly evasive?
Regarding the image as being the true body itself, Master Zhizhao was once asked: "The sutra states that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are the Dharma-realm body, which enters into all things..."
Within the thoughts of sentient beings, they now fashion images from wood and other worldly materials, taking these as the Buddha;
yet they do not realize this is improper. He replied: "The body of the Buddha is without marks (*animitta*), yet it is not separate from marks.

Because it is without marks, there is not a single phenomenon—whether mundane or supramundane—that is the Buddha. Even the eighty-four thousand marks and the thirty-two major characteristics are likewise [without marks]."
It is not even a mark; how much less so other things? Therefore it is said: "To be free from all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas.
Because they do not depart from marks, there is not a single dharma—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not the Buddha; how much less so the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana)?
Therefore it is said: "One should know that all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma. If one can realize this, then marks are non-marks. Not...
Phenomena are themselves the manifestation of reality. Thus, mountains, rivers, lands, grasses, trees, and atoms; the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence;
and all that flutters, flies, crawls, or moves—all are none other than the substance of the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas.

How much more so for those cast in metal, molded from clay, carved in wood, or fashioned by painting and sculpture—these images adorned with the marks and signs of perfection—are they not uniquely the Buddha? Those who possess wisdom should contemplate these icons: they are but timber, ash, cloth, and glue.

Lacquered, gilded, and painted—these are formed through the conjunction of various conditions. If one seeks among these conditions, they are all worldly things, each possessing its own name and substance;
which of them, then, is the Buddha? Yet, conditions have no fixed characteristics and things have no fixed names.
Since it is designated as "Buddha," every single condition is none other than the essence of the Buddha. How could one abandon these and seek the Buddha elsewhere? Thus, the *Avataṃsaka*...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Physical form is not the Buddha; sound is likewise so. Yet, without departing from form and sound, one perceives the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
If one contemplates in this way, one neither dwells in signs nor departs from signs. Principle and phenomena are of one suchness; the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
Although one faces an image, this is the true perception of the Buddha—the sacred image as a record.
In the fasting quarters, one must not place images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas where ordinary people sit or lie down during their daily lives; this incurs the sin of sacrilege.
When Master Guàn of Zhūān saw students placing images in their fasting quarters, he immediately admonished them, saying: "In your daily activities..."
Regarding ritual propriety: speaking useless words and offering only a modicum of reverence by burning incense does not compensate for the sin of being irreverent and disrespectful all day long.
When Dàtōng Běn Chánshī saw images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in standing or walking postures, he would not dare to sit;

furthermore, he would not eat anything named after fish or meat. Such was his sincere and respectful service, guarding his mind and distancing himself from transgressions. These are the pure regulations.
[This section] admonishes ordinary people against improper conduct: they must pay homage and present superior offerings, replenish the incense, and change the water;

they must not enter the hall without a valid reason, for fear that negligence will diminish their merit and bring about transgression. However, this applies except when one is attending to a person at the point of death who is oppressed by the suffering of illness.

Regarding the practice of visualizing the Buddha’s image and reciting his name to increase right mindfulness and assist those seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, these are not restricted to this specific context.

As for the two modes of cultivation—sudden and gradual—the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas have two types of practice. That which takes emptiness as its object and enters into it is called the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*). That which involves phenomena..."

To practice both [the principle and the conduct] together is called "practicing the practice. Master Daomou’s entry into the Way consists of two aspects: first, entry through principle (*liru*); second, entry through practice (*xingru*).

These are established based on the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*. Some claim that "direct entry" constitutes the sudden (*dun*) and "combined practice" constitutes the gradual (*jian*), but this is not necessarily so.
One should know that what is termed "sudden" and "gradual" within the Buddha-dharma actually resides in the capacity for cultivation.

This depends merely on the depth of one's realization and understanding. To realize that there is no cultivation while cultivating is called "unconditioned practice" (*anabhisaṃskāra-caryā*); it does not mean that one does not cultivate at all.
Furthermore, those who enter directly do so because their faculties are matured, whereas those who cultivate concurrently follow the constant path. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
How could the practices performed across the dust-motes of lands all be gradual? Within the four practices for entering the Way, the third and fourth are the practice of having nothing to seek.
To one who clings to principle, it appears that there is no dharma to be sought; this may be called the ultimate. However, this is merely a refutation of seeking something existent.
As the Sūtra says: "Within that which has nothing to seek, I wish to seek it. The *Avataṃsaka* says: "One should give rise to supreme aspiration and resolve to seek the Unsurpassed."

O Supreme Awakening, how can one dogmatically insist that non-seeking is the ultimate goal? Therefore, the fourth [section] is titled "Acting in Accordance with the Dharma. It cites the *Jingming jing* (Sutra of Purity and Clarity), which says:
"The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings. The Dharma has no self, because it is free from the defilement of the self.
If a wise person can thoroughly comprehend this principle, they should act in accordance with the Dharma. The essence of the Dharma is without stinginess. Regarding...

Regarding body, life, and wealth, one practices the giving of *dāna* with a mind free from stinginess or attachment, thoroughly understanding the three kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and remaining neither dependent nor clinging;
this constitutes one’s own practice. Furthermore, one is able to benefit others and adorn the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*).

As it is with *dāna*, so it is with the other five perfections. To eliminate deluded thoughts, one cultivates the six *pāramitās* while having nothing to practice—this is precisely what is meant by "using non-... [existence].
Abiding in the marks [of practice] and cultivating the six perfections—who could say that one realizes one’s own mind through sudden enlightenment and thus ceases further cultivation and realization?

Regarding the sublation of phenomena by principle, the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states: when a person from Shaozhou asked about the method for practicing the Western [Pure Land], the Sixth Patriarch said, "The Western [Land] is within one's own mind."

Where can one seek the West? If people of the East commit offenses and create karma while seeking rebirth in the West, then if people of the West were to commit offenses and create karma, where would they seek rebirth?
If one is simply able to awaken to their own nature, what could be impossible?
Furthermore, Master Zhi said: "The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant pray to go to the West. The words of these two masters are both based on principle.
The act of "taking away" is likewise medicine for an illness. If one generates understanding merely by following the words, then clinging to the medicine becomes the illness itself.
If one speaks directly from the perspective of ultimate principle, then not a single dharma can be apprehended; what pure land could there be to be reborn in?
Not only is there no pure land, but even one's own mind cannot be apprehended. This non-apprehension is itself non-apprehendable. If this is so, then...
To claim that one’s own mind is the Western Pure Land, or that knowing the mind is Buddha, both result in superfluous growths.

Nevertheless, principle is the principle inherent in phenomena, and emptiness is the emptiness inherent in existence. Precisely at the point where all should be swept away, what prevents the establishment of all dharmas through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land?
Since phenomena are identical to principle, there is mindfulness without mindfulness, and birth without birth.
One who is alive is currently walking on the path of life; they do not cling to words of death.

Later generations fail to understand this meaning and, following the literal words exclusively, give rise to interpretations that slander those who cultivate pure karma. It is like someone traveling by boat across the sea who instead encourages others to travel by land;

failing to accord with the capacity of the recipient, one only increases confusion and delusion. Yongjia said: "To abandon existence and cling to emptiness is likewise a sickness; it is just like avoiding..."
To drown oneself and then throw oneself into fire—is this not so?

The four kinds of pure attachments hold that the Way is neither internal nor external, yet it is not separate from the internal and external. The Way transcends self and other, yet it is not obstructed by self and other; for all phenomena are identical [to it].

Because they are of one essence, "one" is not fixed as one; what hindrance is there to the myriad distinctions? If you comprehend this principle, then the realization of one is the realization of all; the myriad dharmas are all my own self-nature, and there is nowhere one cannot go.

If you take the recollection of a Buddha to be attachment to signs, then the non-recollection of a Buddha would be even more extreme attachment to signs. To explain this by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), there is: [The text continues with the four propositions: 1. There is a Buddha to be recollected. 2. There is no Buddha to be recollected. 3.

There both is and is not a Buddha to be recollected. 4. There neither is nor is not a Buddha to be recollected. Thus it is said: "If there is a Buddha to be recollected, one is attached to signs. If there is no Buddha to be recollected, one is even more attached to signs. Try explaining this using the four propositions. Thus, there is...
"Buddha," "no Buddha," "both Buddha and no Buddha," and "neither Buddha nor no Buddha"—these constitute four kinds of attachment.
To adhere to any one of these is all false view. However, if one can harmonize these four without obstruction, then observing any one of them will result in samādhi.

To cite one example among many, the meaning can be grasped through reflection: the Buddha, by means of his vast power of vows, enables ordinary beings at the very first stage of their resolve to be born in that land and never again fall back;
