yet, some are unwilling to seek rebirth there, preferring instead to endure the cycle of delusion and suffering.

This is precisely what is meant by the saying, "a man starving to death right beside a basket of rice. Bodhidharma said, "The mind must be like a blank wall before one can enter the Way," for the purpose of breaking [through attachments].

Discrimination based on deluded sentiments is likewise a medicine for a specific ailment. If one were to seek directly for a state of no-mind, one would instead incur illness by becoming attached to that very medicine.
The Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures and had attained the fruit of the four dhyānas;

yet, because he associated with evil friends, he falsely claimed that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Nirvāṇa, thereby falling into hell. All of this resulted from his deluded attachment to the emptiness of dharmas.

To deny cause and effect is to invite such a dire retribution. People today do not follow the Buddha’s teachings; they cling to false views as the Mahāyāna and slander the practice of Buddha-recollection as Hīnayāna.
This is precisely to preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and to preach the Dharma as not the Dharma—the grave offense of the Avīci Hell.
How can one escape this? Regarding the discourse on the gain and loss of emptiness, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness to deliver those who are attached to existence; yet some become attached to emptiness itself. This is what the Buddhas [intend].

It is not that [the teachings] are not transmitted; the entire Great Canon of the Teachings is medicine prescribed according to the ailment. One who skillfully employs the medicine will find no illness that cannot be cured;
one who does not skillfully employ it will find even the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) transformed into lethal poison.

Bodhidharma did not establish reliance on words and letters, but instead upheld the direct pointing, which is called the "separate transmission outside the teachings. The Sixth Patriarch said: "These very two characters 'not established' are themselves words."

To utter a single word or phrase of "direct pointing" is already a deviation. For the ancients, in their work of untying the sticky and removing the bonds for students, dispelling doubts, and shattering attachments, their merit was unsurpassed.
One must know that this Way cannot be sought with a mind of intentional effort, nor can it be attained through a state of non-mind;
it cannot be constructed through words and language, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness. It must be reached such that there is absolutely no dependence.
"Leaning" means transcending the emotional and intellectual measures of both the holy and the ordinary; yet it does not rely even upon that state of being utterly without support or leaning.

Only one who transcends the emotional and intellectual measures of the holy and the ordinary is called a man of the Way who stands outside the conventional. Students of later generations engage in arbitrary calculations and perverse attachments, failing to understand the intent of the Patriarchs.
They take the words of the ancients and understand them all as literal truth, believing there is actually a single dharma that constitutes a separate transmission outside the teachings.
They seek only to sweep away all texts, identifying with a state where not even a single dharma exists as their ultimate goal.
Thus they remain perpetually within stagnant water, making their living. If one were to say to them, "Sweep this away of sweeping away," they would be left utterly bewildered.

I understand. Alas, how pitiable! You do not realize that severing the delusive thoughts of the three realms and extinguishing the physical body of the five aggregates leaves not even a hair’s breadth of anything to engage the emotions;
this is merely the view and understanding of the Hīnayāna of the Tripiṭaka.

If you can comprehend the single path of turning back [the mind], then naturally all dharmas will interpenetrate, and you may proceed unhindered upon the living road. Relying on the holy teachings of the Buddha, you should make a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
To pay homage to Amitābha, draw near to virtuous friends, swiftly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression, and extensively deliver all sentient beings—
this is as vastly different from those who cling to the view of biased emptiness and willingly endure saṃsāra without seeking liberation, as heaven is from earth.
To oppose the Classics and criticize the Sages is the way of the ancients. Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; rather, it is defilement that is not permitted.

Take, for example, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which speaks of "giving without abiding in signs. How could this mean that one should not practice giving at all? It is specifically because one [can]...

Cultivating this mind brings one into accord with the principle of the true emptiness of *prajñā*. Although practicing giving all day long, one remains free from all marks (*nimitta*) in order to destroy attachment;
thus, it is said directly that one is "free from marks. To speak exhaustively according to the ultimate principle, one does not even cling to being free from marks.

Therefore, it is said that regarding both attachment and non-attachment, there is no clinging whatsoever. By practicing in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one is free from the attachments to emptiness held by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.

This is because one possesses the view of equality; therefore, it is said that there is no abiding in signs. For all Bodhisattvas practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds, this is invariably the case.
How could it be that one must first practice in a state of vast non-practice before it can be called "non-abiding in signs"?
Now, the single gate of rebirth in the Pure Land is precisely one dharma among the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva, wherein one travels through the ten directions to serve all Buddhas.
Listen. Because one practices in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one realizes that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), and even this signlessness is non-existent.
If this is so, how could it obstruct rebirth in the Pure Land? How could it hinder drawing near to Amitābha?

By riding upon the power of the Buddha’s vows, one swiftly realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*). If one were to dogmatically cling to the view of non-arising as the realization of principle, one would fall into the level of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), clinging to the biased view of emptiness, openly contravene the Buddha’s holy teachings; they oppose the scriptures and misrepresent the Sage—there is no sin greater than this.
They have fallen into error in their declining years.

Sentient beings are deluded; they are addicted to the five desires and do not seek liberation. None among them have yet been able to give rise to a resolute mind, vowing to be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
This remains so even when they encounter enemies and those they hate, suffer the separation from loved ones, or face the signs of old age, sickness, and death.
Pressed by peril, sinking into agony and poison, unable to endure it, one then weeps with sorrow and cries out, taking refuge in the Jewel of the Buddha in hope of escaping death.
Furthermore, those who possess wealth and status often lack the leisure to practice Buddhist affairs;
those who do have such leisure fail to develop faith; and even those capable of faith suffer from an inability to sever their doubts—until they reach a state of utter distress.
Those who resolve their minds [to practice] while suffering often lose the opportunity due to old age.
Thus, one knows that it is no easy matter to give rise to right faith, arouse right mindfulness, and cultivate the conditions for goodness.
Regarding the saying of Layman Longshu:
"Nowadays, those who engage in trade rejoice when they gain two coins' profit for one coin's investment;
those on a journey rejoice when they cover two days' distance in one day. Conversely, they will surely be distressed by the opposite. This is...
One feels sorrow and joy over the minor gains and losses regarding external things.
Yet, while one's own time is limited, it is a great loss when it is wasted and passes away, and one does not regard this as a cause for sorrow.

While the conditions for the Pure Land are difficult to encounter, it is a great gain to have fortunately come to know them, and one does not regard this as a cause for joy. One merely perceives those small losses and grieves over them.
They rejoice; yet, regarding the most significant matters of gain and loss, they remain ignorant. How can their lack of reflection be so extreme?

They do not cultivate the ten methods for transcending faults that the Buddha revealed as the direct path for practice, which would enable all sentient beings to swiftly transcend birth and death; instead, their obstructions are heavy.

There are ten kinds of losses for those who are unwilling to advance in their practice: first, they do not believe the Buddha’s words; second, they do not follow the holy teachings; third, they do not believe in cause and effect;
fourth, they do not value their own spiritual nature; fifth, they do not seek upward progress;

sixth, they do not associate with virtuous friends; seventh, they do not seek liberation; eighth, they willingly endure the cycle of saṃsāra; ninth, they do not fear the evil realms; and tenth, they willingly align themselves with Māra.
Those who practice in contrast to this will obtain ten kinds of benefits and shall forever be free from demonic hindrances.
Master Xuanzang’s *Decisive Clarification on the Right Faith of Nianfo* states: "Some say that at the moment of death, one sees the Buddha emitting light to welcome and lead one away."
"This is a realm of Māra. How is this explained? Answer: "The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states that practicing samādhi may provoke the *skandha-māras*.
The *Mahāyāna-śāstra* and the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* state that practicing samādhi provokes external māras.

These cases all concern those who practice dhyāna through their own power (*svabala*) and who possess latent seeds of māra that are activated by meditative concentration. Provided they can attain clear realization..."
Through this antidote, one accomplishes the noble Dharma; if one follows one's own nature in ignorance, one will be obstructed.
Now, as for the practice of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), one relies upon the power of that Buddha, like being near a sovereign—dare anyone dare to offend?

For Amitābha possesses the power of great compassion, the power of his vows, the power of his majestic spiritual authority (*mahānubhāva*), and the power of his samādhis; he possesses the power to destroy all that is heterodox and the power to subdue all Māras.

[He possesses] the power of the divine eye to see afar, the divine ear to hear from a distance, the thorough discernment of others' minds, and the pervasive illumination of light that gathers in sentient beings.
Since he possesses such powers of merit, how could he not protect those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, ensuring they are free from obstacles at the moment of death?
Furthermore, matters such as the arrival of the golden platform to welcome them originate from the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching), spoken by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha].
If one considers this to be Māra, one is profoundly ignorant.

The *Fanfashi hui zong ji* (Anthology on the Essential Teachings of the Dharma Master) regarding the Perfect Penetration of the Three Powers of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* cites the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, stating that there is rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha.
There are three kinds of power: first, the power of the inherently existing Buddha-nature, which refers to the Tathāgatagarbha within the mind of afflictions;

second, the power of compassionate light that gathers and protects, which refers to Amitābha’s immeasurable radiance gathering and never abandoning those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
third, the power of the *nien-fo* samādhi, which refers to the certainty that by recollecting and mindful of the Buddha, [the Buddha] will appear before one in the present or the future.
One will certainly see the Buddha. These three powers are like three strands of rope joined together to form a great cord, capable of pulling heavy objects.
Furthermore, they are like water, fire, and a mirror: if one holds them toward the sun and uses moxa to collect [the heat], one can obtain fire;
if one holds them toward the moon and uses a lens to collect [the light], one can obtain water. Now, by means of the mirror possessing the natures of both water and fire, the assembly is illustrated.
Birth is the power of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed; that which requires the light of the sun and moon to shine upon it is the power of Amida’s compassionate light to gather beings in;
and that by which the pearl and the moxa can draw forth water and fire is the power of faith and the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
These three things are indispensable; when these three factors harmonize, water and fire are then produced. Thus do the three powers...
Those who rely [on this practice] will certainly be born in the Pure Land.

Regarding the "Lion’s Sinew" bowstring, Master Daochuo of the Tang dynasty’s *Anleji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) asks: "By what causes and conditions can the power of a single recitation of the Buddha's name extinguish all [afflictions]?"

[Question: Is it an obstruction? [Answer: A sutra states: "For example, if someone uses a lion’s sinew to make the strings of a lute, as soon as those strings are plucked once, all other strings are simultaneously severed.
Likewise, if a person cultivates the *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) samādhi within the mind of bodhi, the roots of all afflictions (*kleśa*) are entirely severed and extinguished.
It is also like a person who takes the milk of cattle, sheep, donkeys, or horses..."
Place them in a single vessel and cast a single drop of lion’s milk into it; all the other milks will be transformed entirely into water.
Likewise, if a person cultivates the *nien-fo* samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) within the bodhicitta, all evil Māras and obstacles will pass through directly without difficulty.
The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* states that a boat with stones does not sink. Long ago, there was a king who asked the śramaṇa Nāgasena: "The karma of sentient beings is heavy;
how is it that by merely recollecting the Buddha, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land? Nāgasena replied: "It is like a person who takes a large stone, numbering in the thousands..."

One hundred [yojanas]. Just as one who wishes to cross the great ocean reaches the other shore by the power of a ship, so too are the sins of sentient beings like a massive boulder, while the vow-power of Amitābha is like that great vessel.
Although the stone would naturally sink, it can be crossed because of the ship.
To traverse the sea of birth and death entirely depends upon the Vow-King of one’s own Buddha. At all times, He serves as a virtuous guide, leading one directly to that [Pure Land].
The shore is not beyond one's own mind. Thus, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The fool falls into evil even for a small transgression;

the wise are liberated from suffering even for a great transgression. It is like a lump of iron that sinks in water even if it is small, while iron fashioned into a bowl can float even if it is large."

Upon raising this thought, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) was immediately produced. It asks: "The Western Land is ten thousand billion lands away from here; ordinary beings are weak and inferior.

How can they possibly arrive there? The answer is: "The Western Land being ten thousand billion lands away is spoken only in relation to the physical eyes and the birth-and-death mind-capacity of ordinary beings."
Provided that sentient beings have perfected their pure karma, the mind of meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the mind for receiving birth in the Pure Land.
A single movement of thought is precisely the moment of being born in the Pure Land; thus, a sutra says: "Amitābha Buddha is not far from here.
Because the power of karma is inconceivable, one is born there in a single thought-moment. One need not grieve over the distance. It is also like a person's dream, where the body—
Although one remains on one's bed, the mind, intellect, and consciousness reach other lands no differently than they did during one's lifetime; the same applies to the Pure Land.
As soon as one stirs a thought, one is born there—there is no need for doubt.

Regarding the appearance of images in a mirror, Layman Longshu said: "When sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions recite the Buddha’s name, a single lotus flower arises in the jeweled ponds of the Pure Land, inscribed with their names.
Some may doubt this, so I explain it to them: it is like a pure, bright mirror. When objects [are placed before it], [their reflections appear].
When they come, they appear; how could a mirror have any intentionality? It is simply because it is luminous by nature. Thus it is said:
"As soon as a virtuous thought arises, the precious palace of the heavens is first completed; when an evil notion first sprouts, the fire-city of the underworld is already prepared.
Given this, what is there to marvel at if those who cultivate the practice of purity inscribe their names upon the lotus petals to await their rebirth there? It is but natural.

Someone asked: "If it is said that for one who holds the *Nianfo* (Recitation of the Name) mantra, Amitābha Buddha constantly dwells upon their crown, and that when a practitioner of Pure Land karma approaches the end of life, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas all come to welcome them—given the infinite number of sentient beings, how can [the Buddha] always dwell upon their crowns and always go to welcome them?
I replied: "The single moon universally appears in all waters; the single sun universally shines."
In immeasurable worlds, only turbid water fails to reflect [the light], and overturned basins fail to receive its illumination.
The radiance of Amitāyus Buddha universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions and those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, embracing them and never forsaking them.

That there are those in the world who do not wish to be reborn therein is like turbid water or an overturned basin that alone does not receive the light; how could this be the fault of the sun and moon?

The *Essential Principles for the Repentance Ritual* by the Venerable Master of the Four Clarities states: "In this Sahā world, one does not constantly encounter Buddhas, and adverse conditions are many;

even those in deep stages of realization may still regress. In contrast, those in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) always have the opportunity to behold the Buddha, possessing only supreme [conditions]."
Through these conditions, one attains non-retrogression from the very first thought-moment. Furthermore, by the power of that Buddha’s vows, he universally gathers in all sentient beings;

if one can aspire and seek rebirth there, one will certainly attain it. How much more so when the karmic conditions of good and evil accumulated throughout the past and present come to demand their retribution at the end of one's life?

If, at the time of death, evil thoughts increase and flourish, then all evils will reach completion, dragging one into the evil realms. [Conversely,] if virtuous thoughts prevail at the time of death...

When these increase and flourish, all virtues will be accomplished, leading one to rebirth in the happy realms. Now, since you seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (An-yang), you must adorn yourself with pure karma.
Without the powerful drawing force of the power of aspiration, how could you maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death? Therefore, you must sincerely make this vow.
Having resolved upon the essential vow and desiring rebirth in the Pure Land, one should be single-mindedly earnest.
Master Zhao requested the Buddha’s protection, saying: "Someone asked: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states, 'This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Since the mind is already..."

Question: Why is it necessary to be mindful of another Buddha? Answer: It is precisely because the mind is fundamentally the Buddha that one is instructed to single-mindedly be mindful of that Buddha.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts state: "One must always know for oneself: 'I am a Buddha who has not yet attained completion; the various Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained completion.

Your own mind-Buddha is the Buddha who has not yet attained completion; Amitābha Buddha is the Buddha who has already attained completion. [Regarding] the Buddha who has not yet attained completion...
Those who have long been submerged in the ocean of desire are fully possessed of afflictions and have no foreseeable end to their stay;

those who have already attained Buddhahood have long since realized Bodhi, are endowed with majestic spiritual power, and are able to protect sentient beings. For this reason, all Buddhas exhort one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
this is simply to seek the protection of other Buddhas who have already attained realization, by means of oneself who has not yet become a Buddha. Therefore, sentient beings—

If one does not contemplate the Buddha, the holy and the ordinary will be forever separated, father and son will be estranged, and one will dwell long in saṃsāra, remaining far removed from the Buddha.
Chapter Eight: Refuting Errors.
Ordinary beings are deluded and inverted; they do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom. They take the entire realm of the Buddha to be the realm of Māra, rooted in the view of self. They cling...
To sever attachment to permanence, the sixty-two views, and the one hundred and eight afflictions—there is nowhere that does not involve Māra.
To raise the mind or stir a thought is the work of Māra; to still the mind and eliminate delusion is also the work of Māra. As the Sūtra says:
"In the final age, sentient beings mistake illness for the Dharma; though they exert themselves with diligence, they only increase their various ailments. Now, I wish to clear the path of awakening.
It clears away the thorns and brambles [of heterodoxy] and refutes the evil doctrines of divergent schools; this is the reason for the composition of this work on the rejection of errors.

It is like the state issuing proclamations and commands to punish the good and warn the wicked, aiming for a state where there is no need for punishment—how could it be done for the sake of mere expediency?

In his *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*, the Great Master Tiantai Zhiyi explains the character "contemplation" (*guan*) by means of the threefold contemplation within a single mind, and explains "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*) by means of the three bodies as a single essence. He states:
"By citing the primary [the principal], the dependent is subsumed; by describing the master, the retinue is encompassed. Although there are sixteen contemplations...
To say that the Buddha’s teaching is thus complete means that all sixteen contemplative objects (*viṣaya*) are the perfect and wondrous Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).
Master Yuán of Gūshān on Qiántáng Mountain, relying on the posthumous writings of his teacher, the late Master Qīng, composed the *Kānjùjì* (Record of Revision and Correction) to explain them.

However, he departed from the fundamental school and lost its essential meaning by treating all sixteen contemplations as mere mundane conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), asserting that the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) were unnecessary. The Venerable Zōngzhě of Sìmíng could not bear this and [wrote the *Guānkānjì*].
Jin initially composed the *Rongxin jie* (Explanation for Melting the Mind), and later wrote the *Miaozong chao* (Commentary on the Subtle Pivot) to remedy the corruptions of his time.

His teachings perfectly captured the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and were widely disseminated. Subsequently, Master Shenzhi Yishi and Master Jianming Zhan, both of whom followed [the lineage], turned their backs on their teacher’s doctrines and produced their own writings.
This continued until Master Tōkō Eikyō established a thesis that regarded the *Mohe zhiguan* as...

The contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*) constitutes the sixteen contemplations as views of arising; though they claim to follow the Tiantai school, they fail to grasp the Master’s intent and instead offer divergent theories that are shallow, vulgar, and laughable.

Guishan adheres to the view that principle-contemplation (*li-guan*) is merely a matter of conceptual thought (*xiang*), while Tongjiang restricts the understanding of the sages to the sentiments of ordinary people (*fan-qing*).
Those who study the Buddha-dharma should not fail to examine this carefully.

The Dharma Master Jingjue, who erroneously clung to a biased view of emptiness, said: "In the world, there are those who cite Master Dazhu as saying, 'To abandon defilement and grasp at purity is the karma of birth and death.
And Master Pang said, 'If one abandons afflictions to enter bodhi, one does not know where else a Buddha-land might exist.'"
All these are words intended to dispel attachment; one must not cling to them to disparage the Pure Land.
Furthermore, the teaching that there is neither defilement nor purity is the very meaning of "the mind is itself Buddha. Who among those who receive the teachings of Śākyamuni does not know this?

How can one discard the methods of causal cultivation and realization simply because of discourses on the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Even a Bodhisattva of the Sixth Stage still remains subject to the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).
Even the True Persons of the four fruits of arhatship undergo the death of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*). How can one claim that passing away is eternally *nirvāṇa*?
One must know that from the time a Bodhisattva has not yet realized wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and prior, they constantly cultivate the myriad practices with a mind of emptiness.

Throughout the day they contemplate the Buddha, yet there is no Buddha to be contemplated; throughout kalpas they deliver sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings to be delivered. They temporarily proceed toward the purity of empty flowers.
The earth is provisionally based upon the illusory Amitābha; one shatters the dust and toil of last night’s dream and enters the stage of the city of *gandharva*.
Even until the attainment of Buddhahood, although one’s own practice is dark and silent, the benefiting of others remains manifest.

Therefore, it is compared to a body like a clear mirror, appearing as images according to the various types of beings. People of the world do not inquire into this great meaning, but rejoice only in sudden enlightenment. Directly—
Entering the state of non-arising, one does not contemplate it. Yongjia said:
"If there truly is neither arising nor non-arising, yet one takes up emptiness with such vast openness, I fear that such boundless wandering will invite calamity.

This is similar to the case of those from Yue who practiced archery but could not shoot beyond a few paces, or those from Longxi who studied swimming but instead drowned within the swirling waves. Such companions should not be sought out for study.
Regarding those whose doubts are deep and hindrances heavy, Yang Cigong said: "In this world there are virtuous gentlemen who give rise to three kinds of faithless thoughts.
Those who do not seek rebirth in the Pure Land are especially pitiable. The first is: 'I shall transcend Buddhas and patriarchs; the Pure Land is not a place where I ought to be born. The second is:"
Every place is a pure land; it is not necessary to be born specifically in the West. Third, [it is said]: "The Holy Realm of Ultimate Bliss is a place where we ordinary beings cannot be born.
Now, the ocean of practice is inexhaustible, and Samantabhadra’s vow is to behold Amitābha. Although the Buddha-land may be empty, [the aspiration remains].
Vimalakīrti constantly cultivated the Pure Land; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions praised him with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions shared his resolve to go there.
Try to reflect for yourself: who among us can compare with these holy ones? To say that one is unworthy to be born there—how self-deceptive this is!
As for the patriarch Nāgārjuna, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic record concerning him, and so does the teaching of Vasubandhu.
This is the core principle. The *Wuliangshou lun* contains verses on seeking birth [in the Pure Land], and Ci'en’s *Tongzan* begins by extolling the "Ten Superiorities.

Zhiyi analyzed the principles and clearly resolved the "Ten Doubts. These were all men of supreme wisdom who diligently strove for rebirth there. To claim that birth is not necessary is nothing short of self-contempt.
Even the fiery chariots of hell can be extinguished; even a boat with stones will not sink. As for those who manifest immediate karmic rewards, none are more striking than Zhang [Daoling].
By ten recitations, one may transcend to a superior realm. For those entering hell, none can do so more swiftly than Xiongjun, who was restored to life and realized the wondrous cause.
The transgressions of worldly people need not necessarily be like this; to say that one cannot be reborn—how self-abandoning is that!
Deceiving oneself, being self-conceited, and abandoning one's own spirit, one flows into the cycle of saṃsāra. Whose fault is this?

Regarding those who preach deceptive and false doctrines, National Teacher Wuye Dada of Fenzhou said: "Those in the world today who understand Chan and understand the Way are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Numerous teachings have been spoken by the Buddhas, yet if there is even a speck of dust of thought not exhausted, one cannot escape saṃsāra;
if there is even a single thread of a notion not forgotten, one will entirely fall into decline.

Those of such a kind cannot even recognize the karmic fruits for themselves, yet they falsely claim to benefit both self and others, considering themselves superior to all preceding masters. They merely say that everything before their eyes is nothing but the Buddha-work. To raise [this point]...

Every footstep is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Yet, when examining their habitual practice, they are not even equal to a single ordinary person who observes the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action.
When observing their speech, they disparage the *śrāvakas* and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages. Now, the supreme flavor of clarified butter (*sarpis*) is that which is prized by the world.

Encountering such people as these turns [even the Dharma] into poison. Even if one’s talent rivals that of Aśvaghoṣa and one’s understanding equals that of Nāgārjuna, one may only avoid losing the human body for one or two lifetimes;
yet at the moment of death, even a hair’s breadth of the dualistic conceptualization of "saint" and "ordinary person" will not have been exhausted.
Not even a speck of thought has been forgotten; following that thought, one takes birth.

With the five aggregates—light or heavy—one is entrusted with a physical form within the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse, or is scorched and boiled in cauldrons of boiling water and glowing coals. All former memory, recollection, and understanding are lost at once.
Returning as before to the state of ants, and starting again from the beginning as mosquitoes or gadflies, though these were once virtuous causes, they now invite such evil retribution.
Master Yongming Yanshou Jingjue said: "I deeply lament that in this degenerate age, people falsely claim to practice Chan, studying only empty posturing while possessing no real understanding at all.
Step by step they walk in existence, yet mouth after mouth they speak of emptiness; they themselves do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma."

Furthermore, they teach others to deny cause and effect, claiming that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi, and that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder Prajñā.
Such people encounter the laws of the state while alive and fall into the Avīci Hell after death;

having undergone the sufferings of hell, once their karma is exhausted, they enter the realms of animals and hungry ghosts for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, with no prospect of liberation unless they suddenly turn the light back upon themselves in a single thought-moment.

Thus, one turns what is heterodox into what is correct. If you do not personally repent, personally regret, personally deliver yourself, and personally cultivate, then even if all the Buddhas were to appear, there would be no way for them to save you;
you have not attained what you claim to have attained.
Zen Master Yuanwu said: "There is a class of people who say, 'Originally there is not a single thing;

one simply drinks tea when meeting with tea and eats rice when meeting with rice. This is a great falsehood—to claim what has not been attained as attained, and what has not been realized as realized.
When they see others speak of mind, nature, the profound, or the wondrous, they immediately dismiss it as mere idle talk, claiming that originally there is nothing at all."
This matter may be called "one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. They have been struck down within the realm of non-action;
they do not even bow to the Buddha nor burn incense. It may seem so, yet it is fundamentally not right. As soon as one questions them, it seems as though they have reached the ultimate limit;
yet as soon as one presses them, they fall apart in seven pieces and eight fragments. They sit in a state of empty stomachs and haughty hearts. And when the third day of the twelfth month arrives—
Ten days have passed; changing hands and beating one’s breast is already too late.

Regarding the *Taisi Xielun* (Discourse on the Deviant Theory of Embryonic Respiration), Zen Master Yuanwu said: "Alas! I see a certain class of blind, wild fox progeny who have never even dreamed [of the truth]."

The Patriarch, however, falsely transmitted the claim that Bodhidharma passed on *tāixī* (embryonic respiration) to others, asserting it was "the transmission of the Dharma to save deluded sentiments.
He cited examples such as National Teacher An, Zhaozhou, and others from previous years who all practiced this breath-control.

Furthermore, he boasted that the single shoe of Bodhidharma and the empty coffin of Puhua were both proofs of the efficacy of this art, leading eventually to the complete shedding of the physical body. Thus he claimed—

To claim that their form and spirit are both wondrous, to gaze at one's shadow on New Year’s Eve, to call out to the "host" to divine the passage of days and months, to listen for the watch-tower drum to verify the jade pond, or to peer into the light of the eyes as a means to transcend birth and death—this is truly a deception of the common folk.
It is a fabrication of falsehoods that invites the derision of the high-minded. Let me briefly explain Zhaozhou’s *Song of the Twelve Hours* and Layman Pang’s *Verses on Turning the River-Cart*.
They instructed one another in secret, transmitting and upholding [the teachings] in order to seek longevity and ensure their own physical survival.

When they eventually passed away, those who were bold, heroic, and exceptionally brilliant—those who engaged in lofty discourse and grand sophistry and looked down upon the Patriarchs—often believed them. Thus, they attempted to paint a tiger but ended up producing a wildcat.

When those with true discernment perceive this, they see that those within the realm who study this [teaching] are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds. Those of lofty insight and far-reaching vision do not follow such complacency;

fearing that those who have newly resolved their minds may not yet have entered the profound depths, they worry that such individuals might encounter those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who lead them into this forest of false views.
Once a single error occurs at the end, one will sink forever without the possibility of turning back. This current flows ever more widely, and none know how to stem it.
I have therefore uttered these explicit words, so that those with aspiration may discern the gate of great liberation and together enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) which is non-arising.

Regarding silent illumination (mozhao) heterodox Chan, Zen Master Zhenjing Wen said: "In these times, there is a certain class of people who cling to the notion that 'ordinary mind is the Way' as the ultimate principle.
They say, 'Heaven is heaven; earth is earth; mountains are mountains; waters are waters; monks are monks; laypeople are laypeople.'"
In the secular calendar, a "large month" has thirty days and a "small month" has twenty-nine; both are merely like grass clinging to trees—unknowing and unawakened, one is led straight into delusion.

Miaoxi said: "Donglin Zhaojue took 'ordinary and effortless' as his standard, not establishing views or knowledge, nor seeking profound enlightenment through intellectual understanding; instead, he used the seeing of nature by all Buddhas and Patriarchs [as his path]."

This Dharma gate is established to refute those who slander the former sages and leave future generations deaf and blind—those who have no sinews in their eyes and no blood beneath their skin, who follow the crowd in their inverted views while remaining complacent and unaware; they are truly to be pitied. The *Nirvana Sutra* says:
"Sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age, though seeking virtuous friends, may encounter those with false views and fail to attain correct awakening; this is called being 'external' (*bāhya*)."
The nature of the Way-seeds (mārga-jāti) and the errors of false teachers are not the fault of sentient beings;
how could this be empty talk?

Regarding the "Secret Formulas for Longevity," the Layman of Longshu said: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are ten classes of immortals (*ṛṣi*) who live for millions of years and dwell in profound [seclusion].

Mountains. When their merit is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth once more because they have not realized the true nature (*tathatā*). Thus, they share the same name as the "seven destinies" (*sapta-gati*) of the sentient beings of the six realms.
Among those in the world who study the arts of the immortals, not one in ten thousand succeeds;

and even if they do succeed, they cannot escape the cycle of rebirth because they remain attached to the physical form and spirit (*rūpa* and *manas*), being unable to relinquish them. Furthermore, these physical forms and spirits are merely manifestations within the true nature.
Forgetful thoughts are all unreal. In recent centuries, those who attained the rank of Immortal were only Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin.
Yet those who studied under Zhongli and Lü have numbered in the millions; among my own personal acquaintances, such individuals were likewise not few.
Yet they have all died and been buried beneath the earth; not a single one has been seen ascending to heaven in broad daylight. If you wish to seek long life, nothing compares to [this method].

Regarding the Pure Land, they do not know to cultivate it, yet instead study the arts of the immortals. This is like discarding a beautiful jade gem before one's eyes to seek an unobtainable piece of *wǔfū* stone;
is this not delusion? The Layman of Mount Xiang in the Tang dynasty composed a poem for the Mountain Man Wang, which says:

I have heard that you have reduced your sleep and food, daily listening to the discourse of the immortals. You wait in secret for an extraordinary person, secretly seeking the secret formula for longevity.

But what is long is fundamentally contrasted with what is short; one has not yet departed from the tracks of birth and death. Even if one were to attain longevity, it could only serve to surpass premature death.
The pine tree withers after a thousand years; the hibiscus flower fades in a single day. In the end, they are both identical to empty space; why need one boast of years and months?
Peng and Shang differ only in their duration, yet in birth and death there is ultimately no distinction. It is better to study non-arising; where there is no arising, there is no ceasing.

For those practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] who negate cause and effect, whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, they all comply with the holy teachings and entirely accord with the Buddha’s mind.

If it were the case that generating a thought or stirring a thought through mindfulness of the Buddha constituted deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then the cessation of the mind and the absence of thought would likewise constitute deluded conceptualization. *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*...

The Sūtra says: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere reflection of the discrimination of dharma-dusts.
If even mindfulness of the Buddha is considered a fault because it involves conditioned phenomena, then those who cling to emptiness suffer from an even greater affliction.
Yongjia said: "To reach for emptiness while disregarding cause and effect leads to a vast, boundless state that invites calamity; to abandon existence and cling to emptiness is a sickness."

It is likewise so; it is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire. If one considers seeking another Buddha externally to be a failure to reach the truth, then clinging internally to one's own mind is an even greater failure to reach it.
Changsha said: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, simply because from of old they have identified with the spirit.
This is the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas; the deluded call it the 'original person. If [one acts] thus...
To seek a separate pure land is a biased view; however, those who cling to the present moment as being the pure land commit an even greater error.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that those who fall into the path of Māra all point to what is immediately before them as the Buddha-land, claiming there is no other pure abode nor the golden marks [of a Buddha].
They are fond of saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are...
This is bodhi. Both the disciples and the master fall into royal calamity; deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

If one takes the cultivation and realization of "existence" to be a provisional teaching, yet clings to the cultivation and realization of "non-existence," one falls into the ranks of the external paths (tīrthikas), and the disaster is even more severe.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Such a person initially does not realize they are possessed by a māra, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa."

This refers to those who claim that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment; who, even in their hearts, hold the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of lower stations;
who do not pay homage to stūpas and temples; and who destroy scriptures and images, claiming they are merely made of gold, copper, clay, or wood.
To fail to show reverence for one's own physical body—which is truly eternal—and instead to venerate earthen and wooden images is truly a perversion.

Those who deeply believe in this [perversion] will follow it by destroying [the true body], burying it in the ground; thus they mislead sentient beings and fall into the Avīci Hell. The Buddha’s words on this matter were repeated with great earnestness.
Should one not believe this?
The Great Wisdom Vinaya Master (Dazhi Lishi) said:
"Among those in the world who study Buddhism, there are none at the outset who do not say that they do so for the sake of the matter of birth and death."
Alas! When moved by fame and profit or muddied by worldly conditions, they set aside the great matter of birth and death without discussion.
Or, when questioned by others, they evade with pretexts and excuses, unable to reach a resolution; or they say, "There is no need to ask about this."

Some say that knowledge is not required; some say that when the talisman arrives, one simply carries it out without making calculations; some say that one takes birth wherever appropriate, entering and exiting with ease;
others say that for now, one will be born into a family that is neither high nor low, and again as a male body.
Some say one must "hold fast to the spirit" so that when the signs of good and evil appear, one does not follow them; some instruct one to wait in anticipation to know the moment [of death];
some teach one to "seize the yin" at the point of death; some say that while the hundred bones disintegrate, a single entity remains eternally spiritual;
others say that when the form disperses and the breath vanishes, one returns to quiescent extinction. Such various conjectures and distortions do not go beyond the realm of ordinary worldlings.

The path cuts through the two views of permanence and annihilation. When one reaches the point where the four elements dissolve and the body is overcome by the suffering of illness, it is certain beyond doubt that consciousness has no master and wanders through saṃsāra according to karma.
Even if one were to fix a date and set a time to depart this life while sitting or standing, achieving such worldly virtue would not be considered extraordinary.
This is because one has not seen the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* and does not understand the signs of rebirth in the nine grades.
To believe in the power of Amitābha’s vow while stubbornly clinging to one's own views, willingly casting oneself into the mire and flames—how could one not feel sorrow for such a person?
○ This refers to the ninth path of practice within the *Guanjing* (Contemplation Sutra).
Its essential point lies in the single-minded upholding of the Name; by this, one immediately attains rebirth. How [could it be otherwise]?

One must rely upon many words. As for the subtlety of its essential meaning and the profound refinement of its realization of the Way, these could not be manifested without the breadth of scriptural texts and the detail of their exposition.

Therefore, the partial praises of the various sutras and the elucidations of the many sages have resulted in writings so vast that they would exhaust oxen and fill the rafters of houses; were it not for those of extensive learning, one could not discern their essentials.
Now, drawing from the broad to the concise, I have recorded one or two items so that students may investigate them, grasp the essential meaning, and cultivate themselves accordingly.
Is this not what the Confucians mean when they say, "Study extensively and explain in detail, so as to return to a concise understanding"?
This is precisely what it refers to.
The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta* of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the section on the Prophecy, states: "If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
during the final five hundred years, there should be a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teaching, at the end of her life here, she shall immediately— "
One shall go to the world of Sukhāvatī, the abode where Amitābha Buddha dwells surrounded by a great assembly of Bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne.
There, one will no longer be afflicted by desire, nor afflicted by anger or ignorance, nor afflicted by pride or envy;
one will attain the supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva and the realization of the non-arising of dharmas.

Regarding "Patience" (*kṣānti*): Miaole states that hearing this sutra and practicing according to its teachings constitutes the cause for the Pure Land; there is no need to point further to texts such as the *Contemplation Sutra*.
Establishing practice based on the sutra is detailed in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit. One directly contemplates the four lands within this very realm.
Because they are fully endowed [with these qualities], this Buddha-body is itself the three Buddha-bodies, and this great assembly is itself the entire assembly.

Because delusions have not yet been severed, the "Practice of Peaceful Abiding" (Anrakugyō) is the functional aspect of the practice for the Pure Land of Common Dwelling (*sōjū jōdo*). Fourth, Ming Rongxin’s *Jie* (Commentary) states: "If delusions are not yet severed, it is the Pure Land of Common Dwelling;
this refers to the three truths of the stage of contemplative practice (*kan-gyō*). When the afflictions of views and thought (*kenshi*) are exhausted, it is the Land of Expedient Means (*hōben*)."
Purity corresponds to the three truths of semblance. When ignorance is broken, there is the purity of the true-recompense land; this is the three truths of partial realization.
When ignorance is exhausted, there is the purity of the land of tranquil light; this is the three truths of ultimate perfection.

When one cultivates the single mind and the threefold contemplation with the aspiration to seek birth in the Pure Land, one takes the three delusions as the cause of the defiled land and the three truths as the fruit of the pure land.
In the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva instructs Sudhana to make the ten great vows, saying: "If a person receives,
maintains, reads, and recites these great vows, at the time of their death, all their faculties will completely disperse."
All things will perish; all kinsmen will be utterly forsaken; all power and majesty will completely fade away.
Only this King of Vows will not abandon them, leading them at all times before him. In a single instant, they shall attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Upon arrival, they shall behold Amitābha Buddha and be born within a lotus flower, receiving empowerment from the Buddha.
Recorded. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, by the power of wisdom, he brings benefit to sentient beings according to their inclinations.
Before long, he shall sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), subdue the armies of Māra, and attain perfect awakening (samyaksaṃbodhi).

If one does not take birth in the Pure Land, that is one thing; but once born, one shall forever be without regress. An ordinary person bound by all fetters first relies upon faith and aspiration to attain birth.
In that land, although the three poisons and false views have not yet been suddenly forgotten, how is it known that they are non-retrogressive?

It is because they are constantly sustained by the power of Amitābha’s vows; the great light shines perpetually; they are gathered among those of supreme goodness; their lifespan lasts for eternal kalpas;
and the waterfowl, trees, forests, winds, sounds, and music proclaim the wondrous vehicle. Those who hear these sounds practice mindfulness of the Buddha and mindfulness of [the Dharma].
This is because the mind that recollects the Dharma and the Sangha has never been interrupted. Sentient beings are like those afflicted by illness;
the Buddha is the King of Physicians, the Dharma is the excellent medicine, and the Sangha are the attendants who nurse the patient. When these three are present before one, the illness cannot arise.
Speaking from this perspective, how could there be any regression once one has been born in the Pure Land for a lifetime?
The *Sūtra on the Differences in Karmic Retribution* states that there are ten kinds of merit for chanting the Buddha’s name and reciting sūtras with a loud voice: first, it can dispel drowsiness;
second, it causes the heavenly Māras to be terrified; third, the sound pervades the ten directions; fourth, suffering in the three evil realms is stilled; fifth, external sounds... [are silenced].
1. Not entering [into distraction]. 2. Causing the mind not to be scattered. 3. Courageous and diligent effort. 4. Bringing joy to all Buddhas.

5. The manifestation of samādhi. 6. Rebirth in the Pure Land. Master Ciyun’s Repentance Text states: "When reciting the Buddha’s name, one should use the mind to follow along with each syllable, making every word distinct.
Only when the mind and mouth are thus bound together can a single thought extinguish the karmic hindrances of eighty billion kalpas."
[This is] the sin of death. If it is not so, it is truly difficult to extinguish the sin. If you fear that the mind will scatter, you must call out loudly and swiftly;

then the mind will easily become settled and samādhi will easily be accomplished. Therefore, in the *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts), Master Huigan quotes the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Sūryagarbha-parivarta*, which says:
"With small mindfulness one sees a small Buddha; with great mindfulness one sees a great Buddha. The commentary explains: "Great mindfulness..."

"Chanting the Buddha's name with a loud voice" means chanting the Buddha's name with a great sound; "chanting with a small voice" means chanting the Buddha's name with a low voice. Both are the teachings of the Sages—what cause for confusion is there? I exhort all people of the world:
chant the Buddha's name with a forceful voice, and the samādhi will be easily attained. By chanting with a small voice, the mind often becomes distracted and scattered.

Only those who study [the Dharma] realize that this is not something ordinary people can understand. Even those of the lowest of the lower grades attain rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death. What is lacking? It is nothing more than the intensity of the voice.

At that time, one must be fierce and sharp, with a mind of resolute discernment; this surpasses the power of vows made over a hundred years. Nowadays, those who recite the Buddha’s name are for the most part not single-minded;
with distracted minds and slow voices, they cause few to achieve success in the present life and rare instances of spiritual response at the moment of death.

Therefore, this method is specifically shown to encourage that when reciting the Buddha’s name, one should be single-minded without distraction, reciting aloud with each sound following the next in uninterrupted succession. Thus, [one will attain success].
Success will be achieved before long.

The *Lifó gōngdé yèbào chābié jīng* (Sūtra on the Differences in the Karmic Retribution of the Merit of Bowing to the Buddha) states: "In a single prostration to the Buddha, from the knees down to the vajra-realm, there is not even a single mote of dust [that is not purified]."
A universal monarch (cakravartin) attains ten kinds of merit: first, he obtains a sublime physical form; second, people believe whatever he says;

third, he is fearless when among the multitude; fourth, he is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas; fifth, he possesses great dignified deportment; sixth, all people draw near to him with affection.

7. All devas will love and revere them. 8. They will possess great merit and virtue. 9. At the end of their lives, they will be reborn in higher realms. 10. They will swiftly realize *nirvāṇa*. The Venerable Master Siming said:
"When a practitioner prostrates to the Buddha, they should deeply realize that the Buddha-body is not separate from their own mind.

They share the same source of awakening, which perfectly illumines all phenomena. The Buddhas have awakened to this fundamental nature and give rise to compassion based on our shared essence; sentient beings, however, are deluded regarding the Truth and undergo suffering."
All illusions are suffering; when compassion and suffering meet, a resonance is thus established. With a single body, one reaches before all Buddhas;
with a single prostration, boundless sins are universally extinguished.

Regarding the attainment of blessings in the present life, Longshu said: Some claim that seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is a matter for after death, failing to realize that it is of great benefit even before one dies.
Why is this? For the Buddha’s teaching of people consists entirely of what is wholesome; since seeking rebirth in the Pure Land...
Take earth as your mind. Whatever the mind contemplates, whatever the mouth speaks, and whatever the body performs—let there be nothing that is not good.
In this present life, you may thus become a gentleman or a great sage; others will revere you, the spirits will assist you, your fortune and rank may increase, and your lifespan may be prolonged.
Should you, however, be deprived by karmic conditions and unable to focus single-mindedly on this, [the result will be otherwise].
Thus, evil conditions will be diminished by this means, while wholesome conditions will increase from this point forward.

Even those who are ignorant of propriety and righteousness, who fear neither legal punishment nor social censure, and who esteem only physical strength and pursue only power and profit—if they but come to take the Pure Land as their core concern, they will surely examine themselves and reproach their own past actions. Although they may not be able to conform entirely to [the teachings],...
If one acts in accordance with ritual and righteousness, one will surely remain close to ritual and righteousness. How could such a person willingly fall back into the reach of punishments?
If everyone were to act in this way, it would gradually be possible to escape the realm of the petty person and ultimately find refuge as a gentleman.
Those among one’s fellow villagers who know them would all regard them as virtuous people. From this perspective, by following the Buddhist teachings, and...
For one who takes the Pure Land as their resolve, who would say that it is of no benefit before life ends?

Regarding those who serve as monks and practice *nianfo*, Longshu said: "Those who serve as monks and study the Buddha should reflect within themselves: 'I am an ordained person; I have fully understood the nature of life...'"
Death is one's fundamental duty; if one cannot act in this way, one will eventually be submerged in the dust of worldly affairs. When the day of one’s great limit arrives, what reliance can there be?
Although one may have accumulated good karma throughout one’s life, one cannot avoid following the cycle of saṃsāra; once the retribution for that good karma is exhausted—
Furthermore, [if one merely practices this] and falls back, it is not as good as exclusively cultivating the Pure Land to directly escape saṃsāra;
only then will one have fulfilled the purpose of leaving the household life. Chan Master Yongming Shou, Chan Master Changlu Yi, and Chan Master Wanan Yi all cultivated this path.

Furthermore, since they have transformed themselves to manifest as humans, how can one not emulate them? If one does not take birth in the Pure Land, one cannot avoid receiving retribution according to one's karma.
For instance, Chan Master Haiyin Xin, due to a single moment of error, was born into the family of Defense Official Zhu as a female child;
only after being enlightened by Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben did she manage to escape that state. One must consider what will happen in her second lifetime.
Furthermore, how is this so? An elder of Taiping Monastery in Shuzhou, also known as the Venerable Master Xing, was reborn after his death into the family of a high minister.
Having enjoyed wealth and status, he committed evil karma and fell again into the evil realms; what end to this can there be? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"A practitioner is like turbid water that is difficult to clarify. As long as the dregs have not been removed, stirring it will only make it turbid again. (2)

This is what is meant by "aging. If one is born in the Pure Land and dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, yet returns to this realm to save sentient beings, it is like having scrubbed away turbidity;
even if the feet stir the water, it will no longer become murky.

Regarding the study of the Way by those of wealth and status, Longshu said: "Though people of wealth and status enjoy every kind of pleasure as they desire, time passes swiftly and this illusory body is difficult to preserve.
Since antiquity, who among those of the highest rank remains? It is better to cultivate pure karma so that one may be reborn in a superior realm after death."
How joyful this dwelling place is! In our own dynasty, Wen Lü Gong was in the capital and, together with Chan Master Jingyan, gathered ten thousand monks and laypeople to form a Pure Land assembly.

Even such eminent figures as Minister Wang Minzhong, Circuit Intendant Yang Cigong, and Palace Attendant Feng Jichuan all cultivated the practices of the Pure Land and were all able to attain rebirth there. How could this not be so?
Look up to and emulate these!

Longshu said: "Providing offerings to the Buddha and providing meals for the Sangha, constructing stupas and building monasteries, reciting mantras and performing repentance rites, and filially supporting one’s parents—these are the virtues of elder brothers."

He was respectful toward his friends and younger brothers; among his kinsmen, there was no lack of harmony and concord. Within his village and neighborhood, he shared kindness and courtesy with others.

When serving his sovereign, he offered his sincere heart for the sake of the state; when acting as an official, he was benevolent and compassionate for the benefit of the people; and when serving as a leader, he was skillful in bringing peace to the masses.
When serving those below, they diligently attend to their superiors. They may instruct the ignorant and deluded; support the orphaned and weak;
rescue those in urgent distress; bestow gifts upon the poor; construct bridges and lay wells; distribute food and dispense medicine;
reduce their own sustenance to benefit others; yield to others when faced with wealth through self-reflection; teach others to do good; or protect...
Cease evil and perform only all manner of wholesome deeds, whether mundane or supramundane, regardless of their size or quantity—
be it giving a single coin to another, or quenching someone’s thirst with a single drop of water— even down to a virtue as minute as a hair-tip.
One must simultaneously give rise to the thought: "May these virtuous conditions be dedicated toward the Western Land. Through the mutual support of all merits, may we surely attain rebirth there.
This is the benefit of encouraging practice.

Longshu said: "The Tang dynasty official Fang Zhu died suddenly and arrived at the underworld. The magistrate of the underworld told him, 'According to the records, you once exhorted an elderly man to recite the Buddha’s name;
he has already been reborn in the Pure Land. By virtue of this merit, you too ought to be reborn there.
Zhu replied, 'I still intend to recite one hundred thousand volumes of the Diamond Sutra and pay homage at Mount Wutai; therefore, I do not wish to go to rebirth yet.'"
The official of the underworld said, "To recite sutras and prostrate yourself is indeed a virtuous deed; however, it would be better for you to first be reborn in the Pure Land.

Realizing that his resolve could not be shaken, the official released him to return to the human realm. Thus, we know that those who exhort others to cultivate the Pure Land not only ensure their own rebirth there, but also move the spirits of the netherworld.
Regarding the failure to act due to procrastination, Jishi said: "When people of the world wish to cultivate pure karma, they say, 'I am too busy now; I will wait until I have leisure.
Or they say, 'I am too poor now; I will wait until I am wealthy. Or they say, 'I am still young and strong; I will wait until I am old. If one's lot were fixed and constant..."
One is busy. One’s lot is fixed as poverty; one’s lot is fixed as an early death. Thus, there is no opportunity to cultivate pure karma.
To perish suddenly—what use would repentance be then? I exhort all people: while your bodies are strong and healthy, strive with diligence to practice it.
One should contemplate the silent chamber after death, thinking: "Worldly people know only to nourish and provide for this body during life, seeking out its necessities;
yet they do not consider that after casting off this body, the consciousness does not perish. If there are no virtuous causes, one will fall into the miserable realms. For what purpose was one born?"
At such times, you cherish this body; yet, even though the consciousness does not perish after death, do you not contemplate liberation?

Furthermore, worldly people devote themselves entirely to their wives, children, and kin, laboring extensively to provide food and clothing without the slightest negligence, yet they do not contemplate the moment of their own death.
At that time, although wives, children, and kin may love one another to the marrow of their bones, they cannot save each other; one must go forth alone. Now, I exhort you:
People of the world should not, for the sake of nourishing life, forget the fear of death; nor should they, for the sake of others, forget what they must do for themselves.
One must prepare in advance for unforeseen calamities.
Longshu said: "It is like a person entering a city on business who must first seek a place to stay.
When evening falls and it grows dark, there is a place to lodge. Seeking a place to stay beforehand is the cultivation of pure karma.
'When evening falls and it grows dark' refers to the arrival of one's great destiny. 'Having a place to lodge' means being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms."
Furthermore, it is like traveling a long distance during the spring months: one must prepare for rain gear so that when a sudden downpour arrives, one suffers no distress from being drenched.
Preparing the rain gear beforehand is the cultivation of pure karma; the sudden arrival of the downpour is the sudden onset of impermanence.
One who suffers from no chronic ailments will not fall into the evil realms. Furthermore, by first seeking a dwelling place, one does not hinder the execution of one's tasks;
by first preparing for the rain, one does not hinder long journeys. Thus, for those who cultivate the Pure Land, it does not obstruct any worldly affairs.
Why would a person not cultivate it?
The merit lies in reaching full maturity.
Longshu said: "Mencius stated that for the benevolent person, it also simply depends upon becoming mature in it. Therefore, the gentleman—
"One does not depart from benevolence (*ren*) for even the duration of a single meal; one must remain thus even in moments of haste, and remain thus even in times of distress.
If one can do so, then there is nowhere one goes where one is not practicing benevolence. It is the same for those who cultivate the Pure Land (*śuklā-viṣaya*).

In all activities—whether rising or reclining, eating or drinking, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still—one never forgets the Pure Land. Then, although this body dwells within the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the mind has already [reached it].
"I am in the Pure Land. Chaaan said: "The shape of the setting sun resembles a suspended drum. Sit upright in the full lotus posture, facing the western direction.
Although your body has not yet reached the Flower Pond, first send your mind back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is precisely what he meant.

Regarding the ten kinds of benefits, the Venerable Master Ciyun stated: "The Great Teacher of the Three Realms, the Compassionate Father of myriad virtues—those who take refuge in him have their transgressions extinguished;

those who revere him give rise to blessings. This is fully explained in the various sutras. If one can take refuge in the Triple Gem and uphold the name of even a single Buddha, [the benefits] will manifest..."
The world shall obtain ten kinds of benefits: first, day and night one will constantly receive the protection of all the great powerful divine generals of the heavens who remain invisible;
second, one will constantly receive the protection of twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others;
third, one will constantly be protected and remembered day and night by all Buddhas, and Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit [light].
1. Radiant light will embrace this person. 2. None of the evil spirits, yakṣas, or rākṣasas will be able to harm them. 3.

Neither venomous snakes nor poisonous drugs will have any effect upon them. 4. They shall not suffer death by water, fire, enemies, bandits, swords, arrows, shackles, fetters, imprisonment, or any other untimely demise.
5. All previously committed sins shall be completely extinguished. 6. The lives of those they have killed as enemies shall [be restored].

All shall receive liberation and no longer harbor attachments or oppositions. Seventh, they will experience auspiciousness in their dreams at night, beholding the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha Buddha.
Eighth, their minds will be constantly joyful; their complexions will be radiant and lustrous, their physical strength abundant, and all their undertakings will be auspicious.
Ninth, they will always be honored and prostrated to by all the people of the world, just as if they were honoring the Buddha. Tenth...
At the time of their death, they will have no fear; with right mindfulness manifest before them, Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy beings will appear,
welcoming them upon a vajra pedestal to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.
*Jingtu zhiguī jí*, Scroll Lower (End).
*Zhiguī zhíyī lüèxùn*:
The name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara is established with two pronunciations. Dīpaṃkara is the name of a Buddha.
"Ti-si" (提撕): "Si" (撕) means to admonish by pulling at the ear. "Mei" (玫) has the pronunciation of "mei" (梅);
it refers to the *móguī* (玫瑰) pearl. "Seng" (僧) is a name;
"zhào" (肇) has the pronunciation of "zhào" (兆), meaning the beginning.
*Qú*: The pronunciation is *qú*. It refers to the lotus flower. *Chuǎn*: A corruption;
it has the third tone (*shàngshēng*). It means "erroneous. *Xia*: The pronunciation is *é*.
It means "mistaken. *Tiáo*: The pronunciation is *tiáo*. It refers to the hanging hair of a young boy.
"To rush toward sounds" means to gallop in disorder;
it is a vulgarization of the term "sound.
"To be submerged in sounds" means to be drowned; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to be submerged" refers specifically to being immersed in wine.
*Jun-zhai* (捃摭): "To gather" (*jié*). *Zhī* (隻) is the phonetic component. *Cai-zhai* (采摭): "To collect and gather the words of many.
*Zhuān* (諄) is pronounced as *zhūn* (純). It refers to repeated instruction.
*Chàng-chàng* (暢唱): "To proclaim and chant. It means to penetrate and communicate.
"Bi" (俾) means "to cause. "Chou" (讐) refers to an enemy;
the upper radical is "man" (人), and the lower is pronounced "qi" (乞) with the tone "ni" (逆), meaning resentment.
"Xie" (褻) is pronounced "xue" (薛); it refers to private clothing. It also means to draw near to petty people, as in the aforementioned [passage].
*Xiùn* (pronounced *shùn*): The name of Prince *Amakṣu*. *Keng*:
A river name (the *qū* and *shēng* initials are combined). *Jù*:
Sudden or urgent (the *jǔ* and *qù* tones are combined).
"Jie" (藉) is pronounced as "xie" (謝) and means to borrow. It also carries the sense of containing and encompassing.
"Lian" (連) is pronounced as "zhu" (燭). It means to connect and to continue; it is like to join together.
*Zàng* (奘) is pronounced with a departing tone; it is the name of a translator.
*Jìjì* (罽計) is the sound [of the first syllable]; *Bīn* (賓) is the name of a country.
*Wàn* (簐) has the pronunciation *fàn* (犯); it means a model or pattern.
In utter disarray, wherever the wolf lay, the grass was strewn and trampled. *Huǒn yào* (焜耀) is a compound;
in older editions, *huǒn* is incorrect. *Yào* (曜) is pronounced "guāngyào" (光耀), meaning radiance.
"Yì" (睿) is pronounced with the *rèi* rhyme. It is the name of a Dharma Master.
"Lún" (掄) has the sound of *lún*. It is an official title.
"Wěi" (偉) has the sound of *wěi*. It means extraordinary; it also means great.

"Kang" (糠) is pronounced with the initial *k* (as in *kāng*). It refers to the husks of rice. "Bi" (粃) is pronounced with the initial *b* (as in *bǐ*). It refers to grain that has not formed properly. In the *Zhuangzi*, it says:
"Dust, grime, husks, and chaff—these will be used to mold and cast Yao and Shun."
The character "詵" (shēn) is pronounced as "qiè. It is the name of a Dharma Master.
The character "闉" (yīn) is pronounced as "yīn. It is an official title.
The character "叵" (pō) is pronounced as "pō," meaning "impossible."

The character for "huò" (攉) has the phonetic value *huò*. The older editions read "yí" (怡) instead of "huò," which is incorrect. Consulting various rhyme dictionaries now, [the character with the radical] "shǒu" (hand) refers to a hand-gesture game;
it is also written as "huò" (霍) or "huī" (揮). "Huò" (霍) denotes suddenness and urgency.
*Bǐng* (pronounced *bǐng*) means light; it is the name of the Dharma Master.
*Shào* (pronounced *shào*) is an official title.
*Bō* (first tone, rising intonation) means a person with a lame foot.
"Wu" (窹) and "mi" (寐) refer to awakening; "jue" (覺) is also used for awakening. "Mi" (迷) is pronounced with a departing tone. "Mu" (目) means closed; "shen" (神) means hidden.
"Qing" (圊) and "hun" (溷)—the former with a level tone, the latter with a departing tone—both refer to the latrine.
Yí (頤) has the sound *zé*; it means "deep. It is the name of a Dharma Master.
Kǎi (鎧) has the sound *kǎi*; it is the name of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*).
Jué (厥) has the sound *jué*; it means "his" or "that."
"Gāohuáng" (膏肓): the upper character is pronounced yīn; it refers to the liquid of the spirit. The lower character is pronounced huāng. "Xīnshàng" (心上): above the diaphragm. "Wóuzuì" (疣贅):
the upper character is pronounced yóu; it means a tumor. The lower character is pronounced zhuì; it means a black mole.
*Chuo* (綽) and *chang* (昌) are pronounced with the entering tone; they are the names of Dharma Masters.
*Kan* (闞) and *kan* (勘) are the pronunciations; they are official titles.
*Ta* (墖) and *ta* (塔) are identical.
*Āng-yǔ*: "Āng" means high; it means to look up. "Yǔ" (with the upper radical *yōu*) means a curved spine. *Mó-léng*:

The first character is *mó* (model) and the second is *léng* (edge). When Sū Wèidào served as Chancellor, he did not wish to decide matters with clarity, preferring instead to remain vague and ambiguous.
*Yu*: the phonetic reading. A title for an official.
*Du* and *dǔ* are synonymous, both meaning "to see.
*Baddhaparyaṅka*: the right foot rests upon the left thigh, and the left foot rests upon the right thigh.
*Wú* (upper character): pronounced like *wū*, meaning "to deceive. (Lower character): pronounced like *wǎng*, meaning "to deceive. *Xī*:
pronounced like *xī*, referring to sunlight; it is the name of the Dharma Master. *Líu*:
pronounced like *liú*, an official title.
*Xi-xi* means "of the same class" (*sabhāga*).
*Lian-bao* (the character for *bao* pronounced as *páo*) means "growing in clusters. In the *Shijing*, it says, "Just beginning to bud, just beginning to form.
*Hua-ji* (the character for *ji* pronounced as *kè*) refers to a flower vessel used in foreign countries.
Yù (彧) and Yù (郁) have the same pronunciation; they denote "literary style" and "appearance," respectively. Fǎshī (法師) is a title for a Dharma Master.
Tián (闐) and Tián (田) have the same pronunciation; it is the name of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*).
Yàn (雁) and Yàn (鴈) are identical.
Jùnyǐng (俊穎): "yǐng" is pronounced with the third tone (rising tone). Xiùyǐng (秀穎) refers to one of eminent virtue. Hóng (洪): [The character for] "hóng" is used here. Zhēndú (酖毒):
"zhèn" is pronounced with the second tone (falling tone). It refers to food and drink that kill people.
Kuī (巋): Pronounced as "kuí". Língkuī (靈巋) is a monastic name.
